Nd2 f6!?, making the gambit sincere, has been analyzed by Schiller, building on work by Silman and Donaldson, but has never been played at the highest level. Of course, White can also capture on d5 before considering the gambit: 4. cxd5 cxd5 and now any of 5. dxe5, 5. Nf3, 5. e3, and even 5. e4 are playable. 5. dxe5 gives Black an isolated queen's pawn, but after 5...d4 6. Ne4 Qa5+ 7. Nd2 Nc6 8. Nf3 Bg4 he will regain his gambit pawn at the cost of the bishop pair, with the d pawn potentially becoming passed after e.g. 9. g3 Bxf3 10. exf3 Qxe5 11. Qe2 Qxe2. 5. Nf3 gets kicked around twice by 5...e4 6. Ne5 f6 7. Qa4+ Nd7, with complex, unclear positions after either 8. Nxd7 Bxd7 9. Qb3 Bc6 or 8. Ng4 Kf7. 5. e3 allows Black to equalize with either the space-gaining 5...e4 or simply 5...exd4. 5. e4 is perhaps the strongest of White's fifth-move choices, and is always followed with 5...dxe4. Then the main continuation is 6. Bb4+ Bd7 7. dxe5 Bb4 8. Bd2 Bxc3 9. Bxd7+ (9. Bxc3 would be a losing mistake) Nxd7 10. Bxc3 Nc5, offering a queen trade while threatening ...Nd3+. 6. d5 bears mention mainly for the historic game Marshall-Winawer, 1901 rather than any great strength. Finally, White can decline the gambit immediately with either 4. Nf3 or 4. e3. After 4. Nf3, Black equalizes with 4...exd4, or can try for more with 4...e4, where after 5. Nd2 Nf6 6. e3 a reversed French results. 4. e3 is best met with 4...exd4 5. exd4 Nf6. 4. e3 e4 results in a reversed French, but unlike the previous example, White can put the extra tempo to immediate use with 5. Qb3 etc.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.name: 3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.description: With the most common move in the Slav, 3. Nf3, White develops their knight and exerts more control over the e5-square. Similar to 3. Nc3, Black should avoid 3...Bf5 as 4. cxd5 cxd5 5. Qb3 effectively wins a pawn. However, unlike 3. Nc3, 3...dxc4 should also be avoided as White is better after 4. e3 and 5. a4 since White will win back the pawn as the knight on f3 is not vulnerable to a b5-b4 pawn push. As such, Black only has 2 main responses. 3...Nf6 is by far Black's most common reply, and play from White typically transposes into a Semi-Slav with 4. Nc3, although some unique lines exist such as 4. e3, the Quiet Slav, where Nc3 is delayed or not played at all. 3...e6 is occasionally seen, and play typically transposes back to 3...Nf6 variations, with some exceptions. 3...a6 is also a solid option for Black, albeit rarely seen. Play typically transposes to the main line of the Chebanenko variation of the Slav, although White can opt for a Catalan-style setup with 4. g3 instead.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.name: Modern Line
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.description: Black begins development of his minor pieces with 3...Nf6, which is invariably the best square for this knight, as it exerts control over the e4 square and adds protection to the d5-pawn. White can respond to this move in a variety of ways:

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N2N2/.name: 4...Bf5?!
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/2N2N2/.description: This move looks natural, but it allows the annoying cxd5 cxd5 Qb3, losing a pawn if the bishop does not retreat to c8.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.name: Chebanenko Slav
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.description: The move 4...a6 introduces the Chebanenko (or Chameleon) Slav. Though it seems a small move, it prepares ideas of ...b5 (either to attack White's c4 pawn or to shore up Black's after ...dxc4) and eases the problems of developing Black's light-squared bishop, as now Qb3 can be met with ...Ra7. The weakening of the b6 square, however, invites White to simply push - 5. c5 is the most common response, gaining space on the queenside. In the resulting positions, it is very common for Black to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, where it is a lot more useful by eyeing White's center. Alternatively, White can play 5. e3, solidifying their d pawn and adding their light-squared bishop to the fight, while accepting 5...b5. Less common are 5. a4, preventing ...b5, and 5. cxd5, releasing the central tension but leaving Black to show what purpose ...a6 now serves.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/P.name: Advance System
rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/P.description: White plays 5. c5 to control the weak b6 square and forestall any ...dxc4 or ...b5 ideas. If White can make this space advantage permanent, they will have a very comfortable game, so Black needs to start planning a pawn break on either b6 or e5. To support this, the main move is 5...Nbd7, developing the queen's knight to its best available square and preparing whichever break Black chooses. The main alternatives are 5...Bf5, developing the bishop before it gets blocked in by ...Nbd7, and 5...g6, preparing a fianchetto. 5...Bg4 is also played occasionally, with the idea of pressuring the e5 square indirectly, but there is no reason White cannot simply occupy it at once with 6. Ne5.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.name: Slav accepted
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2P.description: Black finally takes the sacrificial pawn with dxc4. Despite being known as the "Pure Slav," this move has about half the popularity of 4...e6, the Semi-Slav. The idea of this move is to threaten a pawn advance onto White's queenside. White can choose to either allow the queenside expansion and gambit the c-pawn, or they can prevent it and give Black time to develop the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.name: Alapin variation
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P2.description: The advance of the a-pawn prevents Black from playing 5...b5, which in turn leaves the c4 pawn available for capture. This is White's most popular and ambitious response. Over the last century, there have been four major lines played by Black. 5...Bf5, the Czech variation, is by far the most testing and theoretical line. The bishop eyes at the center and makes it harder for White to play e4. 5...Bg4 is the Steiner variation. It is played quite often at the amateur level, but requires Black to understand the positions well to be played successfully. White's knight isn't pinned and can move to e5 with a tempo on the bishop. 5...Na6 is the Smyslov variation. While it looks odd at first sight, the goal of the move is quite understandable: Black wants to maneuver the knight to b4, where it can't be chased away by pawns. 5...e6 is the Soultanbeieff variation. Black opts to play in more of a Semi-Slav style and temporarily locks the light-squared bishop behind the pawn chain.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.name: Czech Variation
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N2N2/1.description: Black develops their light-squared bishop. This is possible now because the threat of Qb3 is no longer present thanks to the pawn on c4. White should try to regain their pawn, which can be done in two ways. 6. e3 is the Dutch variation. This is the classical main line. White tries to capture the pawn with 7. Bxc4 and continues the game by castling and preparing to play e4. 6. Ne5 is the central variation. Instead of recapturing the pawn with the bishop, White tries to do so with their knight instead. This is White's most ambitious option and leads to sharper positions. 6. Nh4, the Bled attack, is the chief sideline for White. Instead of going after the pawn, White first tries to get rid of Black's light-squared bishop. This move can be played in the Dutch variation too, and the positions may transpose into each other.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.name: Central Variation
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.description: White places their knight into the center to recapture the pawn on c4 while leaving the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop open. There are two theoretical responses for Black. 6...Nbd7 is the main move, letting White take on c4 and preparing to either put the knight on b6 or to play e5. 6...e6 is the Wiesbaden variation. This line involves White attempting to gain a lot of initiative and Black preventing it by sacrificing a piece for three pawns, generally leading to an endgame where Black tries to march an army of pawns down the board.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.name: 6...Nbd7
r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.description: This is a simple developing move. White's only real follow-up is 7. Nxc4, keeping the knights in the center and recapturing the c4 pawn.

r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.name: 7. Nxc4
r2qkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.description: White recaptures the c4 pawn. Black can now choose to either enter the Carlsbad variation with 7...Qc7 or to transfer the knight to b6 with 7...Nb6.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/1np2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.name: 7...Nb6
r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/1np2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2.description: Black intends to trade off White's active knight. This move poses an immediate threat, so White's options are fairly limited. 8. Ne5 puts the knight back in the centre and declines the trade. This is the main line. 8. e3 intends to recapture the knight with the bishop. 8. Ne3 retreats the knight with a tempo on the bishop. The knight is not entirely misplaced here, since White's idea is to clamp down the d5-square and develop the light-squared bishop to g2 instead.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2P.name: 7...Qc7
r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N5/1P2P.description: Black develops the queen to c7 in order to prepare e5. This will likely lead to the Carlsbad variation. White's main response is 8. g3 preparing to develop the dark-squared bishop to f4 where it can put pressure on the knight after 8...e5 9. dxe5 Nxe5. This also prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1P.name: 8. g3
r3kb1r/ppqnpppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1P.description: This move prepares to develop both bishops; the dark-squared bishop to f4 and the light-squared bishop to g2. This move doesn't deter Black from playing 8...e5 which has been prepared with Black's previous moves.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4pb2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1.name: Carlsbad variation
r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4pb2/P1NP4/2N3P1/1.description: Black finally pushes the e pawn forward, releasing the dark-squared bishop and fighting for the center. If White ignores the pawn and prepares to castle with 9. Bg2, Black can start building pressure with 9...Rd8, aiming at White's queen, and 10...Be6 pressuring the knight (if 9...O-O-O then 10. a5! followed by 11. Qa4 starts a nasty attack on the queenside). Therefore, White's best option is 9. dxe5, exchanging pawns in the center.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4Pb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P.name: 9. dxe5
r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p2n2/4Pb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P.description: White exchanges the pawns in the center. Black doesn't have many valid options other than 9...Nxe5, recapturing the pawn.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P2.name: 9...Nxe5
r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N5/2N3P1/1P2.description: The central pawns have been exchanged. White can, and should, play 10. Bf4, developing the bishop and pinning the knight on e5. This also justifies White's previous move 8. g3. White's knight on c4 is hanging, so there isn't many alternatives. 10. Nxe5? doesn't develop any of White's pieces and allows Black to quickly catch up in development.

r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.name: 10. Bf4
r3kb1r/ppq2ppp/2p2n2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.description: This move pins the knight on e5 to the black queen, which is its only defender at the moment. Moving the knight isn't an option, so the only move to add another defender is 10...Nfd7. 10...Bd6?? fails to defend the knight because it loses a piece. The d6 square is attacked by both the c4 knight and the queen on d1 and only defended by Black's queen on c7.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.name: 10...Nfd7
r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.description: This move defends the pinned knight. White no longer has any moves to increase the pressure on the e5 knight, so play usually continues by developing the light-squared bishop with 11. Bg2.

r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.name: 11. Bg2
r3kb1r/ppqn1ppp/2p5/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1P.description: White develops the light-squared bishop and prepares to castle short. From this position, two moves have been played historically: f6 and g5. 11...f6 is the old mainline, defending the knight. 11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black.

r3kb1r/ppqn2pp/2p2p2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.name: 11...f6
r3kb1r/ppqn2pp/2p2p2/4nb2/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.description: This is the old mainline. Black protects the knight with a pawn in order to protect the knight. The usual continuation after f6 is 12. O-O Nc5 13. Ne3 Bg6 14. b4.

r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.name: Morozevich variation
r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P1N2B2/2N3P1/1.description: 11...g5 is the most popular line nowadays and is considered the best move for Black. Because the kingside pawn structure is significantly weakened, Black will usually resort to castling queenside. 12. Bxg5?? would blunder 12...Nxc4. The bishop can't stay on the same diagonal as the black queen, so some pieces have to be traded. 12. Bxe5 allows Black to secure the bishop pair after 12...Nxe5 but White gets compensation after 13. Qd4 f6 14. O-O-O preventing Black from castling queenside. 12. Ne3 is played most often, planning to take the light-squared bishop. After 12...gxf4 13. Nxf5 O-O-O 14. Qc2 Black has two isolated pawns on the kingside, but a four on two majority on the queenside and has control of the d-file. White should soon castle short.

r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P4B2/2N1N1P1/1.name: 12. Ne3
r3kb1r/ppqn1p1p/2p5/4nbp1/P4B2/2N1N1P1/1.description: White decides to exchange the bishop pair with Black. After 12...gxf4 13. Nxf5 both sides will have one bishop left. There are no alternatives to 12...gxf4, as they all lose material or give White a lot of initiative.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.name: Wiesbaden variation
rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N5/1P.description: Black prepares to develop their dark-squared bishop to b4 where it stands uncontested thanks to White's move 5. a4. If White tries to recapture the c4 pawn immediately with 7. Nxc4?! Black can strike back 7...c5, putting pressure on White's centre and garnering an advantage in development. The only move that preserves White's advantage is 7. f3, trying to play e4 on the next move. This threat cannot be stopped by Black, who has to play for piece activity, potentially sacrificing a piece to destroy White's centre.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N2P2/.name: 7. f3
rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/P1pP4/2N2P2/.description: White doesn't capture the c4-pawn. Instead, they prepare 8. e4, which comes with tempo on Black's bishop. With the support of the f-pawn, Black can't stop e4 from being played, so they must find an advantage by different means. 7...Bb4 is the main line. This move removes the knight's defence from e4 and has the idea of sacrificing the light-squared bishop on e4 in exchange for three pawns. 7...c5 tries to disrupt White's centre. After 8. e4 both 8...cxd4 and 8...Bg6 have been tried, but results have generally been favourable for White. This variation was also played in games 3, 5 and 8 of the 2010 World Chess Championship. Modern engines prefer the move 7...Bg6, but this is rarely played and usually transposes after 8. e4 c5.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpP4/2N2P2/1.name: 7...Bb4
rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpP4/2N2P2/1.description: Black makes use of the weakened b4-square, pressuring the knight on c3 and gaining a bit more control over e4. The main line continues with 8. e4, also known as the Sharp line. Black has to sacrifice their light-squared bishop for three pawns if they want to retain any winning chances. 8. Nxc4 is White's main alternative, avoiding many of the complications that ensue from 8. e4. The position branches out after Black castles. 8. Bg5 is a rare continuation that has lost it's popularity over time. Usually Black responds with 8...h6, which gives their light-squared bishop a nicer square to go to if e4 happens.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpPP3/2N2P2/.name: Sharp line
rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/4Nb2/PbpPP3/2N2P2/.description: White takes over the centre, attacking Black's bishop and opening up an attack on the c4-pawn. Retreating the bishop would be a mistake, since this gives White the full centre without any compensation. Sacrificing the knight with 8...Nxe4? doesn't work, since after 9. fxe4 Qh4+ White can move their king to safety on the kingside. If 9. fxe4 Bxe4 Black doesn't have any pressure on the c3-knight, so 10. Be3 keeps everything held. Thus, 8...Bxe4! is the main move to not have a passive position. White doesn't have much better than 9. fxe4, after which 9...Nxe4 threatens 10...Nxc3 11. bxc3 Bxc3+ 12. Bd2 Qxd4 to pick up a fifth pawn for the piece. White has two options in this position.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP3N/2N5/1P.name: Bled Attack
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP3N/2N5/1P.description: White immediately goes after Black's light-squared bishop. The usual response is 6...e6, opening up the dark-squared bishop and preparing to recapture with the e-pawn. 6...Bc8 has also been tried, retreating the bishop to its home-square and arguing that the knight on h4 is misplaced. In practice, Black scores poorly in this line.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.name: Dutch variation
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.description: White opens up the light-squared bishop in order to recapture the pawn on c4. In doing so, the movement of the dark-squared bishop is temporarily restricted in the hopes to open it up later with e4. 6...e6 is played almost every time, looking to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which has been weakened by White's choice to prevent b5 with 5. a4. 6...Na6 is a rare sideline called the Lasker variation, where Black tries to place their knight on b4, instead of the dark-squared bishop.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.name: Lasker variation
r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.description: This move has a similar idea to the Smyslov variation: to bring the knight to the outpost on b4. White can continue playing in their usual fashion: 7. Bxc4 Nb4 8. O-O e6 9. Qe2, after which White will be able to play e4 without any issues. 9. Ne5 transposes to a line that can be reached from the Krause attack with 6...Na6, as can be seen in Carlsen - Vladimir, 2008.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.name: 6...e6
rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1pP4/2N1PN2/.description: Black prepares to develop the dark-squared bishop to the b4-square, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4. White can now simply recapture the c-pawn with 7. Bxc4.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1BP4/2N1PN2/.name: 7. Bxc4
rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/P1BP4/2N1PN2/.description: White reclaims their lost pawn. Black should follow up with 7...Bb4, pinning White's knight and putting it on a square where it can't be kicked out by pawns. 7...Nbd7 is also possible, but will most likely transpose back into the main line.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.name: 7...Bb4
rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.description: Black develops the bishop to its most natural square. White should simply castle kingside 8. O-O to get out of the pin and start preparing e4.

rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.name: 8. O-O
rn1qk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.description: White castles their king to safety to unpin the knight and to start preparing e4. Black can now choose to either play 8...Nbd7 or 8...O-O. Play is very likely to transpose, but different deviations from the main line are possible depending on which move Black plays first. The main difference is that after 8...O-O, Black has many possibilities of fully preventing e4, while after 8...Nbd7 trying to do so is more dangerous for Black. In both positions, White is likely to play Qe2, preparing e4. There is, however, another option.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.name: 8...Nbd7
r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.description: White chooses to develop their knight instead of castling. This move prevents White's knight from jumping to e5 and chasing away the bishop. White does still have the option of 9. Nh4, transposing into the Bled attack and claiming the bishop pair. More common, however, is 9. Qe2, preparing e4 and going into the main line.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.name: 9. Qe2
r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.description: White prepares to push e4. Unlike after 8...O-O, Black has no real way of preventing this. 9...O-O transposes to the main line, while 9...Bg6 still gives Black room for deviation.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.name: 9...Bg6
r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.description: Black prophylactically retreats the bishop so that 10. e4 doesn't come with tempo. This allows for Black to win a pawn at the cost of giving White a big initiative.

r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/1.name: 10. e4
r2qk2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/1.description: White takes up the full center. If Black simply plays 10...O-O we are once again following the main line. One thing that sets this position apart from 8...O-O 9. Qe2 9...Bg6 is that White was actually able to play e4. Black can take the pawn but it is not free. 10...Bxc3 removes an important defender of e4. After 11. bxc3 Nxe4 12. Ba3! =/∞ Black is up a pawn, but White has prevented them from castling king-side. Black will have to castle queen-side, where White has the open b-file and the far-advanced a-pawn. If Black gets greedy and tries to win more pawns with 12...Nxc3? White is quick to get the upper hand after 13. Qb2!, forking the knight and the pawn on b7.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/.name: 10...Bg6
r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBPP3/2N2N2/.description: Black retreats the bishop, keeping an eye on e4. White must either protect or push the pawn. 11. Bd3 defends the pawn and threatens to trade off the light-squared bishops after 12. e5. 11. e5 immediately chases away the knight, but is likely to transpose to the lines with 11. Bd3.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2.name: 9...Nbd7
r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2.description: This move develops the knight to it's most natural square, but also invites White to play 10. e4. This move also sets up Nb6, attacking the light-squared bishop and uncovering the black queen's attack on the d4-pawn. This tactic can cost White a pawn if they are not careful with their pawn-advance.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.name: 8...O-O
rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.description: Black quickly castles their king to safety. This gives Black the option of playing 9...Bg6, which prevents 10. e4 and results in positions where White doesn't get as much central control. White's main option is still 9. Qe2, threatening to play 10. e4. White can also opt for 9. Nh4, transposing into the Bled attack.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.name: 9. Qe2
rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBP4/2N1PN2/.description: White is threatening to play 10. e4 with a tempo on the bishop. If Black allows this, they will have to fend off White's king-side attack, which comes in very quickly.

rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.name: 9...Bg6
rn1q1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pnb1/8/PbBP4/2N1PN2/1.description: Black prevents e4 tactically. By retreating the bishop, 10. e4? is no longer played with tempo and in response Black plays 10...Bxc3! 11. bxc3 Nxe4 ∓. Instead, White should chase Black's light-squared bishop with 10. Ne5. Some players have played 10. Rd1?! in this position, since this move is played anyways. But this is inaccurate, because 10...Nbd7 now prevents the knight from jumping to e5 and trading off the bishop. While chess engines evaluate 10. Rd1 as approximately equal, Black outperforms White in practice.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBPP3/2N2N2.name: 10. e4
r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/5b2/PbBPP3/2N2N2.description: White has been building up to this move for a while. This central expansion hits Black's light-squared bishop with tempo. Black has two squares to retreat the bishop to. 10...Bg6 lets the bishop keep an eye on the e4-pawn, which must now either be pushed to e5 or protected by White's bishop. 10...Bg4 immediately pins White's knight on f3, making the e5 pawn-break possible and also allowing various tactics revolving around the d4-pawn unless defended again.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/7b/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.name: 11...Bh5
r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/7b/Pb1PP3/2NB1N2.description: White can finally go through with their plan of taking over the center with 12. e5.

r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/4P2b/Pb1P4/2NB1N.name: 12. e5
r2q1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/4P2b/Pb1P4/2NB1N.description: White finally takes over the centre, with tempo on Black's knight. Black's main response is 12...Nd5, trying to trade it off for White's c3 knight. Nearly all games continue 13. Nxd5 cxd5 14. Qe3. White unpins their knight and prepares Ng5 to start an attack on Black's king-side. Black has a few possible responses. 14...Be7 defends the g5-square immediately. White can however still go for 15. Ng5, initiating a trade of minor pieces and queens 15...Bxg5 16. Qxg5 Qxg5 17. Bxg5⩲, after which Black re-positions the knight to c6 through b8. White's advantage lies mostly in the bishop pair and the advanced pawns. Apart from 15. Ng5, White can keep the pieces on the board with 15. Bd2, after which Black usually executes the previously mentioned knight manoeuvre. There is many more ideas for both sides which I recommend exploring through the lichess openings database. 14...Re8 is a more modest move, making place for the knight to defend h7. White can choose to tactically trade off pieces with 15. Ng5 Nf8 16. Nxh7!? Nxh7 18. Bxh7 Kxh7 19. Qh3 g6 20. g4 = 14...Bg6 15. Bxg6 fxg6!? trades off the light-squared bishops and opens up the f8 rook. However, after 16. Ng5 Black has to defend their pawn with 16...Re8 not only to defend the pawn, but also to free the f8 square for the knight for if White were to play 17. Qh3, threatening Qxh7 and attacking the e6 pawn.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP2b1/2N2N2/1.name: Steiner variation
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/P1pP2b1/2N2N2/1.description: Instead of the usual 5...Bf5, Black opts to put the bishop on g4, harassing White's knight. However, because the e-pawn hasn't advanced, the knight isn't actually pinned to the queen, so White can play 6. Ne5 with a tempo on the Bishop. After the bishop retreats with 6...Bh5, White has the option to go for either 7. f3, preparing e4, or 7. g3, preparing to fianchetto.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P.name: Smyslov variation
r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/n1p2n2/8/P1pP4/2N2N2/1P.description: Black develops the knight to a6 in order to later transfer it to b4, which was weakened by White's move 5. a4. This does however give White time to occupy the center with 6. e4, or to support the d-pawn with 6. e3. Regardless of whether White pushes the e-pawn one or two squares, Black's response is going to be 6...Bg4, pinning the knight on f3 to the white queen. This is different from the Steiner variation, where the knight isn't actually pinned and can move to e5, gaining a tempo on the bishop. After 6. e4 Bg4 7. Bxc4 it is possible for Black to play 7...Bxf3, doubling White's pawns since 8. Qxf3 would lose the d4 pawn. Despite being a pawn down, this position is still fine for White who can choose to create doubled pawns on Black's a-file with 9. Bxa6. A more modest approach is 7...e6, blunting White's light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3.name: Slav gambit
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3.description: White occupies the center with his pawns. In doing so, Black gets the chance to hold onto the c4-pawn with the move b5, expanding on the queenside. The main line continues 6. e5 Nd5 7. a4 e6 8. axb5 Nxc3 9. bxc3 cxb5 after which Black has to ward off White's attack on the kingside. In practice, Black scores well in this line. This is also backed by computer evaluations, which tend to prefer Black. A better try for White is to play 6. Be2, where White tries to castle quickly and chip away at Black's queenside pawns with moves like b3.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.name: Schlechter variation
rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/P.description: Black intends to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop. White has the option of transposing into an exchange variation with 5. cxd5. This is quite a popular way to meet the Schlechter at the master level, since 4...g6 isn't a very useful move for Black in the exchange variation. Apart from that, White can try to develop the dark-squared bishop outside of the pawn-chain with 5. Bf4 or 5. Bg5. More popular, however, is 5. e3, preparing to develop the light-squared bishop and defending c4.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1.name: 4. Qc2
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1.description: This move is a proper sideline of the Slav defence. White defends the c4-pawn and prepares e4 at the same time. Despite defending c4, it does not prevent its capture: 4...dxc4 is the main move in this position. After 4...dxc4 5. Qxc4 Black can safely develop the light-squared bishop before playing ...e6. White usually employs a kingside fianchetto. Qb3 is usually met with ...Qb6, recapturing with the a-pawn to open up the a-file if White takes. Instead of holding onto material equality, White can play the more aggressive 4...dxc4 5. e4. Black should protect their pawn with ...b5 whenever given the chance in the Slav and this position is no exception. White will chip away at Black's queenside with b3, since there is no knight on c3 that can be kicked by the pawns. The ensuing position is very delicate for Black, so good preparation is required. Black doesn't have to take the pawn however. 4...g6 prepares to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and has many similarities to the Grünfeld defence. White usually tries to develop the dark-squared bishop before closing up the pawn-chain with e3. Another popular response is 4...e6, which closely resembles a Semi-Slav defence. White commonly fianchettos on the kingside, after which 5...dxc4 6. Qxc4 b5 allows Black to fianchetto their own light-squared bishop with tempo on the queen.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3P4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.name: Exchange variation
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3P4/3P4/5N2/PP2PP.description: After this move, the tension in the center is relieved, often allowing Black equality. Because of this, this variation often ends in a draw. Black's only decent move is to complete the exchange of pawns with 4...cxd5. After the exchange, Black will find it difficult to win unless White is overly ambitious. The most draw-ish line of them all is the symmetrical line. Black keeps copying White and both sides exchange minor pieces: 4...cxd5 5. Nc3 Nc6 6. Bf4 Bf5 7. e3 e6 8. Bd3 Bxd3 9. Qxd3 Bd6 10. Bxd6 Qxd6 11. O-O O-O =. Most players agree to a draw in this or any of the following positions.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3.name: Quiet variation
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP4/4PN2/PP3.description: White plays the quiet move 4. e3, introducing more positional play as white is yet to commit the b1-knight to c3. As such, the position remains flexible for both sides and a variety of openings can occur. Black's most common responses are 4...Bf5 and 4...e6, with the latter frequently transposing back into a mainline Semi-Slav defence. However, White can avoid such a Semi-Slav transposition on move 5 with a variety of options, such as Bd3, b3, Nbd2, and Qc2 rather than Nc3. Other responses from Black include 4...a6, 4...g6, and 4...Bg4, all of which are frequently played. White tends to score similarly in this quiet variation compared to the mainline Slav variations.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/4PN2/P.name: Schallopp defence
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2PP4/4PN2/P.description: Black makes use of the opportunity to develop the light-squared bishop. They don't have to be afraid of 5. cxd5 cxd5 6. Qb3 Qc7 since the f6-knight prevents Qb3 from being an effective fork of the b7 and d5 pawns. White's most promising response is 5. Nc3, developing the pieces actively and putting more pressure on d5. The most popular alternatives are 5. cxd5, transposing into the exchange variation where White's dark-squared bishop is stuck behind the pawns, and 5. Bd3, trading off the light-squared bishops.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP2b1/4PN2/P.name: Pin defence
rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2PP2b1/4PN2/P.description: Black develops the bishop to g4, pinning the f3 knight to the queen. White will generally want to get rid of this pin quickly, and has many ways to do so. 5. h3 immediately asks Black the question of whether they want to exchange their bishop for the knight. Both 5...Bh5 and 5...Bxf3 are viable options. After 5...Bh5 White will usually strike back with g4 soon. 5. Nc3 doesn't address the pin yet, but White will likely play h3 soon, often transposing into lines where White begins with h3 instead. 5. Qb3 breaks the pin by moving away the queen, threatening to take the b7 pawn. After either 5...Qb6 or 5...Qc7 White has the looming threat of playing Ne5 with tempo on Black's bishop. 5. cxd5 exchanges the central pawns, resembling the exchange Slav. Black usually responds by trading off the f3 knight, which has the potential of becoming an important attacking piece when transferred to e5.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/R.name: Exchange Variation
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3P4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/R.description: After this move, the tension in the center is relieved often allowing Black equality due to the symmetrical position. Because of this, this variation often ends in a draw. Black's only good move is to complete the exchange of pawns with 3...cxd5, and accept a symmetrical position. However, Nf6!? might be interesting as the position transposes to QGD, Marshall defence, Tan Gambit although this is rarely seen in high-level games. 3...Qxd5?! should be avoided as 4. Nc3 gains a lot of tempo, and allows White a crushing spacial advantage in the center. After 3...cxd5, either side will find it difficult to win unless the other is over-ambitious.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.name: 3...cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.description: This is Black's best option, accepting a symmetrical position. While normal development moves will suffice, White can try to make it harder for Black to get the light-squared bishop out by delaying the combination of Nf3 and e3, which would allow Black to pin the knight to the queen with Bg4. The most popular continuation for White is the combination of Nc3, Bf4 and e3. Usually White starts with 4. Nc3 which is more flexible than the immediate, but totally viable, 4. Bf4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.name: 4. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.description: White doesn't reveal their intentions yet and simply develops the knight to its most natural square, putting pressure on d5. Black's main response is 4...Nf6, overprotecting the d5 pawn and developing the kingside. Black can also play 4...Nc6, often transposing to the same lines as 4...Nf6. However, this move does give White additional options. One of those options being 5. e4, which would have been prevented by 4...Nf6, transposing into a position resembling the French defence.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.name: 4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.description: The most common move for Black. White now has to reveal their opening plan. 5. Bf4 is the most common move, delaying Nf3 and developing the bishop. 5. Nf3 is the second-most common move. This allows a completely equal position and is often used if playing for a draw, especially the variation 5...Nc6 6. Bf4 Bf5 7. e3 e6 8. Bd3 Bxd3 9. Qxd3 Bd6 10. Bxd6 Qxd6 = 5. f3 is the Boor attack, a rare sideline where White tries to take over the center by preparing e4. After both 5. Bf4 and 5. Nf3 Black can try to continue copying their opponent or break the symmetry with the waiting move 6...a6 (played after 5...Nc6). This is a multi-purpose move: it prevents White's light-squared bishop from developing to b5, pinning the knight, and it is useful as a waiting move. If White plays both Nf3 and e3, Black can usefully develop the light-squared bishop to g4 where it pins White's knight to the queen.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/8/PP2PPPP/RNB.description: The Queen's Gambit Accepted has a rich heritage in chess, both sides played by many of the world champions through the years. It is not really much of a gambit since White can recover the pawn immediately with 3. Qa4+, though unless White wants the queen placed on c4, this is unnecessary. Black does better not to hold on to the pawn. Attempts to immediately support it with either 3...b5 or 3...Be6 are not advisable. 3...b5 is countered by 4. a4, threatening Black's pawn chain at its base, and 3...Be6 allows 4. e4, with White grabbing a large share of the center and threatening a later d5 to kick away the bishop. Black's biggest concern is to take advantage of the time it takes White to recover the pawn to get the pieces active and prepare for key pawn breaks in the center (usually ...c5 or ...e5). White usually has better control of the center and has an easier time developing an advantage, but must play well to achieve this. Major continuations: 3. Nf3 - The classical main line. White develops while maintaining some flexibility and preventing 3...e5. 3. e4 - Making use of the fact that Black no longer controls any central squares. This is the oldest and most ambitious response for White. 3. e3 - Not as aggressive as 3. e4, but otherwise similar in intention. This often transposes into 3. Nf3 lines since White ends up playing e2-e3 anyway. 3. Qa4+ - This is a more modern continuation. While classical theory shied away from developing the queen early, this line aims at posting the queen in an active role, similar to lines of the Catalan. This also avoids any monkey business in trying to hold on to c4. 3. Nc3 - This move looks misguided, as d4 and e5 are not controlled, and the knight is vulnerable to a ...b5 advance.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.name: 3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.description: Two players have labeled this move misguided, as the knight is vulnerable here to a b7-b5-b4 advance. It also doesn't control d4 or e5, two important squares in Queen's Gambit Accepted positions. The most common and highest-scoring response for Black is to follow up with 3...a6, preparing a future ...b5 thrust which will introduce the idea of attacking the knight with ...b4, whilst also claiming that Black can keep ahold of the pawn with suitable defence. This usually leads to a firefight on the queenside, with a4 usually being played sooner rather than later by White in order to disrupt Black's defence of the c-pawn. The less common 3...c6 transposes to a position in the Slav defence, with a similar idea in mind.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.name: 3...f5?
rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/2pP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.description: This move is too weakening. It weakens the entire e-file, and the c4-g8 diagonal. In Match 1, Game 8, Labourdonnais-McDonnell, McDonnell played f5 and lost quickly.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.name: Classical variation
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/5N2/PP2PPPP/R.description: This is the classical continuation. White pursues its development and increases control over the e5 square. Black's main reply is 3...Nf6.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.name: 4...e6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.description: This move prepares to release the f8-bishop into action. The light-squared bishop is supposed to go to b7, but sometimes has to settle for the passive d7-square. White should follow up on their previous moves and capture the pawn on c4 with 5. Bxc4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.name: 5. Bxc4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PPP.description: White recaptures the pawn while developing the light-squared bishop. This also allows White to quickly castle kingside. Black should try to stay active and strike at the center with 5...c5. Black could also play 5...a6, trying to get in 6...b5 with a tempo on White's bishop. The move a6 is also part of the main line and therefore likely to transpose with 6. O-O c5.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.name: 5...c5
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2p5/2BP4/4PN2/PP3PP.description: Black strikes back at the center, potentially leaving White with an isolated queen's pawn after ...cxd4. White's main option is 6. O-O, getting their king out of the center. An alternative is 6. Qe2, the Furman variation. This supports the advance of the e-pawn and enables dxc5 without trading the queens.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.name: = 3. e3 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pP4/4P3/PP3PPP/RN.description: This move is not quite so popular as the main lines 3. e4 or 3. Nf3, but respectable nonetheless. It is a more conservative move. White opts to defend d4 instead of taking the center with pawns. Black cannot try to hold on to his c-pawn because of the famous trap 3...b5? (black should pursue development with ...e5) 4. a4! (getting the base of the pawn chain) c6? (further weakening the h1 to a8 diagonal) 5. axb5! cxb5?? (it would still be better to develop now, even though white will end with a pawn up or a huge lead in development) 6. Qf3! when Black must part with at least a minor piece because the weak h1 to a8 diagonal can't be defended anymore. Note: 6... Bb7 loses to 7. Qxb7. Common Black continuations include: 3... e5 - a newer, aggressive move that tries to open up the position and likely results in an isolated queen pawn for white (4. dxe5? fails to 4...Qxd1! when white loses castling rights). 3... e6 - The more classical, conservative approach, although it results in limited mobility for the light-squared bishop. 3... Nf6 - Typical developing move. White then usually takes the c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RNB.name: 3. e4
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RNB.description: In this line, white moves immediately to reclaim the "gambit" pawn. The rationale is simple. In most lines of the QGA, white allows black to play ...Nf6 which usually means white has to play f2-f3 in preparation for e3-e4. By playing e2-e4 now, white establishes broad control of the center without losing time. This also has the potential advantage of allowing the c1-bishop to develop unhindered. Also, black is forced to choose a central strategy now or else face being dominated by white's center and development. Black is no worse in these lines, though, than in the classical QGA's, and can obtain counterplay in these lines as well as the others. Here are several options: 3...e5 - The most common reply. 3...c5 - Playing this now can lead to Benoni-like positions. 3...Nf6 - Playing this now can lead to Alekhine-like positions. 3...Nc6 - Takes advantage of the fact white has not played 3. Nf3 to pressurize the d4 pawn. Trying to hold on to the pawn with 3...b5?! is not advised, as even though the e4 pawn blocks the h1-a8 diagonal, it is still quite risky to hold on to the pawn. After 4. a4! c6 5. axb5 cxb5, the weak diagonal is subject to discovered attacks and queen-bishop batteries. The b5 pawn could soon be in jeopardy and white's attacking opportunities and moderate (but still significant) lead in development gives more than enough compensation for the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.name: 3...e5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/2pPP3/8/PP3PPP/RN.description: This is the most common and ambitious reply by Black. This move attacks White's centre and opens up the dark-squared bishop. There is only one move that preserves White's advantage, that being 4. Nf3, attacking e5 and defending d4. 4. Bxc4? doesn't work due to 4...Qxd4! 5. Qxd4 exd4 6. Nf3 c5 ⩱ and Black is able to build a fairly stable centre. 4. dxe5? also does not work due to 4...Qxd1!, forcing a trade of queens with Kxd1, and although material is even, White is exposed in the center and loses castling rights.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.name: = 2...e5 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.description: The Albin Countergambit is an uncommon defense to the Queen's Gambit. Although it is rarely played by masters, it seems to be better than its reputation. The usual continuation is 3.dxe5 d4, where in exchange for the gambit pawn Black has a central wedge at d4 and gets some chances for an attack. Often White will try to return the pawn at an appropriate moment in order to gain a positional advantage. The Black pawn at d4 is stronger than it may appear. The careless move 4.e3? can lead to the Lasker Trap (see diagram below). After 4...Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3!! 6.Bxb4?? is a blunder — 6...exf2+! 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+!! and Black's position is superior. The Lasker Trap is notable because it is rare to see an underpromotion as early as move 7. Instead the game usually continues 4.Nf3 Nc6 (4...c5 allows 5.e3 because Black no longer has the bishop check) and now White's primary options are 5.a3, 5.Nbd2, and 5.g3. Perhaps White's surest try for an advantage is to fianchetto his king bishop with 5.g3 followed by Bg2 and Nbd2. Black will often castle queenside. A typical continuation is 5.g3 Be6 6.Nbd2 Qd7 7.Bg2 0-0-0 8.0-0 Bh3. In the Spassky Variation, White plays 4.e4 to take advantage of the fact that an en passant capture must be made immediately after the enemy pawn moves. Now after 4...Bb4+ 5.Bd2 the en passant capture ...dxe3 is no longer available for Black because of the intervening moves.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/.description: With 2...e6, Black declines the Queen's Gambit in the traditional fashion. 2...e6 bolsters the d5 pawn and opens a diagonal for the development of Black's dark-squared bishop. However, 2...e6 also blocks the c8-h3 diagonal for Black's light-squared bishop. Finding a way to productively develop this piece is a perennial challenge for Black players in the QGD.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.name: 3. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.description: With the move 3. Nc3, White continues development and puts pressure on the d5 pawn, and also controls the e4 square for a possible e4 break in the future. White wants to play e4 at some point in the future, and the move 3. Nc3 helps with this break.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.name: 3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.description: With 3...Nf6, Black begins developing the minor pieces, gets closer to castling, and exerts control over the center. This is the classical main line of the Queen's Gambit Declined. White has several options, though some of these may transpose into each other at some point. 4. cxd5 is the exchange variation. Unlike other exchange variations notorious for yielding a quiet game (e.g. French, Slav), this exchange results in what is known as the Carlsbad pawn structure, which has several aggressive plans, such as a "minority attack" on the queenside. Although it was once relatively uncommon, as Black's usual response 4...exd5 unblocks the queen's bishop from development, it has become the main line after 3...Nf6. 4. Bg5 is a classical continuation that leads to a wide variety of positions. White gets the dark-squared bishop outside of the pawn chain in order to be able to release the light-squared bishop with e2-e3. Black usually unpins the knight with 4...Be7 and tries to castle quickly. After the usual 5. e3 O-O 6. Nf3, Black has a major choice between 6...Nbd7 (the classical variation) and 6...h6. 4...Nbd7 is a notable alternative, often leading to the Cambridge Springs defense (5.e3 c6 6.Nf3 Qa5). 4. Nf3 is the three knights variation. White gives Black many choices on how to continue development, including some of the most aggressive variations of the Queen's Gambit, such as the Semi-Slav (4...c6) and Vienna (4...dxc4) variations, as well as the Ragozin (4...Bb4) and Semi-Tarrasch (4...c5). Transposition to the 4. Bg5 line after 4...Be7 5. Bg5 is also possible, but White has the major alternative of 5. Bf4, the Harrwitz Attack.

rnbqk1nr/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.name: Charousek variation
rnbqk1nr/ppp1bppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.description: Black stops White from playing the immediate 4. Bg5, practically forcing White into one of three options: 4. Nf3, simply developing the knight. This is the most common and flexible response, since White doesn't reveal anything about their setup yet. If Black plays 4...Nf6 then 5. Bg5 transposes back into the main lines. 4. Bf4 develops the bishop to f4 instead. White intends to enter the Harrwitz attack. 4. cxd5 transposes into an exchange variation where Black has already played Be7, preventing White from usefully developing the bishop to g5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.name: Orthodox variation
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP2.description: Black unpins the knight and prepares to castle short. White's two main responses 5. e3 and 5. Nf3 are very likely to transpose, so the order doesn't particularly matter.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1P3/P.name: 5. e3
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1P3/P.description: With the dark-squared bishop developed, White can safely create a dark-squared pawn-chain.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.name: 6. Nf3
rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.description: White proceeds with normal development. Black now has two options. Go into the classical variation with 6...Nbd7. Go for either Lasker's defense or the Tartakower variation with 6...h6.

r1bq1rk1/pppnbppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.name: Classical variation
r1bq1rk1/pppnbppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN2.description: With this move Black enters the Classical variation. This is an older and well-studied variation that has stood the test of time, as it is still played to this day. Due to its age, White has developed many responses to it over time. 7. Rc1 is the main line, developing the rook to the to-be-opened c-file. 7. Qc2 is the Rubinstein attack. White develops the queen to watch over the b1-h7 diagonal. 7. cxd5 releases the tension from the center and transposes into an exchange variation. 7. Bd3 is the Botvinnik variation, in which Black gains a few tempi on White's bishop with 7...cxd5 and, later on, Nb6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN.name: 6...h6
rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4pn1p/3p2B1/2PP4/2N1PN.description: Black pushes the bishop away, likely intending to go for either the Tartakower or Lasker's defence. Apart from White's main option 7. Bh4 they can also avoid these theoretical lines by playing 7. Bxf6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4p2p/3p4/2PPn2B/2N1PN2.name: Lasker defence
rnbq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/4p2p/3p4/2PPn2B/2N1PN2.description: Black centralizes the knight, opening up an attack on White's dark-squared bishop. The mainline continues by trading the dark-squared bishops and later the knights as well.

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bpp1/1p2pn1p/3p4/2PP3B/2N1P.name: Tartakower defence
rnbq1rk1/p1p1bpp1/1p2pn1p/3p4/2PP3B/2N1P.description: 7...b6 enters the Tartakower defence, where Black hopes to develop the light-squared bishop. While it looks like Black intends to fianchetto the bishop, this isn't necessarily true. If White tries to blunt the a8-h1 diagonal immediately with 8. cxd5, Black will nonetheless be able to develop the bishop: 8. cxd5 Nxd5 9. Bxe7 Qxe7 10. Nxd5 exd5 = and Black can now put the bishop somewhere on the c8-h3 diagonal instead (usually going to e6).

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.name: 4...Nbd7
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4pn2/3p2B1/2PP4/2N5/PP.description: With 4...Nbd7, black intends to play the Cambridge Springs Defense, which continues 5. Nf3 c6 6. e3 Qa5. The Cambridge Springs Defense is a solid line of the QGD and is often played both in the amateur level (because of the easier to understand theme) and the grandmaster level. This move also sets a trap that has ensnared quite a few players. White can continue 5. cxd5 exd5, resulting in a position that resembles the QGD Exchange variation (which is fine for both camps), as long as he/she doesn't play 6. Nxd5??. While it superficially appears to win a pawn (because the black knight is pinned), black can capture with his knight with 6... Nxd5!. Then after 7. Bxd8, white has not won black's queen because of 7... Bb4+!, where the only legal move is 8. Qd2, and black gets his/her queen back and emerges a minor piece ahead.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP2.name: Ragozin Defence
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP2.description: The mainlines continues either 5. Bg5 h6 (Moscow variation) 5. Bg5 dxc4 (Vienna variation)

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.name: = Three Knights Variation 4...Be7 =
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.description: This position is often reached from the Indian defence after white tries to avoid the Nimzo-Indian through 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nf3 d5 4. Nc3 Be7

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.name: Harrwitz Attack
rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.description: White develops the bishop to f4. This just looks like a standard developing move, but it is extremely aggressive. With the bishop on f4 instead of g5, White avoids piece exchanges, and often castles queenside while Black castles kingside, leading to sharp opposite-side castling positions. Black has nothing better to do than castle.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined
rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.description: Blackburne Variation After the developing move 6. e3, Black has 3 choices: -She can take advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which doesn’t pressure the d5 pawn, and play 6...c5 without fear of being forced into an IQP structure. However, this line is entry to the rabbit hole and leads to very complicated positions. -6...Nbd7 is a more solid choice and avoids the complications of the main line. However, it allows 7. c5 resulting in white having a pleasant space advantage. -6...b6 is the most solid way for Black to play, resulting in positions resembling the Tartokower Defense.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP1B2/2N1PN2.description: Black immediately strikes the White centre with ...c7-c5. This takes advantage of the Bishop being on f4 instead of g5, which applies less pressure on d5. To demonstrate, after 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 Be7 5. Bg5 O-O 6. e3 h6 7. Bh4, 7...c5 can be met with 8. Bxf6 Bxf6 9. cxd5 exd5 10. dxc5, and Black is left with a suboptimal isolated queen’s pawn structure. White’s only move is the Botvinnik exchange: 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo. 7. cxd5 can be met with ...Nxd5, and 7. Bd3 or 7. Be2 can be met with ...dxc4, which all allow black to equalise comfortably.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2Pp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/.description: White captures the c-pawn with 7. dxc5, forcing the black bishop on e7 to waste a tempo with 7...Bxc5. Note that 7...dxc4 leads to a favorable endgame for white after 8. Bxc4 Qxd1+ 9. Rxd1, where white enjoys more active pieces.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.description: Black recaptures the pawn. Now White can play the unambitious 8. cxd5 and saddle black with an isolani, or continue going down the rabbit hole with the mainline 8. Qc2, where the queen points towards the black kingside. It should be noted that 8. a3 transposes into the mainline.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2/P.description: White activates the queen, who points towards the black kingside. Black develops with 8...Nc6

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/2N1PN2.description: Black simply develops. White continues with 9. a3, an important move to control b4 and prepare b2-b4.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/2bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.description: This move is important to control the b4 square and support b2-b4. Black is forced to play 9...Qa5, which prevents b4 by pinning the a3 pawn to the rook and pins the c3 knight to the king. This also supports ...Nb4.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/q1bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.name: Queen’s Gambit Declined, Blackburne Variation, Main Line
r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/q1bp4/2P2B2/P1N1PN.description: This move is forced, pinning the a3 pawn to the rook, preventing b2-b4 and supporting ...Nb4 ideas. White has a sideline and 2 mainline moves. 10. Nd2 is the sideline, avoiding the complications of the mainlines. As Nb3 is threatened, black responds with ...Be7. The mainlines 10. Rd1 and 10. O-O-O are not for the faint of heart, as they lead to wild, extremely complicated positions.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.name: General concepts
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.description: Unlike the regular Tarrasch, in the Semi-Tarrasch Defense Black does not accept an isolated pawn, since he intends to recapture on d5 with the knight (as after 5.cxd5, 5...exd5 has long been known to be dubious after 6.Bg5), but he cedes a spatial advantage to White. After 4...c5, White usually plays 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.e3 or 6.e4, which leads to different types of middlegame play and has attracted the interest of strong players with both colors since the early twentieth century.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.name: Vienna variation
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.description: 4...dxc4 is a very aggressive response by Black leading to very double-edged positions. Black gives up some central control, allowing for White to build up a big center that Black tries to tear down later. 5. e4 is White's main response, taking up the entire center and preparing to recapture the pawn with the bishop. 5. e3 is the quiet variation. Positions often resemble those of the Queens Gambit accepted with 3. Nf3. 5. Qa4+ is a sideline with positions similar to the Semi Slav defence.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.name: 5. e4
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2pPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.description: White takes up the center and opens up the light-squared bishop to recapture the pawn on c4. Black can choose to go into the sharp mainline with 5...Bb4 or to hang onto the pawn a little longer with 5...b5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.name: 5...Bb4
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP3P.description: Black pins the c3 knight, removing the only defender of the e4 pawn. 6. Bg5 is White's main response, pinning the f6 knight to the queen which indirectly defends the e4 pawn. 6. Bxc4 is a sideline, letting Black take the e4 pawn for faster development.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/6B1/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP.name: 6. Bg5
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/6B1/1bpPP3/2N2N2/PP.description: White pins the f6 knight, indirectly defending the e4 pawn. Black's main option is 6...c5 striking at White's center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.name: Queen's Gambit Declined - Exchange Variation
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.description: With this move, Black frees up his light squared bishop, which was originally blocked with the move 2...e6. In addition, the classic Carlsbad pawn structure is entered, in which White has a pawn majority in the centre, and Black has a pawn majority on the queenside. White wants flexibility on where to place the knight on g1 in this position. In the cases in which White goes for the minority attack, a knight on f3 is usually preferred, and in cases in which he prefers a central expansion with f3 and e4, a knight on e2 is preferred. As a result, White usually prefers to develop the light squared bishop first (almost always to d3), so ...e3 is played before deciding on a placement for the knight. However, playing 5. e3 immediately would block in the dark squared bishop, so White almost always continues with 5. Bg5, pinning the knight on f6 and adding pressure to the pawn on d5, whilst also getting the bishop outside the pawn chain. With this move, White threatens to double Black's pawns with 6. Bxf6, as 6...Qxf6 would lose a pawn to 7. Nxd5.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.name: Tarrasch defence
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pp4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.description: Black aggressively attempts to gain space in the center, with the caveat of a potentially isolated pawn on d5 after a few pawn exchanges. The isolated queen's pawn is one of the reasons many players prefer to play the Semi-Tarrasch instead. White has the options of taking on d5, taking on c5 and protecting the pawn. 4. cxd5 is considered to be the main line, making sure the c3 knight won't be pushed around by Black's pawns and trying to create an isolated queen's pawn to play against. 4. e3 is White's main sideline, which equalizes for Black quite quickly. After both sides have developed the knights the position is completely symmetrical. 4. dxc5 results in Black being able to push the d pawn to gain a tempo on the knight. While the engine evaluates this move as equal, Black performs a lot better in practice.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pP4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.name: 4. cxd5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/2pP4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP.description: White captures the d5 pawn in an attempt to give Black an isolated queen's pawn. Black has two viable responses: 4...exd5 is the main line, replacing the captured pawn to control the center. 4...cxd4 is the Schara gambit, luring White's queen into the center in order to develop quickly with tempo on the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3P4/3p4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.name: Schara gambit
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/3P4/3p4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.description: Instead of the usual 4...exd5 Black opts to gambit a pawn for rapid development. The immediate 5. Qxd4 runs into many tempo gaining moves, the first of which is 5...Nc6, making use of the fact that the pawn is pinned. The line continues 6. Qd1 exd5 7. Qxd5 and black can choose to play 7...Be6 going into the Von Hennig gambit, trading White's queen which was moved three times in the opening already. The main move is 5. Qa4+, forcing Black to block the black queen's vision of the d5 pawn with a piece. This is usually done with the bishop, since the knight will be better placed on c6. After 5. Qa4+ play continues 5...Be7 6. Qxd4 exd5 7. Qxd5 and Black will use the white queen to quickly develop the minor pieces with tempo.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.name: 4...exd5
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/3P4/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.description: Black recaptures on d5, keeping a pawn in the center. White usually continues developing the knights and preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.name: Triangle system
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.description: In this position, by delaying Nf6, Black keeps many opportunities open. They can keep on playing in the normal Queen's Gambit Declined (QGD) fashion with 4...Nf6 (whether White plays e3 or Nf3), or can try other options. 4. Nf3 can lead to regular QGD games or alternatively the Noteboom variation: 4...dxc4. Here, Black aims to get two passed pawns on the flank in exchange for White's big center. The middlegame is critical, but if Black survives, the endgame will be in their favor. On the other hand 4. e3 can lead to a stonewall defense position with 4...f5, where Black's usual plan is a quick attack on the king side and can often involve a rook lift to f6. Another option for White, though less popular, is the Marshall Gambit of the Semi-Slav, with 4. e4. This move aims at exploiting Black's lack of control over the e4-square, not having played Nf6. The main line continues 4...dxe4 5. Nxe4 Bb4+ 6. Bd2 Qxd4 7. Bxb4 Qxe4+ with a sharp game. Usually White blocks with Be2 and leaves the g2 pawn hanging. Black can capture it, but not the rook (Bf3 wins the queen). In return, White can have lasting pressure and tactics involving the d6 weakness. An example game played in this line is Bacrot - Morozevich, Biel Rd2, 2012.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.name: 4. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.description: White develops the knight and leaves the opening choice to Black. The move 4...Nf6 transposes into the Semi-Slav defence, while 4...dxc4 enters the sharp Noteboom variation.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.name: Semi-Slav defence
rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.description: A highly theoretical opening. Black willingly keeps the light-squared bishop behind the pawn-chain, intending to free it later with either the e5 or c5 pawn breaks. In response, White has two main options with very different playstyles. 5. Bg5 leads to sharp, tactical positions, where Black can choose to play the Botvinnik variation 5...dxc4 or the Moscow or Anti-Moscow. 5. e3 leads to calmer, more positional variations. White will generally decide whether to go into the mainline Meran with 6. Bd3 or avoid it with one of the many Anti-Meran variations. Some less popular options include 5. cxd5, leading to either an exchange Slav or exchange Queens gambit declined. 5. g3 is also a viable alternative, dodging theoretical lines of the Semi-Slav and potentially resulting in Catalan-esque positions. This opening can also be reached through the queen's gambit declined by the move order 2...e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nf3 c6.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.name: Noteboom variation
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/2pP4/2N2N2/PP2PP.description: With this move Black enters the aggressive Noteboom variation. White can attempt to win back the pawn like in the Alapin Slav with 5. a4 but Black can take advantage of that move with 5...Bb4. After 6. e3, attacking the pawn, Black can defend it with 6...b5, making use of the fact that after 7. axb5 cxb5 White's knight on c3 is still pinned and can't capture the pawn on b5. White's other option is to try to win back the pawn with the immediate 5. e3 but Black will respond with 5...b5, defending the pawn. After 6. a4 Black has successfully provoked White into weakening the b4-square, where Black will once again place the dark-squared bishop, transposing into the previous line. White can also choose to avoid the Noteboom with either 5. Bg5 the anti-Noteboom variation or with 5. g3 the anti-Noteboom gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.name: Marshall gambit
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2PPP3/2N5/PP3P.description: This move controls the center and creates a huge pawn roller. Black's c8-bishop will be blocked and inactive for some time. However, White will have to sacrifice a pawn in a few moves if they want to fight for the edge. Black hasn't moved a single piece yet and put all their central pawns on light squares. White quickly got e4 in.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP3PPP/.name: 5...Bb4+
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP3PPP/.description: This move is Black's best option to fight for an advantage. It forces White to either gambit the d4 pawn for activity, or to retreat the knight back to c3, "losing" a tempo in the process. 6. Bd2 is the main move, blocking the check and attacking Black's bishop at the same time. This does however block the white queen from defending the d4 pawn, allowing 6...Qxd4, which gambits the pawn in exchange for quick development and active pieces. 6. Nc3 is the Forgotten variation, a sideline where White holds onto the d4 pawn, keeping material equal. 6. Nd2? is a mistake, since it contains all the drawbacks of 6. Bd2 (losing d4) and none of the advantages (getting a very active dark-squared bishop). To add insult to injury, it also hampers the development of White's queenside by locking up the c1 bishop.

rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP1B1PP.name: 6. Bd2
rnbqk1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPPN3/8/PP1B1PP.description: This move blocks the check and attacks Black's bishop, but loses sight of the d4-pawn. 6...Qxd4 picks up the gambitted pawn and threatens the knight on e4.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPqN3/8/PP1B1PP.name: 6...Qxd4
rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1bPqN3/8/PP1B1PP.description: Black takes the gambitted pawn and will be up material for the time being. This opening doesn't come without compensation for White. After 7. Bxb4 White will have dominance over Black's weakened dark squares.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BPqN3/8/PP3PPP/.name: 7. Bxb4
rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BPqN3/8/PP3PPP/.description: White takes Black's dark-squared bishop. White's dark-squared bishop is now placed on a very active diagonal, cutting through d6, e7 and f8. Black should play 7...Qxe4+ to not be down a piece.

rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BP1q3/8/PP3PPP/.name: 7...Qxe4+
rnb1k1nr/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/1BP1q3/8/PP3PPP/.description: Black recaptures the piece. This is the starting point of the Marshall gambit. White has two main ways of blocking the check, both leading to complex positions where White has to find a way to convert their lead in development into a tangible advantage. White should generally avoid trading pieces, especially queens, as any endgame will favour Black. 8. Be2 is the main line, blocking the check with the bishop. This leaves the g2-pawn undefended, but taking it would be unwise, since it allows White to develop even more quickly with Bf3, Ne2 and then Rg2 comes with tempo. 8 Ne2 is less popular, but still very often played. This leaves the c4-pawn undefended, but taking it is once again way too dangerous for Black because of Qd6!, infiltrating on the weakened dark squares. The main continuation in this line ends up restoring material equality.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.name: 3...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.description: Here white can take an interesting departure from the typical QGD lines by playing 4. g3, transposing into a main line of the Catalan Opening. This colorful opening can be very aggressive, especially if black opens the long diagonal with ...dxc4 at some point. The piece play white obtains from such an opening of lines is often dangerous for black. At this point, white's other main continuations are 4. Nc3 and 4. Bg5, though 4. cxd5 is certainly possible.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP1.name: 3. g3
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2PP4/6P1/PP2PP1.description: White prepares to fianchetto their bishop. White chooses a Catalan-style set up, an approach that combines c4 and d4 with a king's side fianchetto. This is a less common move order. Black usually develops their knight next, 3...Nf6, and the same Catalan position is reached as if the game had played out in the order 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. g3 d5.

r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PP.name: 4...Nc6
r1bqkb1r/ppp1pppp/2n2n2/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PP.description: This move is the main move and where is diverged most of the lines of the Kurtz opening, some like the main line, the Benz Variation, the Silent Game, etc. It is a door for a big center attack, and White does everything to stop 5... e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: Blackmar-Diemer gambit
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: White offers their e4 pawn in exchange for quick development and open lines. At the professional level this move is considered somewhat suspect, but Black must be careful if they choose to take the pawn as there are many traps in this opening. 2...dxe4 accepts the gambit. Black has three ways to decline the gambit. 2...e6 transposes to the French Defence 2...c6 transposes to the Caro-Kann Defence 2...Nc6 transposes to the Nimzowitsch Defence 2...c5 is a largely unexplored countergambit.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 2...c5?
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2pp4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: An unusual countergambit to the Blackmar-Diemer or Smith-Morra gambits. It superficially resembles a reversed Albin countergambit, but with White to move. White can capture either of the pawns and come out ahead. If 3. dxc5 dxe4 leads to a queen trade. Most common in amateur games is 3...d4?, which seems to take space but just leaves the pawn stranded after 4. Nf3 (preventing ...e5) Nc6 5. c3. 3...Nf6 is an improvement. If 3. exd5 Qxd5 then 4. Ne2 is best to defend the d-pawn (if 4. Nf3 then ...Bg4, pinning the knight, cannot be met with f3) 4...Nf6 5. Nbc3 Qd7 6. d5±. Otherwise this probably leads to a queen trade too, e.g. 4. Nc3 Qxd4 5. Qxd4 cxd4 6. Nb5 Na6⩲.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: 2...d5
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: This is the main line of the Caro-Kann defence, a semi-open game that tends to contain lines with minor piece play. Black's threatens to capture ...dxe4. White has four main plans to deal with the central tension: close the centre, capture first, or prepare to recapture with knight or pawn. 3. e5 is the advance variation. White closes the centre and takes more space. This is the modern-day main line at all levels. The main line continues 3...Bf5 4. Nf3 e6 5. Be2, and Black either plays for an early ...c5 pawn break or contents themselves with developing in a cramped position. White has a choice of several sharp sidelines, including 3. Nc3 & 4. g4, sometimes called the Shirov attack. 3. exd5 is the exchange variation. Black retakes 3...cxd5 and frees the c6 for their knight again. Then White's main options are the Rubinstein variation, 4. Bd3 Nc6 5. c3 Nf6 6. Bf4, which leads to a Carlsbad pawn structure, or the sharp Panov attack, 4. c4, where White is willing to accept an isolated queen's pawn position for rapid development and attacking chances. 3. Nc3, the classical, and 3. Nd2, the modern variation, prepare to recapture with the knight. Usually, both moves reach the same position after 3...dxe4 4. Nxe4. The two move orders differ in how they may answer the sideline 3...g6. 3. f3, preparing to recapture with the pawn, is the Maróczy or fantasy variation. Black doesn't usually want to allow White to retake in the centre with a pawn (though 3...dxe4 4. fxe4 e5 is playable) and the main continuation is 3...e6 and a closed, manoeuvring game.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.name: = 2...dxe4 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.description: White has given up his king's pawn, in hopes of an aggressive game. Since there is no way White can win a pawn back immediately, he can expect this set-up most times he plays the Blackmar-Diemar Gambit. The best move for White would be Nc3, putting pressure on the e4-pawn and preparing the move f3, as 3. f3 is well met by 3...e5!, with an edge for Black. One example: 4. dxe5 (other moves are even worse, for example 4. fxe4 Qh4+ and Qxe4 with an extra pawn and an attack, or d5 Nf6 c4 c6 when d5 will soon fall) Qxd1+ Kxd1 Nc6 fxe4 (f4 Bg4+ Ne2 O-O-O+ with a winning attack) Nxe5 with an obvious advantage. Black normally plays 3...Nf6, though 3...f5 and 3...Bf5 are interesting ways to avoid mainline theory. Now, if f3 e5?, dxe5 gains a tempo on the knight. Sometimes Bc4 is played, to hopefully trap Black quickly with a variation of Scholar's Mate.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: = 3. Bc4 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: This move develops the bishop to its most active square. The most common response is Nc6.

r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/7Q/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP.name: = 4. Qh5 =
r1bqkbnr/ppp1pppp/2n5/7Q/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP.description: White threatens to win a queen by checking on f7. Black should play g6 to stop the threat. However, if he, in his hotheaded desire plays Nf6??, Black faces doom with Qxf7+ Kd7 Be6+ Kd6 Bf4+ Ne5 Bxe5+ Kc6 Nc3 Bxe6 Qxe6+ Qd6 Bxd6.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.name: = 3. Nc3 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/R.description: White has brought his minor piece into action and taken control of the middle. Simultaneously, he has put pressure on Black's e4-pawn, which Black must now try and defend. Nf6 or Bf5 would most commonly be used to defend the lone pawn, while e5 gives the option of a pawn transfer. f5 defends the pawn using Black's f-pawn, a less optimal response. Rarer responses include Nc6 transposing to the Nimzowitsch Defense and adding an attacker to the d4 pawn, and c5, a rather unexplored countergambit.

rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.name: 3. Bf5
rn1qkbnr/ppp1pppp/8/5b2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.description: Bf5 defends the pawn on e4 and develops the queenside bishop, with intentions of keeping the pawn as it is a thorn to White who can't play Nf3 or Bd3, otherwise the knight/bishop will be taken by the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.name: = 3. Nf6 =
rnbqkb1r/ppp1pppp/5n2/8/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.description: Black has developed his knight, to prevent White from taking the black pawn on e4.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.name: 3...c5 - Reversed Albin Countergambit
rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/8/2p5/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.description: This rare and rather unknown countergambit adds pressure to White's d-pawn. The name of this opening is the Reversed Albin Countergambit as it resembles an accepted Albin Countergambit with colors reversed and an extra knight on c3. This is sometimes considered slightly dubious or bizarre, but it is nonetheless playable.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.name: = 3... e5 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/4p3/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP/.description: Black has advanced their pawn to e5 and offers a pawn transfer. If White takes the e5 pawn, then Qxd1 forces White to either give up the right to castle with Kxd1 or undevelop the knight with Nxd1. However, there are better options such as Nxe4, encouraging Black to take d4 with the queen and make a queen trade, or Nge2, declining the countergambit and protecting the d4 pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.name: 3...f5 - Netherlands Variation
rnbqkbnr/ppp1p1pp/8/5p2/3Pp3/2N5/PPP2PPP.description: Instead of opting for the standard 3...Nf6 or even 3...Bf5, Black chooses to defend their e4 pawn with their f-pawn, an opening named the Netherlands Variation. This is inferior to other ways of defending the pawn as it weakens the kingside and creates a hole on e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 2...e5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: = Center Game: Beyer Gambit = Black copies White's d4. Although this approach of pushing ...d5 can be plausible against the King's Gambit (in the Falkbeer Countergambit), here it is simply unfavorable for Black. With good play, White can gain a good and superior position. The Beyer Gambit can be met with two responses. 3. exd5?! is not bad, but gives away White's advantage. After 3...Qxd5, Black's position is quite playable with no big problems and no material deficit. 3. dxe5 is testing of the Beyer Gambit. White captures the free black pawn on e5. if Black copies with 3...dxe4, 4. Qxd8+! Kxd8 leaves White with a very favorable endgame where the black king cannot castle and is on the open d-file. Black can play a gambit with 3...d4, but it will be hard for Black to prove compensation for the lost pawn. 3. f4!? transposes to the Hinrichsen Gambit of the Falkbeer Countergambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: 2...d5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: 2...d5 challenges White's centre. Black would love to take dxe4: how will White answer this threat? There are four main options. 3. exd5, the Exchange variation, White takes first before they are taken. This leads to an open, symmetrical game with a reputation for being drawish.
