That wouldn't be a disaster for White, who would have two rooks and two pawns for the queen, in fact it's quite possibly a winning advantage still. But White's rooks would be stuck in the corners, and the Black queen would be running around in the middle of the board, and accidents can happen.

r4bnr/1ppq1k1p/6p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.name: 13. Nb5
r4bnr/1ppq1k1p/6p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.description: Black's c7 and e4 pawns are threatened. 13...c6 saves one and, by kicking the knight, gains the necessary tempo to save the other. Black still isn't worried about 14.Qxh8 which can be met by 14...Nf6 15.b3 Re8 16.Bb2 Bg7 or the quiet 16...Be7 ( 16...Bc5 is a well-known blunder because of 16.Qxf6+ Kg8 17.Qh8+ Kf7 18.Qg7+ Ke6 19.Qf6#) winning the queen for two rooks.

r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.name: 13...c6
r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N2Q3/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.description: It's now time for White to offer to take the queens off with 14. Qd4 and hope that the two extra pawns will be sufficiently healthy to win the day. The retreat 14.Nc3 has been played too, but the attack on e4 is an illusion as long as the e-file is open for the a8-rook (14...Nf6 15.Nxe4? Nxe4 and now 16.Qxe4?? Re8 is a train wreck while 16.Qxh8 Nf6 is just a free piece for Black compared to the earlier Qxh8 lines) so the knight won't be well placed on c3.

r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N6/2PQp3/8/PP1P1PP.name: 14...Qe7
r4bnr/1p1q1k1p/2p3p1/1N6/2PQp3/8/PP1P1PP.description: This is White's last chance to grab the h8-rook, otherwise Black is going to shut the door with ...Nf6. Alternatively, White can take advantage of the fact that Black has blocked the e-file with her queen, and go after the e4-pawn with 15.Nc3. This is a better move than 14.Nc3 would have been, because Black can't pin and win the queen with ...Re8 any more.

r3kbnr/Nppb2pp/3q4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP.name: 10. Qh5
r3kbnr/Nppb2pp/3q4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP.description: Black doesn't have an obvious way of escaping the check. 10...Qg6 would allow White with her next two moves Qxg6 and Bxd7 to a) ruin Black's pawns, b) swap off material when ahead and c) prevent Black castling. Fleeing to either d8 or e7 with the king followed by 11.Bxd7 Kxd7 12.Qb5+ would ship yet another pawn, as would 10...Ke7 11.Bxd7 Qxd7 12.Qe5+. The computer recommends 10...Kd8 11.Bxd7 Qxd7 as the least bad option, although White could then swing the queen over to a5 threatening Nc6+ and so forcing the king straight back to e8, while potentially saving a tempo by not having to move the knight immediately. So the modern, active way of defending this position as Black is with 10...g6 followed by 11.Bxd7+ Qxd7!? It doesn't sacrifice a whole rook, "only" an exchange, because White hasn't got time to capture on h8 and also save the knight.

r3kbnr/Nppb3p/3q2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.name: 10...g6
r3kbnr/Nppb3p/3q2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PP.description: 11. Bxd7+ is necessary to free the b5-square if the knight is ever going to get out of a7.

r3kbnr/NppB3p/3q2p1/7Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/.name: 11. Bxd7
r3kbnr/NppB3p/3q2p1/7Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1PPP/.description: 11...Qxd7 is necessary to avoid losing another pawn to 12.Qb5+. It appears to lose a rook instead by unprotecting e5, but accepting the gift turns out to be fraught with danger.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2Nq4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1P.name: 9. Qh5
r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2Nq4/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1P.description: 9...g6 is the only safe move to block the check, because: 9...Qg6?? 10.Ne5+ wins the queen directly, and 9...Kd7?? 10.Qf7+ and the queen has to be shipped overboard with 10...Qe7, as either 10...Be7 or 10...Ne7 allow the pretty double check 11.Nb8+ followed by mate on e8.

r1b1kbnr/ppp4p/2Nq2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.name: 9...g6
r1b1kbnr/ppp4p/2Nq2p1/1B5Q/2P1p3/8/PP1P1.description: The usual move here is 10. Qe5+, when after the forcing sequence 10...Qxe5 11.Nxe5+ c6 12.Ba4 Bg7 13.d4 exd3 White can simply recapture with 14.Nxd3 and try to untangle her queenside and convert the extra pawn, or alternatively: 14.O-O (to meet ...Bxe5 with Re1 winning the bishop pair) and then 14...Bxe5 15.Re1 is simple enough, but with either 14...Be6 or 14...Bf5 Black can challenge White to the very very long variation: 15.Nxc6 Bd7 16.Re1+ Kf8 17.Nd4! Bxa4 18.Ne6+ Kf7 19.Nxg7 Kxg7 20.b3 Be8 21.Bb2+ Nf6 22.Re7+ Bf7 23.g4 g5 24.f4 gxf4 25.g5 and White has at last won the piece back with, well, approximately a drawn position. 15.Re1 is probably the sane option. 10. Nxa7+ offers to transpose to the 9.Nxa7+ lines, which Black can accept with 10...Bd7 11.Bxd7 Qxd7 12.Qe5+. Since those lines are mostly terrible, Black may be objectively better off with 10...c6, leading to 11.Nxc8 and then either 11...gxh5 12.Nxd6+ Bxd6 or 11...Rxc8 12.Qh3 Ra8, neither of which have been tested by theory.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 7...Qg5
r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: White turns the tables on Black with 8. Qe2, defending the b5-bishop and attacking the e4-pawn. The discovered check isn't as exciting as it looks thanks to the possibility of ...c6 in response. There's nothing to be gained by the panicked retreat 8.Nd4+ c6 9.Bf1, for example.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.name: 8. Qe2
r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2N5/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.description: Black has to defend the e4-pawn, and does so with 8...Nf6, which has the additional benefit of covering h5. 8...Bf5 has a specific tactical problem: 9.f4! is a counter-sacrifice that White wants to play anyway, and with the bishop on f5 the pawn can't be taken: 9...Qxf4?? 10.Rf1 Qg5 11.Rxf5 Qxf5 12.Nd4+ is curtains. Plus, in the current position Black does have a secondary threat of ...a6 and ...Bd7 pinning and winning the c6-knight, which doesn't work if the bishop is away defending e4. Plus, f6 is almost certainly the best square for the knight anyway. Another line that doesn't work is 8...Qxg2. The downside of playing ...f5 in the opening is the need to be vigilant about queen checks on h5. Here 9.Qh5+ g6 (or 9...Qg6 10.Ne5+) 10.Qe5+ punishes Black severely for her pawn-grabbing. 8...Nf6 cuts out this check, turning the illusory threat of ...Qxg2 into a real one.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQP.name: 8...Nf6
r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQP.description: Now Black's attack against g2 is a real one. Defending g2 with moves like 9.0-0 or 9.Rg1 is too slow; Black will have time to execute her secondary threat of ...a6 and ...Bd7. The clever 9. f4 solves this problem by defending g2 with gain of tempo, while threatening to give the knight a beautiful square on e5 to retreat to, at the cost of restoring material equality (9...Qxf4 is the main reply). 9. Ne5+ c6 10.f4 as played by Gyula Sax is just the same moves in a different order. But there is an alternative in the controversial 9. Nxa7+!? as played by Peter Svidler. It has a very positive score for White, but from a very small sample size. If you can't see what a brilliant move 9.Nxa7+ is, it's probably because the Big 9.f4 industry has hired stooges to infiltrate our message boards and talk it down Magnus Carlsen can't see what a brilliant move 9.Nxa7+ is either.

r1b1kb1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.name: 9. Nxa7
r1b1kb1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.description: 9...Bd7 is the main line. Black preserves castling rights and denies the a7-knight the chance of exchanging itself on c8, which would be the coward's way out. It looks as though the move overworks the f6-knight, but in fact there are tactical reasons why grabbing the e4-pawn doesn't lead to any advantage. 9...Kd8 invites 10.Nxc8 and it looks like White has no problems, but Black has a glimmer of hope based on the fact that g2 is still hanging. German correspondence player Peter Leisebein is the main champion of this line. 9...c6? 10.Nxc6! means the c8-bishop will have to go to d7 anyway, but with one fewer Black pawn on the board.

r3kb1r/NppB2pp/5n2/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1.name: 10. Bxd7
r3kb1r/NppB2pp/5n2/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1.description: 10...Nxd7 preserves castling rights for Black. Thanks to the precarious position of the a7-knight, it doesn't matter that it unprotects e4. The alternative 10...Kxd7? would allow the exchange of queens with 11.Qb5+ and the knight is saved.

r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1B1.name: 10...Nxd7
r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP/R1B1.description: 11. f4 is the line adopted by all the top players who have had this variation as White, including Peter Svidler. As in the 9.f4 variation, White is defending g2 horizontally and hitting the Black queen, but now the circumstances are different: without the knight on c6, Black won't be obliged to chop f4 off simply to prevent the knight retreating to e5, and if she prefers to grab the c-pawn instead she can do that with 11...Qc5 (9.f4 Qc5? would have run into 10.d4 when everything is defended). 11. Nb5 allows 11...Qxg2 12.Qf1 Qxf1+ 13.Kxf1 O-O-O or 12.Rf1 O-O-O when Black's greater mobility compensates for the pawn. 11. Qxe4? wins a pawn but loses a piece, because it gives up control of the b5 square that the knight needs to retreat to. 11...Kd8 and now: 12.Qd4 and 12.Qe3 lose to 12...Bc5 12.Qa4 loses to 12...Nb6 12.Qxb7 Rxa7! and the rook is immune because 13.Qxa7 Qg2 picks up the h1-rook (14.Rf1 Bc5 with ...Re8+ to follow makes things even worse). Fun fact: those three moves in descending order of strength offer a pawn, preserve the material balance, and capture a pawn. Collecting pawns in the opening is overrated!

r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ1PP/R1B.name: 11. f4
r3kb1r/Nppn2pp/8/6q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ1PP/R1B.description: Black's queen is attacked by an unprotected pawn. There are two plausible queen moves: 11...Qxf4 accepts the gambited f-pawn, which then allows White to solve most of her problems with the developing move 12.d4 before the a7-knight needs to be extracted to b5. White remains a pawn up and although Black can point to a passed pawn on e4, it's isolated and immobile. 11...Qc5 attempts to imbalance the position a little by grabbing the c2-pawn instead of the f4-pawn, thus isolating White's d-pawn. Sadly, 12.Nb5 Qxc2 13.d4! is still possible, and with 13...Qc6 not sufficing to defend the e-pawn because of 14.d5 (14...Qxd5?? 15.Nc7+) the queens will have to come off and White is a clear pawn up again. Those two lines are Exhibits A and B for the prosecution's case that 9.Nxa7+ busts the whole Classical (7...Qg5) Schliemann Defence. Other moves: 11...Qf5 was tried a bunch of times between 2011 and 2013, with no success whatsoever. White calmly retreats with 12.Nb5 and then has pawn majorities on both sides of the board. 12...O-O-O 13.a4 gets the queenside one rolling. Similarly 11...Qh4+. It's not clear how Black benefits from provoking g3 before retreating the queen to e7. 11...Qa5 was suggested on the ChessPublishing.com message board, but it's completely refuted by Solodovnichenko's 12.Nb5 Bc5 13.b4! Bxb4 14.Rb1 O-O-O 15.Na7+! Qxa7 16.Rxb4 when White's attacking chances are as great as Black's.

r1bk1b1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.name: 9...Kd8
r1bk1b1r/Npp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.description: 10. Nxc8 is the only move to save the knight, since White can't vacate the b5 square with tempo.

r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.name: 10. Nxc8
r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B4q1/4p3/8/PPPPQPPP.description: 10...Qxg2 is a crucial intermezzo, as recapturing the knight will allow White to get the thematic f4 move in.

r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B6/4p3/8/PPPPQPqP/R.name: 10...Qxg2
r1Nk1b1r/1pp3pp/5n2/1B6/4p3/8/PPPPQPqP/R.description: White has tried both ways of defending the rook: 11. Qf1, after which Black can choose between 11...Qf3 and 11...Qxf1 12.Bxf1 Kxc8, and 11. Rf1, after which Black can choose between 11...Qxh2 and 11...Kxc8. If Black doesn't capture the knight while it's on c8, White is going to go Nb6 and ruin Black's queenside pawns. Other than that, the tactics have subsided and Black scores terribly out of the resulting middlegame positions. Even in the line 11.Rf1 Qxh2 12.Nb6 cxb6 where material is level, Black's pawns look silly and White has the bishop pair on a very open board.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ.name: 9. f4
r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B4q1/4pP2/8/PPPPQ.description: 9...Qxf4 is the main line, because why not take a pawn if White's going to leave them lying around. 9...Qh4+ is similar to the main line, in that the Black queen ends up on h3 via h4 in both lines, except without the bonus of having taken a pawn. A pawn is a pawn!

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B6/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.name: 9...Qxf4
r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/2N2n2/1B6/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.description: White now has the simple plan of establishing a knight on e5 guarded by a pawn on d4 (which isn't going to get taken en passant because it'll go there with a discovered attack on the Black queen). The two possible ways of carrying out this plan of Ne5 and d4 are (you guessed it): 10. Ne5+ followed by 11.d4, and 10. d4 followed by 11.Ne5+. The immediate 10.Ne5+ means that the Black queen will definitely go to h4 after 11.d4, whereas 10.d4 gives it the option of retreating to d6 instead. If she declines that option and goes to h4 anyway, the two lines merge into one. White still has the Nxa7+ option. What's different about 10. Nxa7+ compared to 9.Nxa7+? Black no longer has the option of declining the f4-pawn after 9.f4 Qxf4 10.Nxa7+, as she does after 9.Nxa7+ Bd7 10.Bxd7+ Nxd7 11.f4. But Black now has the additional option of 10...Bd7 11.Bxd7+ Kxd7. Recapturing with the king would be a bad idea after 9.Nxa7+ Bd7 10.Bxd7+ because White could trade queens with 11.Qb5+. With f4 and ...Qxf4 inserted, that's not a problem. On balance, those differences are in Black's favour, so if Nxa7+ is going to be played it's best on move 9 rather than 10.

r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.name: 10. Ne5
r1b1kb1r/ppp3pp/5n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1P.description: Black needs to defend against the check while keeping the knight on f6 to deny the White queen access to h5. 10...c6 is a sensible move that leaves two White pieces hanging.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1.name: 10...c6
r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/4pq2/8/PPPPQ1.description: White has two pieces hanging. 11. d4! defends one and gains a free tempo to move the other.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Ppq2/8/PPP1Q.name: 11. d4
r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Ppq2/8/PPP1Q.description: With 11...Qh4+ Black's queen gets off the open f-file and attempts to win a tempo to capture the b5-bishop.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp2q/8/PPP1Q.name: 11...Qh4
r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp2q/8/PPP1Q.description: As the b5-bishop is still hanging, 12. g3 is necessary to deny Black the crucial tempo to capture it.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp3/6Pq/PPP1.name: 12...Qh3
r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/1B2N3/3Pp3/6Pq/PPP1.description: The b5-bishop is finally forced to move, and 13. Bc4 threatens to revoke Black's castling privileges with a check on f7. 13.Nxc6 would be refuted by the same ...a6 and ...Bd7 trick, pinning and winning the knight, that we saw earlier.

r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q.name: 13. Bc4
r1b1kb1r/pp4pp/2p2n2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q.description: 13...Be6 is necessary to deny White access to the f7 square while keeping e4 nailed down. It has the pleasant side-effect of getting another piece off the back rank.

r3kb1r/pp4pp/2p1bn2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q2.name: Ruy Lopez, Classical Schliemann Defence
r3kb1r/pp4pp/2p1bn2/4N3/2BPp3/6Pq/PPP1Q2.description: For the first time since Black played 3...f5, White has no material hanging! So she has a major decision to make about where to develop the last remaining minor piece.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/PP.name: 4. d3
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/4P3/3P1N2/PP.description: The move 4.d3 defended e4 but also threatened to snaffle the f5-pawn into the bargain, because now Black won't have the instant rejoinder ...e4. 4...fxe4 is the only move to justify the Black pawn thrust.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4p3/3P1N2/PPP.name: 4...fxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4p3/3P1N2/PPP.description: With the bishop already developed on b5, there are no clever gambits in this position - 5. dxe4 is played to recover the pawn.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.name: 5. dxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP2P.description: 5...Nf6 is the only move. As well as attacking the e4-pawn, it's a case of making the easy decisions first: the g8-knight is the only Black piece that has an obvious square to go to.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.name: 5...Nf6
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.description: There are a few minor moves here, but if White notices that the e-pawn doesn't need to be directly defended, then 6. O-O makes the most sense, avoiding a potential pin or check after 6... Bb4, which would allow Black to develop the dark squared bishop and play d6 more easily. 6... Nxe4? in response would be a tactical error, allowing 7. Re1 or Qe2 with a strong attack along the e file, as 7... d5 allows 8. Nxe5 with the c6 knight pinned.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.name: 6. O-O
r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.description: Time for Black to develop some more pieces. Spoiler: the pawn currently on d7 isn't going to make it to d5 at this point, because that would leave e5 hanging. So it'll have to go to d6 if the c8-bishop wants to get out. The immediate 6...d6 would shut in the f8-bishop. That's okay, it's got a perfectly good square on e7. 6...Bc5 makes sure that the bishop doesn't get shut in, but becomes a pawn sacrifice after 7. Bxc6 bxc6 8. Nxe5. If ...Bc5 is often a luxury Black can't afford in the Ruy Lopez, surely this applies double in the Schliemann Defence where the Black kingside has already been opened up with ...f5? Black's argument is that firstly, the open f-file is an attacking strength as well as a defensive weakness, and allows Black to fantasize about targeting f2 with ...O-O and ...Nxe4/...Ng4 to go with ...Bc5, so that gives White something to worry about. Secondly, the fact that the d-pawn is gone means that White doesn't have the simple plan of c3 and d4 with gain of time against the bishop. If Black captures on e4 immediately, White has numerous strong options. 7.Nxe5, threatening 8. Qh5+, has to be met with 7...Nxe5, and then 8.Re1 wins the piece straight back with an ongoing attack (8...Nf6? 9.f4!) The immediate 7. Re1 or Qe2 are also strong, as 7... d5 allows 8.Nxe5. Regardless, the e file becomes a huge liability for Black with the king still stuck in the center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.name: 6...d6
r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.description: Now that Black is no longer vulnerable to Nxe5 tricks, the e4-pawn needs to be defended. The economical-looking 7.Re1, normally a very sensible move in the Ruy Lopez, would be dangerous in the Schliemann because it would weaken f2, the target of Black's future pressure along the f-file. 7. Nc3 develops an undeveloped piece to its natural square. Nothing wrong with that! 7. Qd3 is a move that's recommended against 6...Bc5, because after 6...Bc5 7.Qd3 O-O?? White simply wins a piece with 8.Qc4+, so Black is prevented from castling for a while. However, there's currently no bishop on c5 to win, and if White wants to prevent Black from castling after 7.Nc3 she always has Bc4. White may also lose a tempo if Black's light-squared bishop comes to g4 and swaps itself for the f3-knight, because the queen could have recaptured directly from d1. On the positive side, putting the queen rather than the bishop on c4 has the advantage of maintaining the pin on the c6-knight that Black brought upon herself by playing 6...d6. Results-wise there isn't much to choose between the two moves.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.name: 7. Nc3
r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2np1n2/1B2p3/4P3/2N2N2/P.description: Having put the pawn on d6, the only square available for the f8-bishop is e7, so it might as well go there immediately with 7...Be7. The c8-bishop still has options, and the option of breaking the pin on the c6-knight with Bd7 may be particularly useful, so it typically stays put for now. 7...Bg4 is also played, inviting White to transpose to 7.Qd3 lines with 8.Qd3 which gets out of the pin.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/3PP3/5N2/PPP.name: 4. ...fxe4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pp2/3PP3/5N2/PPP.description: If Black takes the e-pawn, White's has two main options. 5. Nxe5 wins the pawn back, but runs into complications after 5. ... Nxe5 6. dxe5 c6. Now if the white bishop retreats, Black has 7... Qa5+ winning the e5 pawn and leaving Black better. (Note that in the Deferred Schliemann, because the white bishop is no longer on b5, c6 no longer comes with tempo, so this line is worse for Black. Thus, 5. d4 is the most common response to the Delayed Schliemann.) Thus, the most common line for white is 7. Nc3?!, a piece sacrifice. Play usually follows 7... cxb5 8. Nxe4 d5 9. exd6 Nf6, with an unclear position. The other option is 5. Bxc6, after which Black enjoys the two bishops in exchange for a worse pawn structure and a white knight on e5 after either recapture on c6. 5... exf3 is less recommended, as after 6. Bxf3 White can quickly castle and place pressure along the e file.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pP2/8/5N2/PPPP1P.name: Jaenisch gambit accepted
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B2pP2/8/5N2/PPPP1P.description: Accepting the "free" pawn is inaccurate, as Black can regain the pawn with extra tempi and space. After 4...e4, White's knight is kicked and is low on squares: g5 and h4 are controlled by Black'[s queen, while Black's knight controls e4 and d5. (The addition of this knight is the key difference between the Jaenisch and Latvian gambits accepted, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 f5?! 2. exf5!) Un-developing the knight to g1 would be a big concession to Black. To make room for the knight to go elsewhere, White has the manoeuvre 5. Qe2, pinning and attacking the e4 pawn, 5...Qe7 un-pins it, 6. Bxc6 with the idea of moving the knight to d4 where it defends the f5-pawn from Black's bishop. 6...dxc6 7. Nd4 =. White may followed with Ne6 in some lines, such as after 7...Qe5. After 6...bxc6 7.Nd4, Black will likely play 7...Nf6, and eventually either Qe5 or c5 and then d5 to try to win the pawn back. 5. Bxc6 dxc6 6. Nd5? ⩱ allows 6...Bxf5 with the threat of ...Qd4. If 6. Qe2 the line can transpose if Black plays 6...Qe7, but better is 6...Bxf5 ⩱.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/5N2/PPPP1.name: 4...e4
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/1B3P2/4p3/5N2/PPPP1.description: = Schliemann Defence Accepted = 5. Ng1 is an interesting move but best to keep a complex position

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.name: Nürnberg variation
r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.description: Black defends their e-pawn with their f-pawn. This is non-standard as it weakens their kingside and prevents the knight coming to f6. It's also unnecessary for Black to defend the e-pawn again: the e5-pawn wasn't hanging because of the tactic Bxc6 dxc6 Nxe5? Qd4!, where Black recovers the material. One idea Black might have is to bait White into playing 4. Bxc6 dxc6 5. Nxe5??. White may suspect they can sacrifice the knight and recover material using the tactic Qh5+. This is the case in the Damiano defence, 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 f6?, where the refutation is 3. Nxe5 fxe5 4. Qh5+. However, it doesn't work out the same here: Black is better after 5...fxe5 6. Qh5+ Kd7! 7. Qxe5 Qf6! (diagram). White doesn't want to trade queens and be down a bishop for two pawns in the endgame. Rather than try to exploit the weakened kingside immediately, White should just develop normally and enjoy the more pleasant position. 4. O-O to get the king to safety, then White threatens to open the centre with d4. One line is 4...a6 5. Bc4 Bc5 6. c3 Nge7 7. d4 b5 8. Bb3 exd4 9. cxd4 Bb6 10. Nc3 ±. White has space and easy development.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2P2N2/.name: Nürnberg Variation, Main Line
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n2p2/1Bb1p3/4P3/2P2N2/.description: In this line, White castles to protect the king and prepares to play d4 to gain more space in the center. Black develops the bishop to c5, which is a natural square for the bishop and also puts pressure on the f2-pawn. White plays c3 to support the d4-pawn advance. The Main Line of the Nürnberg Variation is considered to be better for White, as White has more options and flexibility in the position. White can choose to play d4 immediately or delay it and play Re1, h3, or a4 first. White can also exchange the light-squared bishop on b5 with the knight on c6 at any time, creating a weakness in Black’s pawn structure. Black, on the other hand, has to deal with several problems in the Main Line of the Nürnberg Variation. Black has to find a good square for the knight on g8, which is blocked by the f6-pawn. Black also has to decide whether to castle kingside or queenside, as both sides have their drawbacks. Black’s king is also vulnerable to attacks by White’s pieces, such as Qf3, Qg4 or Qh5. Therefore, the Main Line of the Nürnberg Variation is not very popular among chess players, as Black has to struggle for equality. Most players prefer to play other variations of the Spanish Game, such as the Berlin Defense, the Marshall Attack, or the Open Variation. These variations do not involve the move f6 and give Black more chances for counterplay. 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 f6 4. O-O Bc5 5. c3

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/1B2p1p1/4P3/5N2/PP.name: Brentano gambit
r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/1B2p1p1/4P3/5N2/PP.description: An interesting move where Black threatens ...g4 to push the knight back, and to start a pawn assault if White castles. 4. d4! is the best move. This discovers an attack on g5 with the bishop while attacking the e5 square, the purpose being that now White is threatening 5. Nxg5 to just win the pawn, and if 4...g4? 5. Nxe5 is supported. 4. h3?! is more conservative, preventing ...g4 but is otherwise passive. 4. O-O?! allows 4...g4 5. Ne1 and White's position is far from comfortable.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PP.name: References
r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PP.description: Nunn's Chess Openings. 1999. John Nunn (Editor), Graham Burgess, John Emms, Joe Gallagher. ISBN 1-8574-4221-0. Kasparov, Garry, & Keene, Raymond 1989 Batsford chess openings 2. ISBN 0-8050-3409-9.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.name: The h6 sideline in the Spanish Game
r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/1B2p3/4P3/5N2/PPP.description: The h6 sideline in the Ruy Lopez is a rare and provocative move that aims to prevent White from playing Bg5 and pinning the black knight. It also prepares to play g5 and Bg7, creating a kingside fianchetto. However, it also has some drawbacks, such as: It weakens the g6-square and the dark squares around the black king. It delays the development of the black pieces and the castling of the black king. It allows White to play d4 and gain a strong center. The main line after 3…h6 is 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3, where White has a clear advantage in space and development. Black can try to create counterplay on the queenside with moves like d5, Bc5, O-O, and Rb8, but White can maintain the pressure with moves like O-O, Nc3, e5, and Qf3. Another possible continuation after 3…h6 is 4.O-O g5, where Black goes all-in for a kingside attack. This is very risky and dubious, as White can exploit the weaknesses in Black’s position with moves like d4, Nc3, Nd5, c3, and Be3. For example, after 4.O-O g5 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Bg7 7.Nf5 Bf6 8.Nc3 Nge7 9.Re1 d6 10.Nd5 Nxd5 11.exd5+ Ne5 12.Nd4 O-O 13.Qh5 Bg7 14.h4 Bg4 15.Bg5 Bxh5 16.Bxd8 Raxd8 17.Nf5 Bg6 18.Ne7+ Kh7 19.hxg5 hxg5 20.Re3 Bxd3 21.Rh3+ Bh6 22.cxd3 f5 23.d4 Ng6 24.Nc6 Rde8 25.Ra3 Nf4 26.Rxa7 Rf7 27.Rb7 Nxd5 28.a4 g4 29.a5 f4 30.a6 g3 31.a7 gxf2+ 32.Kxf2 Nb6 33.Rb8 Rff8 34.Rxe8 Rxe8 35.Nb8 Na8 36.Rc1 Re7 37.Nc6 Re8 38.Rc3 Bg7 39.Rb3 Nb6 40.Rxb6 cxb6 41.Nb8 Bxd4+ 42.Kf3 b5 43.Nc6 Bxa7 44.Nxa7 b4 45.Nc6 b3 46.Nd4 Re3+ 47.Kxf4 Rd3 48.Ke4 Rd2 49.Nxb3 Rxb2 50.Nd4 Rxg2 51.Kd5 Rd2 52.Kc4 Rxd4+ 53.Kxd4 Kg6 54.Kd5 Kf5 55.Kxd6 1/2-1/2, White had a clear advantage throughout the game, but failed to convert it into a win. 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 h6!?

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.name: Giuoco Piano
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.description: This is one of the two main branches of the Italian game. Black develops their kingside bishop ahead of the knight: this move order keeps control of g5 until Black is ready to castle. Compared to the Two Knights defence (3...Nf6), where Black develops while making an attack on e4, this is considered the slower and more positional continuation, hence the name which in Italian means "quiet game". White chooses between two sorts of plans: to get their pawn to d4, or to content themselves with d3 (the hallmark move of the giuoco pianissimo, "very quiet game").

r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.name: Jerome gambit
r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP.description: 4. Bxf7+?? is the unhinged Jerome gambit. Though a Bxf7+ sacrifice works in many lines in the Italian, this is far too early and it is objectively woeful for White. However, it is sharp enough that White has some success at the club level. The idea is 4...Kxf7 5. Nxe5+ Nxe5 6. Qh5+, and White hopes that between Black's exposed king and the skewering of Black's pieces on the fifth rank they will swindle compensation. e.g. 6. Qh5+ g6 7. Qxe5 d6?? (better is Qe7∓) 8. Qxh8±. After 4...Kxf7 5. Nxe5+ Nxe5 6. Qh5+ there are several winning approaches for Black. The engine line involves marching their king out to into the middle of the board to guard the bishop: 6...Ke6 7. Qf5+ Kd6 8. f4 Kc6 9. Qxe5 Nf6-+ etc, and despite the weakness of their enemy's king, White's queen alone can't sustain an attack. The simplest approach is to just return the bishop, 6...Ng6 7. Qxc6∓. White has only captured two pawns in exchange for their knight, and the only piece they have developed is their queen. Black can come out swinging.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.name: 4...Kxf7!
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1.description: Black has a clear advantage. White will attempt to mate the black king with a series of checks, but with proper play black will come out ahead. His bishop pair and lead in development make it impossible to find enough compensation.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.name: 5. Nxe5+
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/2n5/2b1N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.description: This move sacrifices another piece, but White will soon get it back with d4 or Qh5+. They will have gotten a second pawn for the piece, but would have lost the bishop pair and their own king would not be able to get out of the center. Therefore, the compensation is not nearly enough and Black is close to winning. Do not sacrifice unless you see reason. Here, White didn't have enough development to attack the king successfully.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: Nxe5
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: This is the obvious response. It seems that black has won 2 pieces, but white will regain one. He will then be a piece down for two pawns with no compensation, however. Since Black has many replies after 6.d4, all of which retain a winning position, the most popular move is 6.Qh5+.

r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 6.Qh5+
r1bq2nr/pppp1kpp/8/2b1n2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: After this, Black has various good replies. 6...g6 and 6...Kf8 are enough to win, but the greedy and probably best 6...Ke6!? shows the unsoundness of White's attack. He simply is not developed enough despite the centralized Black king. He will just be down a piece for a pawn. Lines to avoid are: 6... Kf6?? 7.Qf5+ followed by Qxe5+ and Qxc5 with 2 extra pawns for White, or 6... Ke7?? 7.Qxe5+ with Qxc5 coming next, once again with two extra pawns for White.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.name: 4. O-O
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.description: White chooses a quiet path, that tends to transpose to the Giuoco Pianissimo after white plays 5. d3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/5N2/P.name: = 5.d4 =
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/5N2/P.description: The Deutz (pronounced Doy-ts) Gambit, pioneered by German chess masters Max Lange and George Koltanowski, is an aggressive line by White in the Italian Game, Giuoco Piano. White has a safe king and wants to strike the center of the board with d4, open up many options for their dark-squared bishop (in similar fashion to the Scotch Gambit), and start attacking the black king sooner than later, even at the cost of a pawn. Black is forced to take the pawn on d4 with the bishop, knight, or pawn. Because 5. d4 is a move that Black expects the least due to seemingly hanging a key center pawn three different ways, the Deutz is a dangerous gambit that requires Black to know theory to be able to fight it. The three captures are: 5…Bxd4! This is the strongest variation for black, but not common unless Black knows the theory, since Black is voluntarily giving up a strong bishop for a knight. After the exchange 6. Nxd4 Nxd4, white can play either the Max Lange line of 7. Bg5 or the Johann Deutz line of 7. f4. The 7. Bg5 line pins the f6 knight and prepares 7. f4, leading to tactical attacking chess for White; however, with accurate play, Black can force the queens off the board, leading to an equal endgame. The 7. f4 line is another aggressive tactical option for White which threatens the sole pawn that is holding the center of the board together for Black and is designed to preserve the queens for longer. Black must hold onto this pawn with 7…d6, since they will find themselves well behind if they go with any other option. White still has a very dangerous attack. 5…Nxd4? This move immediately gifts White an advantage and the initiative. White will respond with 6. Nxe5. Notice the pressure white is putting on the f7 square. This is the weakest square for black early in the game because the king is the only piece protecting it. Now white has both the knight and bishop in striking distance of the weakened square. Black might try to play it safe and castle, but that loses to 7. Be3. White has the bishop and queen attacking the knight and black will end up losing a minor piece. If instead black tries 6…Qe7, white can punish black with 7. Bxf7. The f7 square is still under attack from the knight and black is forced to move the king and damage their setup. 5…exd4 After the pawn takes on d4, this transposes into the Max Lange Attack. White will push the center pawn with 6. e5, which is a common idea in Scotch Gambit positions. This is one of the hardest attacks for black to defend against. If black moves the knight back to g8, they lose too many tempe. If they bring it to “safety” with Ng4, black ends up losing after Bxf7, Kxf7, Ng5+, Kg8, Qxg4. Black can also try to block the center of the board with 6…d5, but white is better of with the exchanges after 7. exf6 dxc4 8. fxg7. When contributing to this Wikibook, please follow the conventions for organization.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/5N2/PPP.name: = 6. e5 =
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/5N2/PPP.description: The Max Lange Attack can arise from several different opening lines, including the Two Knights Defense, Petroff's Defense, Scotch Gambit, Bishop's Opening, Center Game, and Giuoco Piano. Two of the most commonly seen move orders are 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 (the Two Knights Defense) 4.d4 exd4 5.0-0 Bc5 6.e5, and 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4 (the Scotch Gambit) Bc5 5.0-0 Nf6 6.e5. After 6.e5, Black has two main replies. Black's 6...Ng4 is playable, but rarely seen. More common is 6...d5, when the main line continues 7.exf6 dxc4 8.Re1+ Be6 9.Ng5 Qd5 (9...Qxf6?? 10.Nxe6 fxe6 11.Qh5+ followed by 12.Qxc5 is a notorious trap) 10.Nc3 Qf5 (10...dxc3?? 11.Qxd5 wins, since 11...Bxd5 is illegal) 11.Nce4 0-0-0 with complex play. Another line for White to try, a critical response, is after 6...d5, White plays 7.Bb5 with strong ideas for both sides, usually resulting in a slight edge for White. An alternative for White is 8.fxg7 Rg8 9.Bg5, analysed by Lev Gutman and Stefan Bücker in Kaissiber, which they consider to be good for White. Black's usual response is 9...Be7 10.Bxe7 Kxe7. When contributing to this Wikibook, please follow the conventions for organization.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/1PB1P3/5N2/P.name: Evans gambit
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/1PB1P3/5N2/P.description: White offers a pawn to divert the bishop away from the centre. White would like to play d4 and put both d and e pawns in the centre. At the moment, Black has too much control over the d4 square for that to be worthwhile. White can prepare d4 with c3, as in 4. c3, the classical variation. However, this gives Black extra time to develop and get ready to castle. The idea of 4. b4 is to achieve c3 and d4 with tempo instead. If Black accepts the pawn, 4...Bxb4, 5. c3 prepares d4 while also forcing Black's bishop to move again. c3 also gives White's queen access to b3. 5...Ba5 (5...Bc5? and the bishop can be kicked again) 6. d4 and the main reply is 6...d6. 6...exd4 appears to be winning because the c-pawn is pinned to the king, White doesn't have to take back immediately and can unpin first. 7. Qb3 (battery against f7) Qe7 8. O-O (unpins) Bb6 9. cxd4 Nxd4 10. Nxd4 Bxd4=, and though Black is up two pawns, White is thought to have compensation. 6. O-O before playing d4, known as the slow variation, avoids the c3 pawn becoming pinned and was popular in the Romantic era. 4...Bb6 declines the gambit and White switches plans to expanding on the queen's side. 5. a4 a6 (to prevent the bishop becoming trapped) 6. Nc3 is the Showalter variation.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/1bB1P3/2P2N2/P.name: = Rare retreats =
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/1bB1P3/2P2N2/P.description: 5...Bf8?! is the Mayet defence. This undevelops the bishop, and is the worst move of the five, as in order to castle kingside, Black must move it again in addition to the g8-knight. White almost always play 6. d4 in order to punish this move, in which he has gained a comfortable advantage. 5...Bc5?! is the McDonnell Defence. This is usually only played by beginners, thinking this move stops the d4 push, but it actually doesn't, and white can then play 6. d4 which also gains a tempo on the bishop. 5...Bd6!? is the Stone-Ware Defence. Although this blocks the d-pawn, it also adds a defender to the e5-pawn, so when 6. d4 happens, it won't come with an attack on the pawn.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.name: 5...Ba5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.description: 5...Ba5 is the main retreat after the Evans Gambit 5. c3, and it is considered the best attempt to "refute the gambit." However, it is not as safe as the retreat 5...Be7. Now, the most aggressive move for White is to play 6. d4, when Black has four options: 6...exd4 6...d6 6...Nf6 6...b5

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.name: 6. d4
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.description: White takes the whole center, attacking the pawn on e5 aggressively. Black can choose from four options: 6...exd4 is usually played. 6...d6 is the most solid move. 6...b5 is interesting. 6...Nf6 is a mistake.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.name: 6...Nf6?
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.description: Black counterattacks the e4 pawn with their knight, but this is not good. White should play 7. dxe5 to exploit Black's mistake and set a trap.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3P3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.name: 7. dxe5!
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/b3P3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.description: White exploits Black's mistake by taking the free pawn on e5. This also sets a trap. The most commonly played move is 7...Nxe4, but that loses the knight to 8. Qd5!. Black should play 7...Ng4 instead, but Black's position is still inferior.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P3/2B1P1n1/2P2N2/.name: 7...Ng4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P3/2B1P1n1/2P2N2/.description: Black correctly avoided losing their knight with 7...Nxe4??, but their position is still inferior. White should strike with 8. Bg5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N.name: 8. Bg5
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N.description: White attacks Black's queen. The only good way to block the attack without losing material is 8...f6. Although 8...Ne7? does not lose material, it unnecessarily cramps Black's position.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2p2/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2.name: 8...f6
r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2p2/b3P1B1/2B1P1n1/2P2.description: Black blocks the attack on their queen. White should now capture the pawn with 9. exf6.

r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2P2/b5B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N2.name: 9. exf6
r1bqk2r/pppp2pp/2n2P2/b5B1/2B1P1n1/2P2N2.description: White takes the pawn on f6. As 9...Nxf6? loses the knight after 10. e5!, Black should play 9...gxf6.

r1bqk2r/pppp3p/2n2p2/b7/2B1P1nB/2P2N2/P4.name: 10. Bh4
r1bqk2r/pppp3p/2n2p2/b7/2B1P1nB/2P2N2/P4.description: White retreats their g5 bishop to h4. White is simply better as Black's kingside pawn structure is ruined and Black's king is weak while material is equal. This is why 6...Nf6? is a mistake.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b2QP3/2B1n3/2P2N2/P.name: 8. Qd5!
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/b2QP3/2B1n3/2P2N2/P.description: White will win Black's knight on e4 as both it and mate on f7 is threatened (for example 8...Nxc3?? 9. Qxf7#). After Black plays 8...O-O or 8...Qe7, White will take the knight on e4.

r1bqk1nr/p1pp1ppp/2n5/bp2p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.name: 6...b5?!
r1bqk1nr/p1pp1ppp/2n5/bp2p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/.description: An interesting gambit, Black sacrifices their b7 pawn to White's bishop on c4. The idea is that after 7. Bxb5, Black can play 7...Nxd4 where White's c3 pawn is pinned to the king, and unlike 6...Nxd4?, Nxe5 wouldn't be possible as the bishop on b5 is also attacked.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.name: 6...d6
r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.description: A solid move, defending the e5 pawn with their d7 pawn. White usually plays 7. O-O or 7. Qb3. 7. Bg5 is a sideline.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p1B1/2BPP3/2P2N2.name: 7. Bg5?!
r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/b3p1B1/2BPP3/2P2N2.description: An interesting sideline, White develops their c1 bishop and attacks Black's queen on d8. Black can choose from 7...Nge7, 7...Qd7, 7...f6 or 7...Nf6.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.name: 5...Bc5
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.description: Black retreats their bishop to c5. This move is usually played by beginners, who believe this stops d4 when it does not. White should play 6. d4, gaining tempo on the bishop and contesting Black's center.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2nb4/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.name: 5...Bd6
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2nb4/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P.description: Black retreats their bishop to d6, defending the e5 pawn so d4 doesn't come with an attack on the pawn, but at the cost of blocking the d7 pawn. White usually plays 6. d4 taking the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppppbppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.name: 5...Be7
r1bqk1nr/ppppbppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.description: Black retreats their bishop to the safest square. White usually plays 6. d4, taking the full center and attacking Black's pawn on e5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.name: 5...Bf8?!
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/P2.description: Black retreats the bishop on f8. This is not good as it undevelops the bishop. White should play 6. d4, taking the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/2bpp3/1PB1P3/5N2/P1.name: = 4...d5 =
r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2n5/2bpp3/1PB1P3/5N2/P1.description: This very fun counterattacking option against the Evans Gambit is called the Hein Countergambit. Here black attacks both the Bc4 and the pawn e4. White has a couple of moves: 5. exd5 5. bxc5 5. Bxd5 5. c3!? 5. Bb3!? 5.exd5 removes the attacker of the c4 bishop, and counterattacks the knight. Black has two pieces hanging in the middle of the board - however, black can escape with 5...Nxb4, saving the knight and remove the attacker of the C5 bishop. 5. bxc5 opts for a bishop trade, but after the trade, the c4 and C5 pawns are both double and weak, and can be attacked easily. 5. Bxd5 captures a pawn - however black can also capture a pawn like with 5...Bxb4 and material is even. 5. c3!? is a dubious choice against the Hein Countergambit as it doesn't deal with most threats, however it defends the pawn B4 that could have been captured by the Bc5. 5. Bb3!? is another dubious choice against the Hein Countergambit that retreats the bishop to a safe square but it leaves a pawn hanging, but material is eventually equal (5...Bxb4 6. exd5 (6...Qxd5?? is not possible due to 7. Bxd5) or 5...dxe4 6. bxc5 exf3 7. Qxf3). 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.b4 d5

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.name: 4. c3
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.description: White reinforces the d4 square, and prepares d4 in order to establish two pawns in the centre. It also stops any Nd4 by black, in the future. White also prepares b4 to try and trap the Black bishop. White's secondary aim is to bring the queen to b3, thus intensifying the pressure on Black's f7-pawn. A drawback to this move is that the pawn occupies a square that should be reserved for the queen's knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.name: 4... Nf6
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.description: The most common reply. It attacks the pawn on e4, develops the knight, and allows black to castle later on.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/2P2N2.name: 5. d4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2BPP3/2P2N2.description: White attacks the center with 5. d4, attempting to create a strong pawn center with the d4 and e4 pawns. Black has to respond with exd4, or else surrender the entire center to White.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.name: 5...exd4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.description: Black takes the d4 pawn with the e5 pawn. White will respond by either pushing the e4 pawn forward to e5 attacking the Black knight, or recapturing the pawn with 6. cxd4, or by playing 6. b4!?.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/1PBpP3/2P2N2/.name: 6. b4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/1PBpP3/2P2N2/.description: White sacrifices the d4 pawn for quick development and an open d file. White also attacks the Black bishop on c5, forcing it to move. Black can play either 6...Bb6 or 6...Be7. In contrast to the Evans gambit, White doesn't sacrifice the b pawn. Because of this White has the threat of b5, forcing the knight to move to a5 or e7. The Dubov gambit is named after the Russian GM Daniil Dubov, who used it to great success against Russian GM Sergey Karjakin in 2020 at the Russian Championship in Moscow. Before GM Daniil Dubov popularised 6. b4, it was used very rarely in high level chess except for a 9 year old Dutch NM that used it to defeat Anish Giri in 2009 and Levon Aronian in 2008 but lost to GM Gukesh in 2009. Recently, the Dubov gambit has been used in online games by very strong players including GM Hikaru Nakamura, former world chess champion Ding Liren and GM Daniil Dubov himself.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P.name: 6...Bb6
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P.description: Black retreats his bishop to b6. White cannot recapture the d4 pawn without hanging the b4 pawn. White can continue with 7. e5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/4P3/1PBp4/2P2N2/.name: 7. e5
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/4P3/1PBp4/2P2N2/.description: = The Egan Variation = 7. e5 White attacks the f6 knight and forces either d5 or Ne4.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P4.name: 6...Be7
r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n2n2/8/1PBpP3/2P2N2/P4.description: Black retreats the bishop to e7. This retreat is generally considered safer, as it blocks any checks on the e file and controls the g5 square. Black will give back the d pawn and try to achieve d5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BPP3/5N2/PP3.name: 6. cxd4
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BPP3/5N2/PP3.description: White plays the natural recapture. Now the bishop will have to move to b4 or b6; in most cases, Black plays 6...Bb4+.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.name: 6...Bb4+
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.description: The bishop must move, and it did. This is actually the only not losing move. White has a couple options here. 7. Bd2 is a natural blocking move. Black can either trade and break the center with 8...d5, or immediately take with 7...Nxe4 which leads to complicated variations and the sacrifice of 8. Bxf7+! 7. Nc3 is a main line that sacrifices the e4 pawn. This is the Greco Gambit, where White then castles and gambits the pawn for development. 7. Nbd2 also exists. It was once very rare but has recently increased in popularity. 7. Kf1, also known as the Cracow Variation, is not usually played, as White can no longer castle and hangs the e4 pawn. For the pawn, White gains initiative and attacks Black who has to find only moves to keep advantage.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.name: Cracow Variation
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.description: This is a weird-looking move that seemingly doesn't make any sense. White can no longer castle and the e4 pawn is undefended. But the compensation exists. White has got a massive center while Black has none, and White are more prepared to attack than Black. The Cracow Variation a tricky opening, Black has to find the only moves to not to get a bad position. Black has several options: 7...Nxe4. Black has grabbed an actually free pawn. White can strike in the center with 8. d5!, kicking the knight back. After 8...Ne7 White has 9. Qd4, grabbing even more space, or a tricky 9. Bb3 with a threat of 10. Qd4 which is somewhy often unseen. 7...d5!. This is the strongest for Black option. After 8. exd5 Nxd5 9. Nc3 Black has to be careful to not to take the knight with their own knight. There is no reason to trade off a central knight. None. Instead, they should take the knight with the bishop, like in the Greco Gambit. 7...O-O?. After 8. d5! Black has giant problems with space and activity. In case of 8...Ne7 or 8...Nb8 White will go 9. e5!, completely paralysing Black, in case of 8. Na5 there is 9. Bd3 with an unstoppable 10. a3 and 11. b4. 7...d6??. This is a blunder. After 8. d5! Ne7 or 8...Na5 there is 9. Qa4+, winning the bishop on b4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/PP.name: Greco’s Gambit
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/PP.description: This is the traditional way to block the bishop check. With 7. Nc3, white does sacrifice the e4 pawn, but aims to get a dangerous initiative

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.name: Greco’s Gambit
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.description: Black accepts the gambit pawn, otherwise she will allow White to maintain a massive center. White follows her plan with 8. O-O

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.name: Greco’s Gambit
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.description: White castles her king. This unpins her knight to her king, causing the black knight on e4 to be hanging. Due to the open e-file creating complications should black retreat her knight, black generally exchanges on c3. While …Nxc3 is appealing to keep the bishop pair, it enters the rabbit hole. Therefore, Black should play …Bxc3, where after exchanging, there is no hanging piece, giving her time to play …d5

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/3P1N2.name: 4... Nf6
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/3P1N2.description: With 4... Nf6, Black develops the king's knight to a good square where it pressures e4, controls the d5 square, and prepares to castle kingside.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1pp2/2B1P3/3P1N2/.name: Lucchini Gambit
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1pp2/2B1P3/3P1N2/.description: With 4...f5!?, Black unleashes the Lucchini Gambit—an aggressive response to the Giuoco Pianissimo that breaks the symmetry and transforms a quiet line into a tactical battlefield. Named after Italian player Marco Lucchini, this gambit challenges White’s center and seeks rapid development at the cost of material. After 5. exf5 d5, Black aims to blow open the center while White is still underdeveloped. If 6. Bb5 Ne7!, Black keeps the kingside flexible while preparing Bxf5 or even queenside castling in sharper lines. Even if White declines the pawn with 5. Nc3 or 5. O-O, Black can still build strong initiative with Nf6, d6, and Qe7. Even sharper is 5. Ng5!?, where the game can explode into tactics. In these lines, Black may sacrifice pieces for open lines and an all-out assault, echoing ideas from the King's Gambit and the Traxler Counterattack. Though not fully sound, the Lucchini is dangerous and practical—especially against opponents who expect a slow positional game and instead find themselves fighting off a storm.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1ppN1/2B1P3/3P4/P.name: Lucchini Gambit
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1ppN1/2B1P3/3P4/P.description: White chooses the aggressive 5. Ng5, eyeing an early attack on f7. This sharpens the game considerably and signals a tactical battle. Black must now decide how to respond to the dual threats of Nf7, forking the queen and rook, as well as Qh5+. If White is able to bring their queen, knight and bishop towards Black's weakened kingside, they'll be in trouble. However, Black has 5...f4!, cutting off White's dark-squared bishop and threatening Qxg5, effectively inviting White to attack their f7 square.

r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1p1N1/2B1Pp2/3P4/.name: Lucchini Gambit: Dubois Variation
r1bqk1nr/pppp2pp/2n5/2b1p1N1/2B1Pp2/3P4/.description: Black plays 5...f4!, the critical move of the Dubois Variation (named after Serafino Dubois, an 1850s Italian master). Here Black threatens Qxg5. Most often, White will continue to fork Black's queen and rook with 6. Nf7. Otherwise, they will force Black's king to move with 6. Bf7+?, a mistake. White's strongest move here is actually h4! to reinforce their knight and stop Black's queen from moving outwards.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p1N1/4Pp2/3P4/P.name: Lucchini Gambit: Dubois Variation
r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bpp/2n5/2b1p1N1/4Pp2/3P4/P.description: After Black calmly sidesteps with 6...Kf8, White’s knight on g5 comes under immediate threat from ...h6, and there’s no safe retreat. For example, 7. h4 h6 8. Bxg8 hxg5 leaves Black with open lines on the kingside and a dangerous initiative down the h-file. Thus, 6. h4 or 6. Nf7 are much better options for White.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.name: = 4.d4 =
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.description: White sacrifices the d-pawn in order to open lines for their pieces and develop faster. The gambit is considered unsound but it's not bad. Black has 3 ways to capture the pawn: 4…exd4 transposes into Haxo Gambit (1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Bc4 Bc5). 4…Nxd4 is playable but allows White to play 5. Nxe5 with pressure on f7, or the venomous 5. b4. But, if Black knows what's he doing, this move is surprisingly strong. 4…Bxd4 is the calmest line and probably the strongest one. Play tends to continue 5. Nxd4 Nxd4 6. Be3 Nc6.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BbP3/5N2/PPP2.name: 4...Bxd4
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BbP3/5N2/PPP2.description: This capture is the best way for Black to proceed without entering the Haxo Gambit. White has nothing better to do than 5. Nxd4 to open lines for their pieces.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPP2PP.name: 5. Nxd4
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPP2PP.description: White captures the bishop to open up the d1-h4 diagonal for their queen. Black usually responds with 5...Nxd4 but 5...exd4 is a sound alternative.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPP2.name: = 4...Nxd4 =
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPP2.description: Even though this move looks very bad, because White can go 5. Nxe5 and it's unclear how to save the f7 pawn and the rook on h8, that's not like that. Yes, after 5. Nxe5 the f7 pawn would be captured in any variant, but black can go 5... Qe7! From now, there are a couple of ways the game can continue: 6. Nxf7!? - the most logical move. It doesn't just capture the pawn, but also trapped the rook in the corner. But this move is awkward because of 6... Qxe4 and after 7. Kf1 Qxc2 the rook will be regained, or a deadly 6... d5! move. 6. Bxf7+! - the best move in this position. Here Black must go 6... Kf8! Now the move 7. Bxg8 is forced because the knight on e5 is attacked. After 7... Kxg8, the knight has to go somewhere, and after 8... Qxe4 black has a better position. Another option would be to go 5. Be3, avoiding all the stuff with 5. Nxe5. This is the most solid and best by the computer move.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1N3/2BnP3/8/PPP2PP.name: = 5. Nxe5 =
r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1N3/2BnP3/8/PPP2PP.description: White has taken the undefended e5 pawn and now threatning to take a pawn on f7 which cannot be protected by any Black's piece.

r1b1k1nr/ppppqppp/8/2b1N3/2BnP3/8/PPP2PP.name: = 5... Qe7 =
r1b1k1nr/ppppqppp/8/2b1N3/2BnP3/8/PPP2PP.description: Black removed their queen from a potential fork on f7, attacked the knight on e5 and the e4 pawn behind it.

r1b1k1nr/ppppqBpp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: = 6. Bxf7+! =
r1b1k1nr/ppppqBpp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: White didn't take the f7 pawn with the knight but took with the bishop, and they did a right choice. Here the best and the most popular move for Black is 6...Kf8.

r1b2knr/ppppqBpp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: = 6... Kf8 =
r1b2knr/ppppqBpp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: Black has moved their king from check. White has the only move 7. Bxg8! because all the other move would lead to either a knight on e5 or a bishop on f7 hanging.

r1b2kBr/ppppq1pp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: = 7. Bxg8 =
r1b2kBr/ppppq1pp/8/2b1N3/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: This is the only move for White to save both the bishop on f7 and the knight on e5.

r1b1k1nr/ppppqNpp/8/2b5/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: = 6. Nxf7?! =
r1b1k1nr/ppppqNpp/8/2b5/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: Taking the pawn on f7 with the knight wasn't the best move for White in that position. It would be better to take this pawn with the bishop. From now, there are 2 main lines: 6... Qxe4. Black has just took a hanging pawn. White has the only move 7. Kf1 and after 7... Qxc2 Black in any variation will be a pawn up. 6... d5!. By computer this move is worse than 6... Qxe4, but for White it would be extremely hard to deal with this move. Yes, after 7. Bxd5 Nf6! black sacrifices their rook and 2 pawns, but the compensation will be Black's wild activity against no White's activity.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1Npp/8/2b5/2Bnq3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: = 6... Qxe4+ =
r1b1k1nr/pppp1Npp/8/2b5/2Bnq3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: Black had just took an e4 pawn with the check to White's king. The only not losing move for White here is 7. Kf1.

r1b1k1nr/pppp1Npp/8/2b5/2Bn4/8/PPq2PPP/R.name: = 7... Qxc2 =
r1b1k1nr/pppp1Npp/8/2b5/2Bn4/8/PPq2PPP/R.description: Black captured the c2 pawn, attacked the bishop on c4 and offered a queen trade. And White have to accept the trade because otherwise black will go 8... Ne7 and save their rook on h8 or capture the bishop on c4.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: 6... d5!
r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: At this moment Black has already sacrificed a pawn and now sacrifices the other pawn and the rook on h8. Here White have only one move to not to lose on spot: 7. Bxd5. Taking the rook isn't the best option as after 7... Qxe4 8. Kf1 dxc4 black has an awesome position because of the trapped knight on h8 and amazing piece activity. The main ideas for Black in this gambit is to open the e file by capturing the e4 pawn (if Black manages to do it, especially if White didn't castle, no matter of material, Black is victorious) and try to develop as fast as possible and open as much files as possible while attacking opponent's pieces.

r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: 7. Bxd5
r1b1k1nr/ppp1qNpp/8/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: White has captured the d5 pawn with their bishop and didn't let Black take the knight on f7.

r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: 7... Nf6!
r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: This is the only move for Black in this position. From now, white has 2 main options: 8. Nxh8??. This move looks natural because White had captured the rook that can be saved the next move, but this move is losing. Here Black can go 8... Bg4!. From now there is quite a lot of variations. 8. Bg5!. This move is much better. Now the knight on f6 cannot capture the bishop on d5 because it's pinned to the queen. But Black has a paradoxal move in this position: 8... 0-0! and after 9. Ne5+ Be6 there are also quite a lot of variations and all of them cannot be described in one article.

r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.name: 8. Bg5!
r1b1k2r/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.description: This is the best move for White in this position. Now Black are unable to take the bishop on d5 because the knight on f6 is pinned to the queen. But here Black can carelessly castle.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.name: 8... O-O!
r1b2rk1/ppp1qNpp/5n2/2bB2B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.description: Despite the fact that the knight from f7 can retreat with check, it hasn't any dangerous for Black squares to go to.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.name: 9... Be6
r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.description: Black has covered a check with their bishop. From this position there is a couple of variations: 10. Bxe6+??. This move is the most obvious one and the blunder. After a natural 10... Qxe6 move White don't have any way of defending both the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4. 10. Bxb7?. The fun fact is that after 10... Rb8 the bishop on b7 is dead. Trying to escape the attack by 11. Ba6? move is bad because of 11... Bd5! and black is victorious again because of the same reason as after 10. Bxe6+ move. 10. c3!. Black will go 10... Nc6 and after the only 11. Ng4! move, after a series of trades Black will end up in a more pleasant position.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4Bn2/2b1N1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.name: 10. Bxe6??
r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4Bn2/2b1N1B1/3nP3/8/PPP2P.description: How tasty this bishop isn't seem, this move is a big blunder. The fact is after Black taking the bishop with their queen White doesn't have any way of defending both the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/2P5/PP3.name: 10. c3!
r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/4bn2/2bBN1B1/3nP3/2P5/PP3.description: This is the only not losing move for White. The knight now has to retreat to c6. White can't take this knight because of the move 10... Bf2+! and the bishop can't be captured because of 11... Nxd5+.

r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/2n1bn2/2bBN1B1/4P3/2P5/PP.name: 10... Nc6
r4rk1/ppp1q1pp/2n1bn2/2bBN1B1/4P3/2P5/PP.description: The knight escaped an attack to it. Here White has the only not losing move 11. Ng4!, and after 11... Bxd5 12. Nxf6+ gxf6 13. Qxd5+ Kh8 14. Be3 Bxe3 15. fxe3 Ne5 Black ends up in a better position. Black's plan is there to create a massive pressure on g file.

r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: 8. Nxh8??
r1b1k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: Look at activities of each side. Black already has both knights, a queen and a dark-squared bishop developed, and the light-squared one is ready to join the party. White has only the light-squared bishop developed since they wasted a ton of tempos by capturing material (and also deactivated their knight). Black can go 8...Bg4!, bringing a new piece to the attack. From now, there are a couple of variations: 9. Qd3 - the most natural move. After that White can go 9... Nxd5, and after 10. 0-0 Nb4 11. Qd2 Nbxc2 Black will regain the lost rook with a bonus. 9. Bf7+. White realises that after 9. Qd3 the bishop on d5 will be captured and removes his bishop with check. Here Black has the only move 9... Kf8!. Now White has to go 10. Qd3 but after 10... Be2! 11. Qh3 Qxe4 Black is winning. If White instead of 10. Qd3 decide to go 10. f3??, Black can go 10... Nxe4! with a totally won position. 9. f3?. Here Black can just simply go 9... Nxd5, and if White takes the bishop on g4, after 10... Qxe4 White will lose.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/8/PPP2PPP.name: 8... Bg4!
r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/8/PPP2PPP.description: Black has attacked White's queen. 9. f3?? isn't the best move for White in this position as Black can safely take the bishop on d5. The bishop on g4 can't be captured because after 10. fxg4?? Black will go 10... Qxe4! with a forced checkmate. 9. Qd3! is a much better option. But after that the bishop on d5 will be captured. So Black often chooses 9. Bf7! to remove their bishop from the danger with check. Black has to go 9... Kf8! and after 10. Qd3 Be2 11. Qh3 Qxe4 (or 11. Qg3 Nxe4) Black has got an overwhelming position.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP3/3Q4/PPP1bPPP.name: 10. Be2
r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP3/3Q4/PPP1bPPP.description: Black has attacked White's queen. If the queen goes to h3, Black would take the e4 pawn with their queen, if White's queen goes to e2, the e4 pawn would be captured by a knight.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3PP.name: 10. f3??
r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/5n2/2b5/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3PP.description: This move looks logical: it saved White's queen, attacked the bishop on g4 and defended the e4 pawn, but Black loses because of the shocking 10... Nxe4!. The knight obviously cannot be captured, but if White captures the bishop, after 11... Ng3+ White will lose.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/5P2/PPP3PP/R.name: 10... Nxe4!
r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/5P2/PPP3PP/R.description: Black bravely sacrifices the bishop on g4 for the e file to be opened. Accepting the sacrifice would be a fatal error because of the move 11... Ng3+! with a forced mate in 6. It's much better to go 11. Be3! and after the same 11... Ng3 either the bishop on e3 or the rook on h1 will be captured the next move.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/4BP2/PPP3PP/.name: 11. Be3!
r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1b1/4BP2/PPP3PP/.description: The best attempt for Black to hold the position. But a simple move 11... Ng3 makes Black's victory inevitable. The knight obviously cannot be captured as after 12... Qxe3+ 13. Kf1 Nxf3+! Black aren't able to defend from the checkmate on f2. If White try to defend their bishop with the move 12. Qd2, Black wouldn't take the rook on h1 but instead go 12... Nxf3+! 13. gxf3 Bxe3 White are forced to sacrifice their queen as there are no other good moves against 14... Bf4+. 12. Qd3 is another defending option, but after 12... Nxc2+! the knight cannot be captured because the bishop on e3 will be captured. After 13. Kf2 Black will go 13... Nxe3! Kxg3 Bf5 White is lost, after 13. Kd2 Bf5 White is lost as well.

r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1P1/8/PPP3PP/RNB.name: 11. fxg4??
r4k1N/ppp1qBpp/8/2b5/3nn1P1/8/PPP3PP/RNB.description: After this move Black's victory is inevitable after the move 11... Ng3+! 12. Kf2 is a worse option as after 12... Ndf5+! White has to sacrifice a queen and the bishop and get checkmated on e3 with the queen. 12. Kd2 is a better option, but it doesn't save the game. Here Black out of nowhere goes 12... Nb3+!!, and after 13. cxb3 (13. axb3 leads to 13... Qe3#) Black is the whole 12 points of material down, but after 13... Rd8+ 14. Kc3 Bb4+ 15. Kc2 Qe4+ 16. Qd3 Qxd3# White loses.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/3Q4/PPP2PPP.name: 9... Nxd5
r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/3Q4/PPP2PPP.description: Black has just captured an undefended bishop on d5. Black's ideas of either 10... Nb4 and 11..Nbxc2 or 10... Be2 and 11... Qxe4 are unstoppable. If White goes 10. Nc3, Black will trade off the knights and then go 11... 0-0-0!.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3P.name: 9. f3?
r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/5n2/2bB4/3nP1b1/5P2/PPP3P.description: This move looks logical: it saved White's queen from being attacked and also threatened the attacking piece. But here Black can simply take the bishop on d5 as the bishop on g4 is innocent (if the e4 pawn dies, White's king will do the same).

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/2P2P2/PP4PP.name: 10. c3?
r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/3nP1b1/2P2P2/PP4PP.description: This is the most tempting move for White: kicking a very active Black piece and unleashing the attack on the knight on d5 if the d4 knight runs away. But instead of moving away Black goes 10... Nxf3!! and after that White is likely to end the game being 13 material points up but with the king on a5.

r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/4P1b1/2P2n2/PP4PP/.name: 10... Nxf3!
r3k2N/ppp1q1pp/8/2bn4/4P1b1/2P2n2/PP4PP/.description: From here White is busted. Taking the knight with the queen would result in losing the queen, if the knight is taken by the pawn, after 11... Qh4! White's king will do a long race and get checkmated on a5 while White would be up 13 points of material.

r1b1k1nN/ppp1q1pp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: 7. Nxh8??
r1b1k1nN/ppp1q1pp/8/2bp4/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: One move earlier Black declined a pawn advantage in the sake of getting a giant piece activity, but in this position Black already takes the pawn on e4. Now a few things can happen: 8. Kf1 leads to 8... dxc4 and 9... Qxc2, so this isn't the best option, even with the fact of this move being suggested by a computer. 8. Be2 is a more popular and intuitive move, but after 8... Bg4 9. f3 Bxf3!! 10. gxf3 Nxf3+ 11. Kf1 Nd2+ 12. Ke1 Nxb1 13. Rxb1 Qxh1+ 14. Kd2 Qxh2 Black is victorious. 8. Be3?? is a very bad option because after 8... Nxc2+ 9. Kd2 Bxe3+ 10. fxe3 dxc4 either a rook on a1 or a rook on h1 will be captured.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPPP1P.name: Blackburne shilling gambit
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPPP1P.description: Black violates an opening principle by moving his knight again. Black hopes to tempt White into taking the unprotected e5 pawn. 4. Nxe5?? falls into Black's trap. After 4...Qg5, forking White's knight the g2 pawn, White is in dire trouble. If White attempts to save the knight, (5. Nxf7?? Qxg2) then White has to give up the rook instead. If they try to hold onto their rook, then they must give up their queen or get mated. (6. Rf1 Qxe4+ 7. Qe2 (7. Be2? Nf3#) 7...Nxe2-+) 5. Bxf7+⩱ is the only way to stay in the game. The gambit is a one-trick pony: as long as White avoids 4. Nxe5??, they are comfortably ahead. For this reason, Black is supposed to exclaim, "Oh my God!" to sell the illusion that they have blundered a pawn. Black's knight is misplaced and they are falling behind in development, so White has a lot of good options. White can simply decline the gambit with 4. O-O or kick Black's knight with 4. c3 (both of these usually induce 4...Nxf3 5. Qxf3). The most critical line is 4. Nxd4. 4. Nxd4 exd4 trades knights and dislodges Black's pawn from e5. This opens up a number of tactical opportunities for White. After 4...exd4, White has an idea of playing e5 themself, e.g. 4...exd4 5. O-O Nf6 6. Re1 Bc5? 7. e5! Ng8 (only safe square for the knight). Another idea is that Qh5 can attack f7 while forking anything on the fifth rank, e.g. 4...exd4 5. O-O Bc5? 6. Bxf7+ Kxf7 7. Qh5+ Ke7 8. Qxc5+ d6 9. Qxd4 nets White two pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 4. Nxd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BNP3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: Instead of accepting the gambitted pawn, white declines it and instead trades the knights in the center.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 4. Nxe5?
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N3/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: This move looks natural, but it is a bad move as there is a strong double attack. It turns out that Black's pawn on e5 wasn't free. After 4...Qg5!, both e5 and g2 are attacked by the queen. White is in a lot of trouble and has to give up a knight to have a playable game with either 5. Bxf7+ or 5. O-O, both with a better position for Black.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.name: 4...Qg5!
r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.description: Accepting the gambit was a mistake, as Black now shows with the accurate 4...Qg5. Attempting to hold on to the knight with 5. Nxf7?? will result in 5...Qxg2!, in which White will lose either the rook, attempt to hold on to the rook and lose the queen with 6. Rf1 Qxe4+, or get checkmated by attempting to keep both the rook and the queen with 7. Be2 Nf3#. Better for White is 5. Bxf7+, which loses a piece for two pawns but keeps White in the game. 5. O-O is another possible option. White castles and defends g2 while giving away the e5 knight to try and get development as compensation for the lost knight.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 5. Nxf7??
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: Here 5. Nxf7?? is a blunder. White would be better off losing their knight for two pawns with 5. Bxf7+, but Nxf7 loses a major piece or the game to 5...Qxg2.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.name: 5...Qxg2!
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.description: Qxg2 is the accurate followup and the dream of Blackburne Shilling Gambit players. White has to give away a major piece to stop checkmate.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.name: 6. Rf1
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2BnP3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.description: Rf1 seems like a defense to the gambit, but Black can play 6...Qxe4+ and White must sacrifice their queen or allow checkmate. Better was 6. Ng5, which gives away the rook but moves the knight to safety and protects the e4-pawn. After 6...Qxh1+ White can play 7. Bf1.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2Bnq3/8/PPPP1P1P/R.name: 6...Qxe4+
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2Bnq3/8/PPPP1P1P/R.description: White is completely lost. Black plays 6...Qxe4+, which allows for two options. The worse of the two options doesn't seem the worst, but 7. Be2? allows the smothered mate (7...Nf3#) where the bishop is pinned. Therefore White must give away the queen with 7. Qe2 and play on without that queen.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/3nq3/8/PPPPBP1P/RN.name: 7. Be2?
r1b1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/3nq3/8/PPPPBP1P/RN.description: The worst of the two legal moves, but White was losing anyway. Black can immediately win the game with 7...Nf3#.

r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.name: 5. O-O
r1b1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4N1q1/2BnP3/8/PPPP1P.description: White resists the temptation to take the 'free' pawn on f7 but instead calmly castles, sacrificing their e5 knight while defending g2 and relocating their king to safety. 5...Qxe5 is obviously the best move. Black captures the free knight and is now up 2 points of material, but they are only slightly better as White will get developmental compensation after 6. c3 followed by 7. d4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.name: Two knights defence
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.description: With 3...Nf6, Black develops a knight and attacks the e4-pawn, getting one step closer to castling. White has several ways to proceed from this position: defend the e-pawn, usually with 4. d3, attack f7 with the aggressive 4. Ng5 (taking advantage of the fact that Black's move 3...Nf6 blocked the queen's control of the g5-square), or sacrifice the pawn for an open centre and swift attack.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/.name: Italian variation
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/.description: White combines the typical Italian game bishop placement, Bc4, with the four knights game. This position arises most commonly in amateur games, from either the four knights or Italian games. White seems to have made reasonable developing moves and is ready to castle. Their bishop on c4 targets f7 and White is ready to castle. However, Black has a tactical trick (4...Nxe4!) which has made masters shun away from this position. 4...Nxe4! is the strongest move. The apparent knight sacrifice is only temporary. After 5. Nxe4, Black plays 5...d5!, forking White's knight and bishop. This is known as the "centre fork trick" and occurs in several lines where White has a bishop on c4 or Black has one on c5. The best continuation is 6. Bd3 dxe4 7. Bxe4: White regains the lost material, but is at a space disadvantage. Black has equalised: "a good Fork Trick has the same approximate value as getting the White pieces." If Black wants to accept a normal game, there is nothing particularly wrong with a natural developing move like 4...Bc5, but 4...Nxe4! is the best move in the position, and White is then fighting for equality.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.name: 4. Ng5!?
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PP.description: 4. Ng5!? is a sideline but the most common amateur move. This Romantic move is an attack on f7 with the bishop and knight, taking advantage of the fact that Black gave up control of g5 and cannot castle yet. However, it is unprincipled to attack before having finished development and Black equalises with best play. Black needs to defend f7: otherwise, as in the common beginner blunder, 4...h6?? 5. Nxf7 Qe7 6. Nxh8, Black gets the house. If Black thinks to counter-attack instead, 4...Nxe4?, the Ponziani-Steinitz gambit, fails to 5. Bxf7+! Ke7 6. d4. 4...d5 is the best way to defend f7. This sacrifices a pawn to 5. exd5. Then there have been several moves tried: 5...Na5, the Polerio defence, is the most serious continuation and main line today. Black counterattacks the bishop, and the line continues 6. Bb5+ c6 7. dxc6 bxc6 8. Bd3 Nd5 9. Nf3 Bd6 10. O-O. White may be ahead a pawn, but Black is considered equal with more active pieces; 5...b5!?, the Ulvestad variation, to drive the bishop on c4 to somewhere less useful; 5...Nd4!?, the Fritz variation, gets the knight out from under the gun; 5...Nxd5?! is more common in amateur games, allowing 6. Nxf7, the audacious knight sacrifice known as the fried liver attack, or 6. d4, the Lolli attack. 4...Bc5? is the venomous but objectively dubious Traxler counterattack. Black can answer 5. Nxf7? Bxf2+! 6. Kxf2 Nxe4+=, but instead 5. Bxf7+ is a free pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/8/P.name: = 4...Bc5 =
r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/2B1P3/8/P.description: The move that signifies the Traxler Counterattack, sometimes known as the Wilkes-Barre Variation. This can quickly lead to mate with the queen. This bold move ignores White's attack on f7 and can lead to wild play as Black can try a bishop sacrifice on f2 if White plays Nxf7. Instead, White will often prefer Bxf7+.

r1bqk2r/pppp1Bpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPP.name: = 5. Bxf7+ =
r1bqk2r/pppp1Bpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPP.description: The preferred move for most modern masters, preferring to capture the pawn and keep the position comparatively calm. This move is considered the best way to maintain an edge.

r1bq3r/ppppkBpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.name: = 5... Ke7 =
r1bq3r/ppppkBpp/2n2n2/2b1p1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.description: The king has only two squares, and as Kf8 blocks in the rook, Ke7 is usually played.

r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.name: = 6.Bd5 =
r1bq3r/ppppk1pp/2n2n2/2bBp1N1/4P3/8/PPPP.description: Bd5 is often given an exclamation mark by theory books. This precise move gives rise to the possibility of a future Bxc6 and overprotects the e4-pawn.

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2p5/2b1p1N1/4P1n1/3P4/P.name: Theory table
r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2p5/2b1p1N1/4P1n1/3P4/P.description: . 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5. Bxf7+ Ke7 6. Bd5 Rf8 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. d3 Ng4

r1bq1r2/ppp1k1pp/2p5/2b1p3/4P1n1/3P3N/PP.name: Theory table
