r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: 5...Be7?
r1bqk1nr/pppnbppp/3p4/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: The position after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 Nd7 4. Bc4 exd4 5. Nxd4 is a critical juncture for Black. The seemingly natural move 5...Be7? is a blunder, and 5...Ngf6 is a safer and superior alternative. White can exploit the blunder with 6. Bxf7+!, intending to win the Black's queen with 7. Ne6 and 8. Nxd8+. The move Bxf7+ is beneficial for several reasons: It sets up the Ne6 threat, prevents the defense of e6 with fxe6, and captures the black pawn on f7. The white knight on d4 can move to e6 to capture the black queen on d8. The white knight threatens the black queen on d8. White utilizes the a2-g8 diagonal to capture the black pawn on f7. Additionally, White can consider playing Qd5, while Black can play g6 and use the 8th rank to control the square d8 with the rook on h8.

r1bqk1nr/pppnbBpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 6.Bxf7+!!
r1bqk1nr/pppnbBpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: This move is a crushing sacrifice. Black loses his queen whether he accepts it or declines it.

r1bq1knr/pppnbBpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 6...Kf8
r1bq1knr/pppnbBpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: This move declines the sacrifice, but actually makes white's winning combination easier. The simple Ne6+ forks the king and queen.

r1bq2nr/pppnbkpp/3pN3/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: 7...Kxf7
r1bq2nr/pppnbkpp/3pN3/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: This move captures the bishop, but drops the queen with check. Unfortunately, it is his only legal move.

r1bN2nr/pppnbkpp/3p4/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.name: 8.Nxd8+
r1bN2nr/pppnbkpp/3p4/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.description: This simple move wins the queen with check. Black is down a decisive amount of material.

r1bq2nr/pppnbkpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: 6...Kxf7
r1bq2nr/pppnbkpp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: This move accepts the sacrifice. White needs to find another brilliant move to win.

r1bq2nr/pppnb1pp/3pk3/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: 7.Kxe6
r1bq2nr/pppnb1pp/3pk3/8/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: This move avoids losing the queen, but gets mated. Better was 7...Ngf6, though the game was lost in any case.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.name: 4...Ngf6
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PP.description: Black develops a knight and controls d5, but this natural move loses a pawn. White can capture 5. dxe5 and Black can't recover it and hold onto it. 5...dxe5 allows 6. Ng5! and Black has to give up at least a piece to prevent Bxf7 Ke7 Ne7!, trapping the queen. Black has to give up at least a piece to prevent it (6...Bb4+ 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4), or accept two pieces for their queen (e.g. 6...Bb4+ 7. c3 Bc5 8. Bxf7+ Ke7 9. Ne6 Kxf7 10. Nxd8+ Rxd8). 5...Nxe5 is better, but allows White to seize the f7 pawn and trade queens (5...Nxe5 6. Nxe5 dxe5 7. Bxf7+ and e.g. 7...Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8).

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.name: 5. dxe5
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/3p1n2/4P3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.description: The critical move. White opens the centre and attacks Black's knight on f6. The pawn must be retaken.: Simply moving the knight loses more material to exd6 and/or Bxf7+, e.g. 5...Ng4? 6. Bxf7+ Kxf7 7. Ng5+ Ke8 8. Ne6 (forking Q and B)+-. Black may think White's e-pawn is hanging and that 5...Nxe4?? kills two birds with one stone. However, 6. Qd5! threatens Qxf7# while forking the knight on e4. 6...Qe7 7. Qxe4+-. These leaves Black with two ways to take the pawn on e5. 5...dxe5?? is a mistake because White can launch a winning attack f7. 6. Ng5! and White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 and Black's queen is trapped. 6...Nb6 is the best attempt. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8+- White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4. 5...Nxe5 is Black's best move. It recaptures the pawn and attacks White's bishop, so White isn't in time to play 6. Ng5. However, after 6. Nxe5 dxe5 White is able to win at least a pawn tactically.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4n3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.name: 5...Nxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4n3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.description: By recapturing the pawn with the knight, Black prevents 6. Ng5: this is because Black's knight is gaining time on White's bishop. 6...Bb3? concedes the initiative and gives Black time to develop. After 7. Bg4= pinning the knight, White still cannot play Ng5. Therefore White must trade knights, 6. Nxe5 dxe5. This is to White's advantage as they will be able to leverage the open d-file to win a pawn (7. Bxf7+).

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/2B1P3/8/PPP2P.name: 6. Nxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4N3/2B1P3/8/PPP2P.description: White trades knights. After Black recaptures 6...dxe5, the d-file will open and White has a tactical way of exploiting that to win a pawn.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.name: 6...dxe5
r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/8/PPP2PPP.description: Black recaptures on e5. There are two tactical features that stand out for White in this position: the queens see each other, and White's bishop is threatening Bxf7+. It might seem that these moves could be played in either order to win a pawn, however 7. Qxd8+? Kxd8 8. Bxf7 allows Black to play 8...Nxe4 and recover the material. The better order is 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8 and White is in time to play 9. Nc3 or 9. f3 to defend e4. Despite appearances, 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 is not a mistake due to deflection, as after 8. Qxd8 Black has 8...Bb4+ discovering an attack on d8 and guaranteeing they recover the queen.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2Bpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 7. Bxf7+
r1bqkb1r/ppp2Bpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: White takes a pawn with check. This leads to a queen trade. If 7...Ke7, to avoid the check while keeping contact with the queen, 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8. The queens have been traded and White is up a pawn. If 7...Kxf7 8. Qxd8, for a moment White may think they have driven away the defender of Black's queen, but Black has 8...Bb4+ (discovered attack on White's queen) 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn.

r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 7...Kxf7
r1bq1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: Black takes the bishop. This moves the king away from defence of the queen: Black can tactically win it back, but only by giving back the bishop too, and White will be up a pawn. 8. Qxd8 discharges the tension between the queens. Black can take back via 8...Bb4+, discovering an attack on White's queen. White can defend the check and remove the queen at the same time: 9. Qd2 Bxd2 10. Nxd2. The queens and bishops are traded and White is still up a pawn. If White avoids the queen trade, they are down a bishop for only a pawn.

r1bQ1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 8. Qxd8
r1bQ1b1r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: White takes the queen. Black can recover the material, but only by giving back the bishop. 8...Bb4+ discovers an attack on White's queen. A move like 9. c3? blocks the check but doesn't deal with ...Rxd8. Fortunately for White they can play Qd2, allowing Black to recover the queen but only if they return the bishop.

r1bQ3r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.name: 8...Bb4+
r1bQ3r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPP2PPP/R.description: Black discovers an attack on White's queen with check. If White blocks the check with 9. Nc3??, 9. Nd2??, or by moving their king, they lose their queen back to ...Rxd8 and are down a bishop. If 9. c3? to block the check while counter-attacking the bishop, then after ...Rxd8 cxb4 Nxe4! White has recovered the bishop but Black regains the pawn. The material and position is equal. The best move is 9. Qd2: interposing the check, counter-attacking Black's bishop while also avoiding ...Rxd8. After 9...Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 (defends the e-pawn), the queens and bishops are effectively traded and White remains up a pawn. good.

r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPPQ1PPP/R.name: 9. Qd2
r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/1b2P3/8/PPPQ1PPP/R.description: White interposes the check while counter-attacking Black's bishop. 9...Bxd2+, recovering the queen, is the only good move of course. After 9...Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 (defends the e-pawn), the queens and bishops have been traded and White remains up a pawn.

r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPPb1PPP/RNB.name: 9...Bxd2+
r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPPb1PPP/RNB.description: Black regains the lost queen with check. Black is also threatening ...Nxe4. 10. Nxd2 is the only recapture that also prevents that, and White remains up a pawn for good.

r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPPN1PPP/R1B.name: 10. Nxd2
r1b4r/ppp2kpp/5n2/4p3/4P3/8/PPPN1PPP/R1B.description: White recaptures the bishop and defends e4. White is up a pawn in the endgame and should win with best play. Black's isolated e5 pawn remains a weakness.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.name: 5...dxe5??
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP2.description: This seems to recover the pawn but loses tactically because the pressure White exerts on f7. 6. Ng5! launches a winning attack. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 trapping Black's queen. 6...Nb6 is the best attempt at defence. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8+- White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PPP2.name: 6. Ng5
r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/5n2/4p1N1/2B1P3/8/PPP2.description: Black cannot guard f7. White threatens Bxf7+ Ke7 Ne6 and Black's queen is trapped. 6...Nb6 is the best attempt. 7. Bxf7+ Ke7 8. Qxd8+ Kxd8+- White is up a pawn in an endgame. Bb3 and Nf7+ forking the king, rook and pawn is threatened. 6...Bb4+ at least allows Black to castle if they give up the bishop. 7. c3 O-O 8. cxb4.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.name: Nimzowitsch variation
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2.description: 3...Nf6 is the Nimzowitsch variation of the Philidor defence. Black leaves their e-pawn undefended to counterattack White's e-pawn instead. White's approaches are to either trade pawns or leave the central tension for now while they continue development.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.name: Exchange variation
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/.description: Black takes on d4, defusing the central tension. This is the main continuation. White now recaptures, usually with the knight 4. Nxd4. Recapturing with the queen 4. Qxd4 is playable but allows Black to develop Nc6 with tempo. Then, having resolved the issue of e5, Black must concentrate on developing their pieces, lest they fall too far behind White. This typically means Black plays ...Be7, ...Nf6, and castles short. Alternatives to dealing with the f8 bishop―...g7 to fianchetto (the Larsen variation) or ...d5 exd5 Qxd5 (the Paulsen attack)―have been tried but are probably too slow.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.name: Morphy Gambit
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.description: White declines to immediately recapture on d4, instead playing Bc4 and offering the pawn for rapid development and pressure on f7. This gambit, famously used by Paul Morphy to defeat the strong English player Thomas Wilson Barnes, exemplifies classical principles of rapid piece activity and initiative over material. By inviting 4...Nf6 and responding with Ng5, White can generate swift threats before Black finishes development. If Black tries to hold the pawn with 4...c5 or 4...Nc6, they risk falling into a cramped and vulnerable position. The safest course for Black is often to return the pawn and prioritize development with 4...Be7 and short castling. While not a mainline weapon at the highest level, the Morphy Gambit is a sharp and historically rich choice that can punish slow or passive responses.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: 4. Nxd4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3NP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: White recaptures the pawn with the knight. 4...Nf6 is the main move, attacking the e4 pawn, and is answered with 5. Nc3 to defend it. To bring more pressure to it, Black must bring the rook to e8, which requires the manoeuvre ...Be7, ...O-O, ...Re8 and ...Bf8. Both sides develop their pieces: Black usually avoids playing ...Nc6 until after they have played ...c5 (with tempo on White's knight) to avoid blocking it in. ...c5 weakens the d6 pawn so committing to it too early can be a mistake, e.g. 4...Nf6 5. Nc3 c5? 6. Bb5+ Bd7 (prevents Q from seeing d6) 7. Nf5 Nc6 8. Nxd6+ Bxd6 9. Qxd6±.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.name: 3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.description: White is threatening the fearsome Qh5+, which, supported by the knight on e5, can't be successfully defended by ...g6. There's also the incidental threat of exf5. So that's the Latvian gambit refuted then? Most top players would say "yes". But there is a particularly optimistic breed of chess player that looks at the pawns on f5 and e4 and thinks that if the knight could just be driven away from e5, it's Black who will be capturing a pawn (fxe4), and possibly even defending it with ...d5. And so the move 3...Qf6 was invented. Yes, it's not usual to move the queen so early, but then again, following up a wild lunge like 2...f5 with solid-looking moves is a recipe for disaster. 3...Nf6!?, which controls the h5 square, may also be tried. White can offer back the pawn with 4. Bc4, not least because 4...Nxe4?? gives up control of the h5 again. To prevent Bf7+, driving the king to e7, Black may try 5. d5 exd5 Bd6 6. d4 O-O 7. O-O Nbd7± or 5. Qe7 to give the king luft on d8. 3...Nc6? is the Fraser variation: "You're threatening to win the exchange? Coward! I shall FORCE you to win the exchange!" Black encourages 4. Qh5+, intending to gain time on White's queen to leverage into an (unsound) attack. Unfortunately for Black the moves to defuse the attack are pretty natural. 4. Qh5+ g6 5. Nxg6 Nf6 (attacks Queen, defends h7) 6. Qh4 Rg8 7. Nxf8 Rg4 8. Qh3 Rxe4+ 9. Be2 Qe7 10. Nc3 Rxe2+ 11. Nxe2 Nd4 12. Qd3 Nxe2 13. Qxe2 Qxe2+ 14. Kxe2 Kxf8+-, White is up more than an exchange in the endgame.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 3...Qf6
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/4Np2/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: Black's queen has come lumbering out to poke the e5-knight in the ribs. Should White hold the line, or retreat? 4. d4 is the (old) main line. It temporarily establishes a classical pawn centre (d4 & e4) allowing easy development of the remaining White pieces. If Black now wants to shift the knight from e5, they will have to play ...d6, shutting in the f8-bishop. 4. Nc4 is the Foltys-Leonhardt variation, recommended by Grandmaster Tony Kosten and now considered a more critical test of the Latvian than d4. White knows they can't prevent ...fxe4, so reserves the option of confronting that pawn with a d2-d3 advance when it arrives on e4. Other knight retreats, 4. Nf3? or 4. Nd3?, allow 4...fxe4 with an attack on the knight, giving Black time to follow up with ...d5 to great advantage.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2N1P3/8/PPPP1PP.name: 4. Nc4
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/5p2/2N1P3/8/PPPP1PP.description: Black remains a pawn down, but White's knight has run off, so Black may now dream of playing …d5 in one move. That pawn on e4 will have to be cleared out of the way first, with 4...fxe4. (If Black delays, White will play exf5 and retain the extra pawn.)

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: 4...fxe4
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: Black threatens to play ...d5 with beautiful development and only a slightly misplaced queen to worry about. But 5. Nc3 covers d5 and gains further time by hitting the e4-pawn. Rarely do such delicate works as Black's encounter such a robust spanner as 5. Nc3.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.name: 5. Nc3
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/5q2/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PP.description: White's c3-knight is threatening to capture on e4 hitting the queen on f6, and taking advantage of this diversion to retreat safely to c3. Were the queen not on f6, Black could turn the tables after Nxe4 with ...d5! picking up a knight. So the queen must move again. In the old days of the Leonhardt Variation, 5...Qg6 was the move, defending e4 and pressuring g2. The modern preference is 5...Qf7, renewing the threat of ...d5.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.name: 5...Qf7
rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/2N1p3/2N5/PPPP1PPP.description: Black is planning ...d5 again. Now comes perhaps the only "unnatural" move with which a White player facing the Latvian must be familiar: 6. Ne3. There's no other way to defend against ...d5.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1PPP.name: 6. Ne3
rnb1kbnr/pppp1qpp/8/8/4p3/2N1N3/PPPP1PPP.description: White has seemingly thwarted ...d5 yet again, and is now asking the Black army how they're going to save Private Ryan on e4. There are two options for Black: abandon e4 and make another non-developing move with 6...c6 to finally establish an iron grip over d5, or continue the charge with 6...d5, the Atars Gambit, accepting the loss of the d-pawn and saddling White with only the minor inconvenience of having to come and capture it. It should be pointed out here that, in fact, the suicidal-looking 6...d5 is one of Black's last remaining attempts to revive the Latvian Gambit. If it doesn't work, the swashbuckling old opening will likely be tucked away on a shelf with a label "suitable only for unprepared opponents".

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1P.name: Mayet attack
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP1P.description: White declines Black's gambit and instead develops a bishop, preparing Nxe5 with a threat on f7. 3...fxe4 is Black's best and main move, otherwise why would Black have bothered with attacking White's e4 pawn? However Black has a few alternatives to consider: 3...Nf6?, the Morgado Defence, is the most common amateur move. It is usually played by people who are used to the Latvian gambit accepted. 3...Nc6 transposes into the Rousseau gambit of the Italian game. 3...b5!? is the rare and dubious Strautins gambit, which triest to distract the White bishop from the a2-f7 diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2B1p3/5N2/PPPP1PP.name: 3...fxe4
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/2B1p3/5N2/PPPP1PP.description: White's only move that makes sense is 4. Nxe5 to regain the pawn lost with fxe4 and attack f7, threatening Nf7 forking the queen on d8 and rook on h8.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: 4. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: Now White takes Black's pawn and threatens Nf7, which would fork Black's queen on d8 and rook on h8. Black can choose to defend this threat, ignore the threat or set a trap. 4...d5, the Polerio-Svedenborg variation, directly defends against the Nf7 threat by blocking the bishop on c4's vision of f7 and attacking it. This is the most common move by far. 4...Qg5!? sets a trap. It seems to blunder the fork 5. Nf7?!, but after 5...Qxg2! 6. Rf1 Bg4! Black has an attack where White has to be precise. 4...Nf6?, the Corkscrew countergambit, is just too much. After 5. Nf7 Qe7 6. Nxh8, Black plays the Corkscrew Gambit with 6...d5 and hopes for 7. Bb3?? Bg4!, but if 7. Be2! is played the gambit is proven unsound and Black is down a rook.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.name: 4...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/4N3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.description: = Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack, Corkscrew Countergambit = This gambit is utterly unsound but venomous if White doesn't know the refutation. It invites 5. Nf7 forking the queen on d8 and rook on h8, but Black will try to create an attack after 5...Qe7 6. Nxh8 d5, the Corkscrew Gambit. Black hopes for 7. Bb3? Bg4!, where White has to sacrifice a queen with 8. O-O Bxd1, or face an overwhelming attack with 8. f3 exf3+ 9. Kf2 Ne4+. However, if 7. Be2! is played instead, Black will find it hard to prove sufficient compensation for the sacrificed rook. 5. Bf7+ is another good move, where after 5...Ke7 6. Bb3 Black has an awkward king on e7 that cannot castle and hinders development of the bishop on f8, without getting into the complications of Nf7.

rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N1q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.name: 4...Qg5
rnb1kbnr/pppp2pp/8/4N1q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.description: = Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack = Black ignores the threat of Nf7 and instead counterattacks White's g2 pawn and e5 knight. 5. Nf7?! seems to win material; it forks the queen on g5 and the rook on h8, but leads to complications after 5...Qxg2! 6. Rf1 d5! where Black is starting an attack and White has to be careful not to be checkmated early. 5. d4! is the true test of Qg5. It gives up a pawn on g2, but when 5...Qxg2, named the Poisoned Pawn Variation, chaos will ensue after 6. Qh5+! g6 7. Bf7+!, where White may want to sacrifice material (probably a rook on h1 and a bishop on c1!) for an attack.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 5. Nf7
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/6q1/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: = Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack = White believes they are winning material, forking the queen on g5 and rook on h8, but Black has other ideas. Black will now play 5...Qxg2!, taking a pawn and attacking the rook on h1. White has to be careful not to get checkmated early.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.name: 5...Qxg2
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.description: = Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack = Black turns the tables on White by taking the pawn on g2 and attacking the rook on h1. White will definitely want to save the rook, so 6. Rf1 is the only move (6. Ke2?? Qf3+! forces the White king back to the first rank where the queen on d1 no longer see the rook).

rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.name: 6. Rf1
rnb1kbnr/pppp1Npp/8/8/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PqP/R.description: = Latvian Gambit: Mayet Attack = White moves their rook to safety. Black will now start an attack with 6...d5!. White will have to navigate safely. 6...Nf6 and 6...Nc6 are also playable but are risky. Any other move and the attack runs out of fuel.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: Polerio-Svedenborg variation
rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN3/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: The best and most common move. Black now is attacking White's bishop on c4 and preventing Nf7. But 4. Nxe5 carried a second threat: 5. Qh5+!. However, if Black finds 5...g6!? to sacrifice the exchange after 6. Nxg6 hxg6 7. Qxh8 Kf7!, the position is objectively equal. It's true that White can save the bishop with 5. Bb5+ or 5. Be2 (5. Bb3?? loses to 5...Qg5!), but it lacks the aggression and force of Qh5+, so 5. Qh5+ is more preferred.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 5. Qh5
rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: White brings their queen out and checks Black's king. 5...Ke7?? would lose to a forced mate in 9 after 6. Qf7+, so Black has to find the surprising 5...g6!?, sacrificing the exchange after 6. Nxg6 hxg6 7. Qxh8, but after 7...Kf7! White's queen is trapped in the corner and White's bishop on c4 is still attacked.

rnbqkbnr/ppp4p/6p1/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.name: 5...g6
rnbqkbnr/ppp4p/6p1/3pN2Q/2B1p3/8/PPPP1PP.description: Black blocks the check with their g-pawn. Now White has two pieces hanging: the bishop on c4 and the queen on h5, so retreating the queen would lose the bishop. White's best and most common move is 6. Nxg6, where Black can choose between the sound exchange sacrifice, 6...hxg6 7. Qxh8 Kf7!, or the unsound (but playable!) queen attack, 6...Nf6, usually played by amateurs. White can play 6. Bb5+, but gives Black the extra tempo of 6...c6 before 7. Nxg6, and so doesn't make as much sense to play.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.name: Damiano defence
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.description: Seeing the threat of Nf3, Black imagines they can protect their e pawn with 2...f6?. Unfortunately, f6's protection is only that: imaginary. 3. Nxe5 snaps off the pawn and opens up White's queen. Then if 3...fxe5? the typical refutation is 4. Qh5+! g6 5. Qxe5+ forking the king and Black's rook on h8. Black can set a trap with 3...Qe7, hoping that White only half-remembers the refutation and proceeds 4. Qh5+? anyway, but this time 4...g6 and White has nowhere to go. (5. Nxg6 Qxe4+ 6. Be2 Qxg6 and Black is up a knight for a pawn.) Instead White should simply retreat the knight and give back the pawn, and be happy with their development lead. 4. Nf3 Qxe4 5. Be2±

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: 3. Nxe5
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: 3. Nxe5 is the critical move that refutes the Damiano defence. White realised that f6 couldn't defend the e5 pawn because of the weakness of Black's kingside. If 3...fxe5? then 4. Qh5+! exploits the open e8-to-h5 diagonal. Then if 4...g6 5. Qxe5+ forks the king and Black's rook on h8. After 5...Qe7 6. Qxh8 (6. Qxe7? and White only has two pawns for the knight) Qxe4+ 7. Kd1, Black has a knight and a pawn for the rook and two pawns they lost. 4...Ke7 does not fare better: 5. Qxe5+ Kf7 6. Bc4+ d5 7. Bxd5+ Kg6 and White has three pawns for their knight, their bishop developed, and Black's king on the run. The Chess Wikibook Sample Game follows the 3...fxe5 4. Qh5+ Ke7 line. Therefore, Black can't afford to take the knight. Instead 3...Qe7 is their best try. 4. Nf3 Qxe4+ 5. Be2 and Black has at least recovered the pawn, but White has a big development lead. The other goal of 3...Qe7 is to bait 4. Qh5+? from an unsuspecting White player, as here 4. Qh5+ is a mistake because after 4...g6 the queen can't take on e5. 5. Nxg6 Qxe4+ 6. Be2 Qxg6 and Black is up a knight for a pawn.

rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 3...Qe7
rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/4N3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP.description: Black realises they cannot afford to take back with the f-pawn, and plays ...Qe7, skewering the knight and e4 pawn instead. This lays a trap for an unsuspecting White player. The usual move, after 3...fxe5, is 4. Qh5+. If White only half remembers the refutation and plays 4. Qh5+? in this position then after 4...g6! White's queen and the knight are hanging. 5. Nxg6 Qxe4+ 6. Be2 Qxg6∓. 4. Nf3 is White's best move. This returns the pawn but White gets a big lead in development, and Black's pawn on f6 is permanently misplaced. 4...Qxe4+ 5. Be2 d5 6. Nc3 (kicking queen)±.

rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.name: 4. Nf3
rnb1kbnr/ppppq1pp/5p2/8/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PPP.description: White retreats the knight to the safer square, where Black will play 4... Qxe4+, regaining the pawn with tempo. However, after 5. Be2, White is up in development and Black's queen is misplaced and will be kicked via 6. Nc3. Also, the pawn on f6 is permanently misplaced, and the development of the g8-knight is hindered.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.name: 3...fxe5?
rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/RN.description: Black is up material, at least for a while. 4. Qh5+ forks the king and the e5 pawn. After 4...g6 5. Qxe5+ wins Black's rook. 4...Ke7 5. Qxe5+ Kf7 is no better. One continuation is 6. Bc4+ d5 (6...Kg6?? blunders mate in 11) 7. Bxd5+ Kg6 and White has three pawns for their knight, their bishop developed, and Black's king on the run.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1pp1/7p/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.name: Truck Defense
rnbqkbnr/pppp1pp1/7p/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1PP.description: The Truck Defense involves giving up the central pawn on e5, allowing the white knight to occupy the square. This defense is very rarely played and considered an offbeat opening. It is not commonly seen in high-level tournaments, but can be used to surprise your opponent, especially in casual play.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/7N/PPPP1PPP/.name: 2. Nh3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/7N/PPPP1PPP/.description: = The Basman Attack = The Basman Attack is an unusual chess opening named after the English International Master Michael John Basman who played the strange 2. Nh3 in a game versus John T Fletcher in 2013. The Basman Attack is offbeat, but slightly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the Ruy Lopez or the Sicilian Defense: Najdorf Variation. White intends to play f2-f4 soon. The Basman Attack incurs multiple problems for White. First, it develops a piece towards the outer edge of the board. The problem with developing your knight to h3 instead of f3 is that on h3 it doesn't control the pivotal central squares of e5 and d4. On h3, the only square the knight can move to that it couldn't move to if it was on f3 is f4. The other problem with this opening is that it loses initiative. In e4 e5 openings, White typically controls the opening. Moves like Nf3 put immediate pressure on the opponent, forcing them to defend. The move Nh3 puts none of that pressure and therefore is an almost pointless move. It is relatively easy for Black to equalise in this opening, for example, 2...Nf6, 2...d5, and 2...Nc6 all equalise, although Black should be careful to avoid an eventual f2-f4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5Q2/PPPP1PPP.name: 2. Qf3?!
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/5Q2/PPPP1PPP.description: The Napoleon Attack, or Napoleon Opening, is weaker than it sounds. Not only does it develop the queen too early, but it blocks the King's Knight from developing to f3, its best square. As with the similar 2. Qh5, White hopes for the scholar's mate: 2. Qf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5?? 4.Qxf7#. In both cases, Black can easily avoid the trap. However, the Parham Attack is more forcing and stronger—first requiring Black to defend his e-pawn (usually with 2...Nc6), then after 3. Bc4 forcing Black to play a sub-optimal move (3...g6 virtually committing Black to a fianchetto rather than a more aggressive placement of the bishop; 3...Qe7 blocking the bishop; or 3...Qf6 taking away the knight's best square). 2. Qf3 places no such impediments on Black's development. Among serious chess players this opening is very rare, but beginners occasionally play it to troll or surprise the opponent. Black has no problems equalizing this game.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P1Q1/8/PPPP1PPP.name: 2. Qg4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P1Q1/8/PPPP1PPP.description: White's 2. Qg4 breaks the chess opening principle of not moving the queen out early, as the opponent will gain tempos by attacking the exposed queen. Not only that, it does not threaten Scholar's Mate, unlike the other early queen attacks Qh5 and Qf3. Black's best replies are 2...Nf6 or 2...d5, which both attack the queen and gain easy tempo. White might move the queen to g3, to keep an attack on e5 and g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: Parham attack
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: This is an aggressive opening move that violates an opening principle by bringing the queen out early. So long as Black doesn't fall into White's traps, they will be able to develop easily and play useful moves that gain time on White's queen. 2. Qh5 both attacks the pawn on e5 and puts pressure on f7. The f7 square is the weakest point in Black's position at the start of the game, because it is the only square guarded only by Black's king. White's usual plan is to follow with Bc4 and deal a swift, knock-out blow with Qxf7#, e.g. 2...Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6?? 4. Qxf7#. This is called Scholar's mate or the four-move checkmate.

rnbq1bnr/ppppkppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.name: 2...Ke7??
rnbq1bnr/ppppkppp/8/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/.description: Black makes a hideous blunder. They allow 3. Qxe5#, with red-faced spectators all about. This move is a curiosity as it leads to the fastest possible checkmate by White at only three moves.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.name: = 2...Nc6 =
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.description: A logical move defending the e5 pawn. Black knight could later move to d4 and threaten Nxc2+ and Nxa1, however Black can't be too hasty as White's Queen is aggressively placed. White has only one sensible move of 3. Bc4 in view of Black potentially playing Nf6 to nudge the Queen away. However in the exhibition game with tennis player Boris Becker vs Garry Kasparov, Becker played 3. Qf3, a move then Kasparov showed led to the better position for Black.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.name: = 3. Bc4 =
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPPP1.description: With this aggressive move, White now threatens checkmate called "Scholar's Mate" by taking the pawn on f7 with the queen. Black has some ways to adequately prevent this mate from happening. The two decent replies are 3...g6 and 3...Qe7. Kasparov chose Qe7 when he met this position in a game against the actor Woody Harrelson in a consultation game. At the lower level many players may be tempted to play 3…Nf6?? attacking White’s queen. However, Black leaves f7 undefended, and White can play the move they were intending to play when 2. Qh5 was played: 4. Qxf7#!, known as the Scholar’s Mate.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP.name: = 3... Nf6?? =
r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP.description: Black's hotheaded desire to prove that the queen was misplaced and to take the queen has backfired. The next move will be 4.Qxf7# (standing for mate). The one natural developing move leads to mate - and that is why black has to always be careful for Scholar's mate.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP.name: = 3...g6 =
r1bqkbnr/pppp1p1p/2n3p1/4p2Q/2B1P3/8/PPP.description: Black counterattacks the White queen, and blocks 4. Qxf7#. White then moves the queen to safety on f3 and attacks f7 from a different angle.

r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2n3p1/4pp2/2B1P3/5Q2/PPP.name: 4...f5
r1bqkbnr/pppp3p/2n3p1/4pp2/2B1P3/5Q2/PPP.description: ...f5 parries the threat of Qf7# by obstructing the queen's vision of the f7 square. It also attacks White's e-pawn, and if Black is able to remove it, they might be able to play d5 and take over the centre. 5. exf5?!, thinking to clear the obstruction, is inaccurate, ultimately because it gives up control of the d5 square. Black can't play ...d5 straight away. If 5...d5?!, apparently with tempo on the bishop, then 6. fxg6! and Black doesn't have time to take the bishop because White's pawn now controls f7: 6...dxc4?? 7. Qf7#!. Instead Black should prepare ...d5 with 5...Nd4 first. This is a double attack on White's queen and the c3 square (threatening ...Nxc3+, Black wins the rook by a fork). Then: 6. Qd1 to defend the c3 square is most natural, which allows 6...d5. 6. Qg3!? allows the fork but sets a trap. 6...Nc3+ 7. Kd1 Nxa1?? 8. Qxe5!+ Qe7 9. Qxh8+-. 6. Qd5?? threatens 7. Qf7# and Qxe5+. This is very common but strictly inferior, and 7...Qf6 deals with both threats. 5. Ne2 is White's best move: controlling d4 so preventing ...Nd4. Then the game may continue 5...Nf6 (threatening ...fxe4, as the knight will prevent vision of f7) 6. Nbc3 (defending e4) d6 7. exf5 Bxf5 8. d3= for an even game.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/6p1/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.name: Wayward Queen Attack
rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/6p1/4p2Q/4P3/8/PPPP1PP.description: = Wayward Queen Attack = This move is a blunder as it allows 3. Qxe5+! creating a deadly fork to the king and the rook and thus loses that h8 rook. If, however, White blunders and Black plays well, the Queen may be trapped near h8, but this is unlikely. Instead of playing 2…g6??, 2…Nc6 defends the e-pawn and gives Black a very slight edge due to White’s misplaced queen. 2…Nf6 attacking the Queen thus preventing the famous Scholar's Mate is another idea, though less common. Although this gives White the opportunity to capture on e5, Black in return gains tempos as White’s queen is far from her home and doesn’t have a clear way to get to safe squares such as e2 and d1 safely. Black also has the ability to play Qe7 attempting to defend the pawn, but it somewhat blunders a whole queen as white can open the bishop to attack the queen on e7 (3. d3/d4, g6 4. Bg5, ...) The queen still has the ability to take, but if the white queen can protect the bishop, the queen will have to go somewhere else, thus it displaces the queen and black is vulnerable to other attacks, if white plays well that is. If black plays Nc6, then white can play Bc4. The bishop would be vulnerable to attacks, but if black attempts to do any other move than guard the f-pawn, black loses. (3. Bc4, g6 4. Qf3, d6 (or any other move that doesn't protect the f-pawn) ?? 5. Qf7#, 1-0). If g6 is played, white can retreat to f3, and deliver a checkmate that way.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP/.name: = 2. a3 =
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/P7/1PPP1PPP/.description: White plays a waiting move instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but timid and concedes White's first move advantage. This is similar to an Open Game with colors reversed, except that White has played a3 to stop Bb4 if Nc3 is played. Black can choose a variety of responses: 2...Nf6 2...Nc6 2...Bc5 2...d5 2...f5!?

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.name: Description
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/1P6/P1PP1PPP.description: Charles' Opening is offbeat, but perfectly playable for White. It is mainly used to avoid highly theoretical lines such as the Ruy Lopez or the Scotch Game: Schmidt Variation, or to surprise the opponent. White intends to play Bb2 soon. After 2...c7-c5, the position is similar to an Anti-Sicilian. Charles' Opening incurs a couple of problems for White. First, it delays the development of a minor piece, disallowing an early castle for White to bring their king to safety. The other problem is that it removes the advantage White has going first. 2. b3 delays the development of another piece with something like 2. Nf3 or 2. Bc4, instead planning to develop their dark-squared bishop to b2, which gives black more time to develop. It is relatively easy for Black to equalise in this opening, for example, 2...Nf6, 2...Nc6, and 2...Bc5 all equalise, although Black should be careful to avoid a quick Bb2 and Nf3, putting intense pressure on the pawn on e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.name: Centre pawn opening
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/2P5/PP1P1PPP.description: White wishes to build a big, two-pawn centre, and plays 2. c3?! to support pushing the pawn to d4. This idea, c3 to support d4, is a common plan for White in many open games (games beginning 1. e4 e5): c3 after developing the knight is the Ponziani (2. Nf3 Nc6 3. c3), and it comes after developing the knight and bishop in the Italian and Spanish games (3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3 or e.g. 3. Bb5 Bc5 4. c3). However, played on White's second move without any pieces developed, it is simply too slow. Black can respond vigorously with 2...d5 to eliminate transpositional possibilities. After 3. exd5 Qxd5⩱, there is no 4. Nc3 to chase the queen away and gain a tempo as the c3 pawn is occupying the square. Staunton suggested that by avoiding taking the pawn, White could keep the game competitive: 3. Nf3 dxe4 4. Nxe5 Bd6!? 5. Nc4 Be6 6. d4 exd3 e.p. 7. Bxd3⩲. However, 4...Qe7! is an improvement, which forces White to move the knight again and gums up White's play for the centre, as d4 will be met with exd3 e.p. and a discovered check. Black sweeps ahead in development to a reach a dominating position. 5. Nc4 Nc6 6. Be2 Bf5 7. O-O O-O-O⩱.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.name: The Whale
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P1P3/8/PP1P1PPP.description: White controls d5 another time with a pawn instead of developing a piece. This move is playable but slow. It concedes White's first move advantage and has the drawbacks of creating a permanent hole on d4 and blocking the f1 bishop from developing to c4 or b5. Black has a wide range of reasonable options, including 2...Bc5, 2...Nf6, or 2...Nc6. 2...g6?! is called the Adorjan defence. This prepares to fianchetto, though the king's bishop could already develop along the a3-f8 diagonal, and invites 3. d4! exd4 4. Qxd4 with tempo on the rook on h8. 4...Nf6 5. Bg5 where 5...Bg7?? loses a piece to 6. e5+-. 2...c6?! transposes into the open variation of the accelerated Panov attack, though this improves White's position. Playing 2...d5? anyway is called the Bavarian gambit.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.name: Kennedy variation
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/8/PPP2PPP.description: The Kennedy variation is a sideline in the Nimzowitsch defence. Black has two attackers on d4 and so threatens to take it next turn. White has three ways of dealing with the central tension: to push the pawn, take first, or defend the pawn. Both pushing the pawn or taking on e5 are very good for White, and the most testing replies, though defending the pawn may allow a transposition to a more familiar position. 3. d5, the Linksspringer variation, pushes the d-pawn out of the way of the attack, gives White more space, and at the same time kicks Black's knight away to a more passive square: 3...Nce7 or 3...Nb8. After 3...Nce7 4. Nf3 Black's knight must move again to keep defence of the e5 pawn, 4...Ng6. 3. dxe5 is slightly more common. White liquidates the centre and this can lead into a lot of trades and a quick endgame. After 3...Nxe5, White usually plays 4. Nf3, the Paulsen attack, where the knights are traded off (4...Nxf3+ 5. Qxf3) and perhaps the queens too (5...Qf6). 3. Nf3 is a transposition into the Scotch game, usually seen after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4. White allows Black to take on d4 and open the position.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.name: Scotch game
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.description: With this aggressive pawn advance, White looks to open up the centre. 3...exd4 is played almost every time. It releases the central tension and leads to a very open game, with a lot of space for both players. 3...Nxd4, the Lolli variation, is playable. White can trade on d4, 4. Nxd4 exd4 5. Qxd4, taking advantage of the fact Black has traded their knight to centralise their queen, or play 4. Nxe5, threatening Qxd4. A few tries have been made with 3...d6, transposing into a Philidor defence, but this affords White a range of good options: 4. d5, kicking the knight and expanding in the centre is the most straight-forward, or 4. Bb5 transposing into an Old Steinitz Spanish.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.name: Modern attack or Steinitz attack
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2P.description: The chief sideline to 3. Nxe5, with 3. d4 White seeks to open the centre immediately and offers Black their choice of pawns to capture. 3...exd4!? is playable but less conventional as it allows 4. e5! to kick the knight. Typically this leads to trading both d- and e-pawns and opening the centre fully: the main continuation is 4...Ne4 5. Qxd4 (the Centre attack) d5 (defends knight) 6. exd6 e.p. Nxd6 7. Nc3, although there are some sidelines (5. Qe2 was advocated by Steinitz; 5. Bb4+ is the Tal gambit). 3...Nxe4 is the main line and leads to a trade of e-pawns. White could retake immediately (4. Nxe5 or 4. exd4) but the normal move order is 4. Bd3 d5 5. Nxe5, where after ...d5 first Black doesn't have ...d6 to shoo the knight away. 3...d5, the Symmetrical variation, passes the decision on what to take first back to White. Since Black has played ...d5 of their own volition, White may choose 4. Nxe5 and the positions can transpose after 4...Nxe4 5. Bd3 (4...dxe4? 5. Bc4 [threatening Nxf7] Be6 6. Bxe6 fxe6 and Black has isolated double e-pawns±). 3...d6 transposes to the Nimzowitsch variation of the Philidor defence.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.name: 3. d4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/3PP3/5N2/PPP2PP.description: White attacks e5 again and threatens to win the pawn. Black must deal with the threat: trade, defend, or counterattack?

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.name: 2...exd4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.description: Black takes White's d-pawn. 3. Qxd4 is the main move. This was Black to develop 3...Nc6 with tempo. 3. c3 is the Danish gambit. White offers to let Black keep the pawn in return for rapid development. 3. Nf3, the Kieseritzky variation, often leads to several transpositions. Black can transpose to the Scotch with 3...Nc6 or 3...Bb4+, to the Philidor with 3...d6, to Petrov's Steinitz variation with 3...Nf6, or to the Lewis Gambit of the Bishop's Opening with 3...Bc5 (followed by 4. Bc4 Nf6). An independent line is 3...Bc5 4. Nxd4 Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.name: von der Lasa gambit
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/RN.description: White gambits their d4 pawn. After either 3...Nf6 or 3...Nc6, this will transpose into other openings. 3...Nf6 is Black's most common move, transposing to the Urusov gambit which is more normally seen from the Bishop's opening with 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nf6 3. d4 exd4. 3...Nc6 is another good move developing the queenside knight. This often transposes to the Scotch gambit after the normal and common developing move 4. Nf3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/.name: 3...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/8/PPP2PPP/.description: Black develops their knight on b8. 4. Nf3 transposes to the Scotch gambit. 4. Nf3 is the most common move, which transposes into the well-known Scotch gambit, more often seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 4. Bc4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.name: Scotch gambit
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2PP.description: White temporarily forgoes recapturing the d4 pawn, instead developing the light-squared bishop to the most active square targeting the f7 pawn. There's no great way for Black to hold on to the pawn they are temporarily up. 4...Bc5, the Haxo gambit and second most common move, is the only way to add another defender to the pawn on d4. Though Black has two defenders to White's two attackers, after 5. c3 Black is best advised to give the pawn back. This is because 5...dxc3?, thinking White wants 6. Nxc3 and Black will still be ahead a pawn, loses to 6. Bxf7+! Kxf7 7. Qd5!+. White can recapture the bishop and if Black still tries to cling onto the material, they fall behind too far in position and development, e.g. 7...Ke8 8. Qh5+ (a little trick to either take the bishop with check or force Black to weaken their kingside) g6 9. Qxc5 cxb2 10. Bxb2+-. Instead, Black's idea is to return the pawn with 5...Nf6, transposing into the Greco gambit for an even game, or 5...d3. 4...Nf6 is the most played move, developing the knight and attacking the pawn on e4. This position can also arise out of the Italian game, after 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. d4 exd4. After 4...Nf6, White usually responds either with 5. e5, where they recover the pawn with the sequence 5. e5 d5 6. Bb5 Ne4 7. Nxd4 Bd7, or 5. O-O, sacrificing the other pawn by allowing 5...Nxe4, the double gambit accepted. 6. Re1 doesn't win the knight outright, rather the game continues 6...d5 7. Bxd5 Qxd5 8. Nc3! (d-pawn is pinned) and 9. Nxe4 after the queen moves.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.name: Kieseritzky variation
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP/R.description: With this move, White brings another attacker to Black's d4 pawn. This often transposes to other openings, though independent lines exist. 3...Nc6 is the most common move, transposing to the Scotch game line, more normally seen from the move order 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4 instead. 3...Bc5 is another normal move, developing the bishop. This can go two ways; 4. Nxd4 Nc6 transposes into the Classical Scotch game, while 4. c3 is the Lanc-Arnold gambit, an independent option.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.name: 3...exd4
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/3pP3/5N2/PPP2PPP.description: Black takes the pawn the centre. 4. Nxd4, recapturing the pawn, is the main line. White centralises their knight, supported by their queen. Black has a chance to take the initiative and develop with tempo, attacking White's centre with 4...Bc5 or 4...Nf6. Alternatively, White can gambit the pawn and not recapture it: 4. Bc4 is the Scotch Gambit. White leaves the pawn in peace and tries to establish attacking pressure with a lead in development. 4. c3 is the Göring Gambit. Similar to the Danish gambit, White offers one or two further pawns to get a lead in development. 4. Ng5? is a trap line, the idea being to sacrifice the knight on f7 to lure out Black's king. It is dubious and can be disarmed by best play, but scores well in amateur databases. 4...h6 5. Nxf7 Kxf7 6. Bc4+ and Black must avoid 6...Ke8??, else 7. Qh5+ leads to forced mate.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.name: Center Game Accepted
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/3QP3/8/PPP2PPP/RNB.description: In the Center Game, White is happy with himself for knocking out Black's only foothold in the center square, e5. At the time, all four central squares are controlled by White. This may seem like a huge advantage for White, but if Black simply plays Nc6, the queen is forced to move. Conversely, it may seem like a bad idea to develop the queen before any other pieces; however, Black can get into trouble if careless.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2Pp4/PP3PPP/RN.name: 3...d3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2Pp4/PP3PPP/RN.description: This moves declines the second pawn sacrifice, but gives White back the advantage because of Bxd3.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/R.name: 3...d5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/3pP3/2P5/PP3PPP/R.description: This is the Sörensen Defense and is also sometimes called the Capablanca Defense. From this position, White almost always plays 4. exd5. Black can safely respond with ...Qxd5, as White cannot immediately attack the Queen. A common continuation is 5. cxd4 Nc6 6. Nf3 Bg4 7. Be2.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP/R.name: 4. Bc4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP/R.description: 4. Bc4 gambits a second pawn. It develops the light-squared bishop to a place attacking Black's weakest square f7. Black almost always accepts the second pawn with 4...cxb2, rather than offering a transposition to the Göring Gambit with 4...Nc6. In one rare line, Black advances the pawn to c2, not wanting to let White develop the dark squared bishop onto the long diagonal.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP.name: 4...Nc6
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2B1P3/2p5/PP3PPP.description: After Nc6, White will usually play 5. Nf3 offering the b2-pawn again and developing the knight to its best square. This transposes to the Göring Gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/8/Pp3PPP/RNB.name: 4...cxb2
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1P3/8/Pp3PPP/RNB.description: = Double Danish Gambit Accepted = This time White has to recapture the pawn with 5. Bxb2 rather than give Black a second queen. (The sacrifice Bxf7 is an important idea in the Double Danish Accepted, just not yet.)

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/R.name: = 5...Nf6 =
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/R.description: Black's knight on f6 is targeting the undefended e-pawn. Turning the tables with 6. e5 is an obvious and strong choice. Defending the pawn with 6. Nc3 or, if you don't want to block the bishop's diagonal, with 6. Nd2 are less popular. Although developing pieces can't be bad, if Black finds the accurate ...d5 in response then the pawn is getting blown up anyway. 6. Nf3 is just a bit too normal to be an optimal move in this crazy line. The moves Black needs to find in response are correspondingly quite normal ones, like castling kingside. 6. Qb3 is obviously devastating if Black were forced to capture on e4, which she isn't. The immediate tactical problem for White is that 6...d5! now can't be met with 7.e5, because the White queen would find herself badly placed after 7...dxc4 8.exf6. The "forcing" 6. Bxf6 is a terrible, horrible, no good, very bad move. Apart from giving up the bishop pair, the Black queen that appears on f6 will target a1 (forcing the passive 7.Nd2) and also f2 in combination with a bishop on c5. 6.e5 is the most popular and strongest move for White.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2B1P3/5N2/PB3PPP.name: = 6. Nf3 =
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2B1P3/5N2/PB3PPP.description: 6…Nxe4? would be a great move to teach chess students about the value of development over pawn-grabbing. The simple 7. O-O sets in motion an overwhelming attack. Part of the reason White wants to play 7. O-O is that it deprives Black of the bishop check on b4, which is otherwise a free developing move. So it makes sense that Black's most popular move is the immediate 6...Bb4+ followed by castling, and that a less popular but higher-scoring alternative is 6...d5 to distract White from castling by threatening a piece. After 6...d5 7.exd5 Black has the nice d6 square for the bishop, Open Ruy Lopez style. Black can opt for passive defence with 6...Be7 or 6...d6, or for a transposition to the Göring Gambit with 6...Nc6.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4P3/2B5/8/PB3PPP/R.name: = 6. e5 =
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4P3/2B5/8/PB3PPP/R.description: Black's f6-knight is attacked by a pawn. How about moving it? 6...Ng8 is an abject retreat that only magnifies White's lead in development. 6...Ne4 and 6...Ng4 both allow the simplifying Bxf7+, leaving White with ongoing pressure for an investment of a single pawn, although 6...Ng4 does set a couple of dastardly traps. Black would ideally like the single pawn without giving White the ongoing pressure, and so the highest scoring moves are those which take preventative measures against Bxf7+: 6...Bb4+ means White can't take on f7 because she's in check; 6...d5 means White can't take on f7 because there's a pawn in the way. Inserting 6...Qe7 7.Qe2 before dealing with the threat only helps White, whose queen isn't blocking her bishop in.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pP3/2B5/8/PB3PPP/R.name: = 6...d5 =
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3pP3/2B5/8/PB3PPP/R.description: Capturing the piece with 7. exf6 is both positionally desirable (threatening to ruin Black's kingside pawns) and tactically forced. Most other moves are punished by a combination of ...Bb4+ and ...Ne4, threatening a second piece. After 7. exd6? Qxd6 Black has the same number of pieces out as White (and two extra pawns), nor does White have any way in after 7. Bb5+? Nd7 (8.Qxd5?? c6).

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/2B5/8/PB3PPP/RN.name: = 7. exf6 =
rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/2B5/8/PB3PPP/RN.description: Black will lose castling rights and have to play around a protected White pawn on g7 if she captures on c4 immediately. So instead she throws in 7...Bb4+. In responding to the check, White must either give up the dark-squared bishop, block the dark-squared bishop's diagonal, block the d-file, or forfeit castling rights herself. All of those are good things for Black!

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/8/PB3PPP/RN.name: = 7...Bb4 =
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/8/PB3PPP/RN.description: White has five legal moves to respond to the check. Ke2 is not the right one. 8. Kf1 is surprisingly popular, but the positive of keeping lines open is outweighed by the negative of losing castling rights, especially since the h1-rook can't get out via h3 while Black's unopposed light-squared bishop is watching it. 8. Nc3 looks natural, but 8...Qxf6! is a very cold shower. Far from stepping into a discovered attack, Black is setting up a devastating cross-pin on the knight that White must waste several moves wriggling out of. 8. Nd2 means it's White, not Black, who will lose castling rights after 8...dxc4. Thanks to the threatened pawn fork on c3, White won't have time to reinforce d2 with Ngf3. So by a process of elimination we have 8. Bc3. This time there's a tactical flaw with 8...Qxf6, so Black must exchange bishops on c3 so as not to lose a piece.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/2B5/P4PPP/R.name: = 8. Bc3 =
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/1bB5/2B5/P4PPP/R.description: Black is temporarily a piece down, and the bishop on b4 is threatened, so 8...Bxc3+ is necessary.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/2B5/2N5/P4PPP/R2.name: = 9. Nxc3 =
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/3p4/2B5/2N5/P4PPP/R2.description: Black recovers the piece with 9...dxc4. (9…Qxf6?? 10.Nxd5 saves both threatened pieces and Black has nothing.)

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK.name: = 9...dxc4 =
rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5P2/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK.description: White has to play fxg7 sooner or later or be a full three pawns down. If she plays 10. fxg7 she can be confident that Black will reply with ...Rg8, as either …Qxd1+ or …Qe7+ would concede possession of the d-file and allow the devastating Nd5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pPp/8/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK1N.name: = 10. fxg7 =
rnbqk2r/ppp2pPp/8/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK1N.description: Black's only move to save the rook is 10...Rg8. Both 10...Qxd1+ 11.Rxd1 Rg8 12.Nd5 and 10...Qe7+ 11.Nge2 Rg8 12.Nd5 are much worse for Black.

rnbqk1r1/ppp2pPp/8/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK1.name: = 10...Rg8 =
rnbqk1r1/ppp2pPp/8/8/2p5/2N5/P4PPP/R2QK1.description: Black is now threatening to trade queens on d1 with a winning advantage, as once the rook has captured on g7, White's Nd5 doesn't come with the threat of a fork on f6, so Black can simply defend c7 with ...Na6. So to limit the damage, White's queen usually makes tracks, with either 11. Qf3 or 11. Qa4+. Another possibility is for White to voluntarily get the queens off with 11. Qxd8+, followed by castling queenside, hoping that an all-out attack on Black's still underdeveloped forces will be enough compensation for the two pawns.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/RN.name: Danish Gambit Accepted: Schlechter Defence
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1P3/8/PB3PPP/RN.description: By playing 5...d5, Black aggressively strikes back at the center, releasing the bishop to catch up in development, returning a pawn in the process. White main move is 6. Bxd5, and the main continuation is 6...Nf6 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 8. Qxd8 Bb4+ 9. Qd2 Bxd2+ 10. Nxd2 with an equal position. Alternatively after 6. Bxd5 Nf6, 7. Nc3?! is tried, but after 7...Nxd5 8. Nxd5 Nd7! (8...c6?? 9. Nf6+ gxf6 10. Qxd8+ Kxd8 11. Bxf6+ and White wins an exchange) Black has an advantage as he is still up a pawn and has the bishop pair, but accurate play is needed. Note that 6. exd5?! is inaccurate because the bishop on c4 is now blocked by its own pawn. After ...Nf6 and ...Bd6, Black's king is safe and White does not have compensation for Black's extra pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2p2N2/PP3PPP/R.name: 4. Nf3!?
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2p2N2/PP3PPP/R.description: This offers another pawn to Black. Black may take 4...cxb2, where White's idea is 5. Bxb2. It is more typical for White to offer this gambit with 4. Bc4 instead, which develops the bishop to pressure f7. Delaying Bc4 with 4. Nf3 is less sharp. The difference can be illustrated in the lines After 4. Nf3 cxb2 5. Bxb2 Nf6 6. e5, Black has 6...Ne4, and 7. Bc4 is a bit too late. 7...Bb4+ ∓ and Black's knight and bishop combine to control the dark squares around the king. Compare the 4. Bc4 line, 4...cxb2 5. Bxb2 Nf6 6. e5, where 6...Ne4? allows 7. Bxf7+ Kxf7 8. Qf3+ Ke8 9. Qxe4 =.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.name: 4.Nxc3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.description: This move was Alekhine's choice. This move regains the one of the lost pawns, thus keeping White's material deficit to a minimum. White now has a huge lead in development and a central pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.name: 4. bxc3?
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4P3/2P5/P4PPP/RNBQ.description: An error. White forgets why the sacrifice was offered in the first place: by retaking with a pawn, White does not develop their pieces in compensation for the sacrifice, and is left with weak and isolated a- and c-pawns to boot. Black should have an easy game.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.name: King's gambit
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.description: White attacks Black's pawn on e5 with the f-pawn, even though that pawn is itself attacked and undefended. White seeks to pry Black's pawn away from control of d4, so that they may place their own pawn there. In addition, White's trying to open the f-file so that once they have castled, their rook is activated on the open file immediately. The king's gambit is a very aggressive opening that comes with severe trade offs. By moving the f-pawn so early, before they have castled, White has greatly weakened their kingside and exposed their king to danger.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/4P3/8/PPPP2PP/.name: 3.fxe5??
rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/4P3/8/PPPP2PP/.description: This move is a well known blunder, since black can now win a whole rook. Qh4+ g3 (Ke2 Qxe4#) Qe4+ picking up a whole rook and the game.

rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/4P2q/8/PPPPK1P.name: King's Gambit Declined 4.Ke2??
rnb1k1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/4P2q/8/PPPPK1P.description: This is a blunder on white's part. The only other legal move would be to play 4. g3, which would force Black's queen to retreat. This move leads to checkmate if Black plays 4...Qxe4#.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP.name: Queen's knight defence
r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP.description: 2...Nc6, a way to decline the king's gambit, is much more common in amateur games than in tournament chess. 2...Nc6 develops a piece and prepares to recapture on e5, though Black's pawn was not actually hanging because 3. fxe5?? can be answered with 3...Qh4+!. 3. Nf3 is the main move, as in many king's gambit lines. This controls h4, therefore preventing the riposte ...Qh4+, and White actually threatens fxe5. Though the engine line is 3...d5 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. Nc3 Qe6, Black's usual idea is 3...f5!?, the Miles defence. 3...exf4 4. d4 transposes to the MacLeod defence. 3. Nc3 transposes to the Max Lange defence of the Vienna gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.name: Falkbeer countergambit
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3pp3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/R.description: 2...d5 is the most common way to decline the king's gambit (at least, for the moment: Black often takes the f-pawn later). White has the choice of two centre pawns they may take, though 3. fxe5?? is a blunder as 3...Qh4+! 4. g3 Qxe4+ 5. Qe2 Qxh1 is most embarrassing. 3. exd5 is the main move, leading to a scramble for control of the d5, e4, and e5 squares. Black's traditional idea (called the Staunton line) is 3...e4, but more common today is 3...exf4 4. Nf3, transposing into the modern line of the king's gambit accepted, as if they had played 2...exf4 3. Nf3 d5 4. exd5. 3. Nf3, the Blackburne attack, postpones taking in the centre to develop the knight. This controls the h4 square, ending with the threat of ...Qh4+, and if 3...dxe4 (attacking the knight) 4. Nxe5!. After 3...exf4 4. exd4 this transposes. Alternatively, 3...Bg4 4. Be2 exf4 5. exd5 Bxf3 6. Bxf3 Qh4+ 7. Kf1= and Black equalises. Other lines include: 3. d4?, the Hinrichsen gambit. 3. Nc3?!, the Milner-Barry variation.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/.name: Modern defence
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/.description: Black attacks White' e-pawn. As with 3...d6, the Fischer defence, moving the d-pawn opens the line for Black's bishop to develop. Moving it to ...d5 is more forcing, however, and by threatening ...dxe4, it compels White to capture the the pawn first, 4. exd5, and robs them of the time to make a developing move of their own. 4. e5? is inferior because after 4...g5 5. h4 g4, White has taken away the e5 square to where they would otherwise like to move their knight. White can end up transposing into the dubious Allgaier gambit.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.name: Falkbeer countergambit accepted
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.description: Accepting the d-pawn is the main move. From here, Black has three choices: 3...e4!? is the traditional idea, but it has fallen out of fashion due to 4. d3!, the Charousek gambit. If 4...Qxd5 5. Nc3 (hits queen) Bb4. If 4...Nf6 5. dxe4 with complications that favour White. 3...exf4 is the main move today. 4. Nf3 (to prevent Qh4+) transposes to the modern king's gambit accepted. 3...c6!? is the Nimzowitsch-Marshall countergambit that offers material for development.

rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/R.name: = 3...c6!? =
rnbqkbnr/pp3ppp/2p5/3Pp3/5P2/8/PPPP2PP/R.description: An interesting move to sacrifice a pawn for development. Nc3 exf4 Nf3 Bd6 is equal. The greedy dxc6?! is bad, as Black has superior development while White's kingside is weak. Bc5 ideas prevent castling kingside unless White diverts the bishop from the diagonal. Qe2 cxd5 fxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Bg4 leads to equality.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4pP2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.name: = 3...e4 =
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4pP2/8/PPPP2PP/RN.description: After giving the pawn on d5, the e4 square is now free so Black pushes the e pawn instead of taking on f4. The idea is to ruin White's plan of opening the f file. The e4 pawn will also be quite a nuisance for White as it prevents natural development of the knight on f3. White will thus try to get rid of this pawn as soon as possible.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/5p2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.name: 4. exd5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/5p2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.description: White takes the d-pawn. After 4...Nf6, the Abbazia defence, White usually allows Black to recover the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/.name: 2...d6
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/4PP2/8/PPPP2PP/.description: This is one way to decline the King's Gambit. This can arise from many different positions, but this transposition to the King's Gambit Declined is most common. This is somewhat sounder than the King's Gambit Declined, Classical Variation, as in the Classical Variation, white can chase the bishop out of c5 and put more pressure on e5, especially with Nf3. Here, on the other hand, if white plays 3. Nf3?!, then black plays 3...exf4! transposing to the King's Gambit Accepted, Fischer Defense. This is similarly true with with 3. Nc3!?, but in this case, white gets a lot more compensation for the pawn compared to 3. Nf3. In fact, the best move here is 3. d3!, defending the pawn on f4 and blocking all transpositions to the King's Gambit Accepted. However, white had to make a concession for this: block his light-squared bishop. Nevertheless, 3.d3 leads to equality with best play. Note: If white plays 3. Bc4 (to not block the bishop), 3...exf4! also works.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/8/PPPP2PP/RNB.name: King's gambit accepted
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/8/PPPP2PP/RNB.description: If Black could make a free move in this position, it would undoubtedly be ...Qh4+. White couldn't successfully block the check with the g-pawn thanks to the Black pawn on f4, and the awkward move Ke2 would be forced. How should White deal with the threat? There are two main approaches, 3. Nf3 and 3. Bc4.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1Pp2/8/PPPP2PP/R.name: = 3.Bc4 =
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1Pp2/8/PPPP2PP/R.description: With this move, White develops the bishop and opens the square f1 for the king if Black elects to prevent White from castling with 3...Qh4+. However, this places the queen on a non-ideal square, with White later being able to play Nf3 and chase it away. Alternatively, Black can develop a piece with 3...Nf6 or play aggressively in the center and give up a pawn with 3...d5 for open lines.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP/.name: = 3...Qh4+ =
rnb1kbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2B1Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP/.description: Black stops White from castling, but in exchange for placing the Queen in poor position. White will later win a tempo by attacking the queen via Nf3.

rnb1kbnr/p1pp1ppp/8/1B6/4Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP/.name: = 5. Bxb5 =
rnb1kbnr/p1pp1ppp/8/1B6/4Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP/.description: Free pawns should be captured. Both players have gambited a pawn now and probably works out better for White, although the position is very unclear. One other famous game that reaches this position was between Garry Kasparov and Nigel Short (1993).

rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP.name: = 4...d5 =
rnb1kbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3p4/2B1Pp1q/8/PPPP2PP.description: A very popular move in this position. Instead of sacrificing the pawn on 4...b5, a better way is to sacrifice the pawn with 4...d5. If 5. exd5, then after 5...Bd6 Black has got active development with the bishops and White's bishop on c4 is blunted. If 5. Bxd5, Black can develop his knight with 5...Nf6. This move gains time on White's bishop in a very productive way and also opens up Black's bishop on c8.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/8/PPPP1KPP/RN.name: Tumbleweed gambit
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/8/PPPP1KPP/RN.description: A joke continuation. Rather than provide for their king's defence, White moves it to a more vulnerable square, where it can be attacked by ...Qh4+ or ...Bc5+.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.name: 3. Nf3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.description: 3. Nf3 develops a knight and controls the h4 square. This is important to prevent Black from playing Qh4+, exploiting the diagonal White opened with 2. f4. White now threatens to play d4 and recover the pawn they gambitted with Bxf4. Black would like to hold onto the f4 pawn if possible. There is a huge variety of approaches, but the most common replies are 3...g5, 3...d6, and 3...d5: the classical, Fischer, and Modern defences.

rnbqk1nr/ppppbppp/8/8/2B1Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP.name: 4. Bc4
rnbqk1nr/ppppbppp/8/8/2B1Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP.description: This bishop move places the bishop on a fine diagonal, helps control d5 and eyes f7. In the case of the check on h4, the king can sidestep to f1. G3?! leads to the Bertin Gambit. While White has very significant compensation, Black is better with best play.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP.name: Shallopp Defense
rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/4Pp2/5N2/PPPP2PP.description: Black answers with 3...Nf6, the Schallopp Defense: an active line named after 19th-century German master Emil Schallopp. Instead of defending the f4 pawn or playing ...g5 immediately, Black develops a piece and prepares to counter in the center. If White plays 4. e5, trying to drive the knight away, Black should respond with 4...Nh5!, defending the pawn on f4 and typically preparing ...d5 to either close the center and dissipate white's fast attacks, or develop black's dark-square bishop on d6 with tempo after white captures en passant exd6 e.p. Black usually also plays ...g5 shortly afterward, but this move order denies White the classical attacking positions associated with the Main Line of the King's Gambit Accepted. The Schallopp Defense can lead to a variety of positions: Sharp lines where Black will counterattack, open positions with liquidated centers that are roughly equal with small advantages for Black, or positions with closed centers that progress slowly where Black tries to solidify their material advantage. It's less tactical than the Kieseritzky or Fischer Defense in most cases, but strategically sound and well-suited for players aiming to neutralize White’s early initiative without deep theoretical preparation.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/5p2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.name: 4. exd5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/5p2/5N2/PPPP2PP/R.description: White takes the d-pawn. After 4...Nf6, the Abbazia defence, White usually allows Black to recover the pawn.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3PP/.name: 4. d4
rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/8/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3PP/.description: d4 grabs the d4-e4 classical center and opens up the c1 bishop's attack on the f4 pawn. Black usually responds with g5, temporarily defending the pawn while planning ...g4 to attack the f3 knight and expose White to Qh4+. The piece sacrifice line: Nc3 g4!? Bxf4 gxf3 Qxf3 Nc6 Bb5 Bd7 O-O-O Qh4 Kb1! (get out of the way of diagonal) O-O-O. This is unclear. Some play h4 to attack the g5 pawn and prevent Qh4+. This is around equal with best play.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2p1p/3p4/6p1/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3P.name: 4...g5
rnbqkbnr/ppp2p1p/3p4/6p1/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3P.description: The most popular move in this reason. It serves 2 purposes. 1 is to defend the f4 pawn temporarily, and the next purpose is to march to g4 next move and attack the knight. White can continue in multiple ways here, such as Nc3 and h3

rnbqkbnr/pppp1B1p/8/8/4Ppp1/5N2/PPPP2PP/.name: 5. Bxf7+!?
rnbqkbnr/pppp1B1p/8/8/4Ppp1/5N2/PPPP2PP/.description: This wild gambit, named the Lolli Gambit, sacrifices a bishop on f7. Although this gambit is unsound, the resulting positions after 5...Kxf7 6. Ne5+ are unclear and chaotic. Black has two legal responses to the check.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1p1p/8/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2P.name: 6. Kf1
rnb1kbnr/pppp1p1p/8/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2P.description: 6...Nh6: Silberschmidt Defence 6...Nc6: Viennese Variation 6...f3: Cochrane Gambit 6...Nf6: Santa Maria Defence

r1b1kbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP.name: 6...Nc6
r1b1kbnr/pppp1p1p/2n5/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP.description: = Salvio Gambit, Viennese Variation = This accurate reply, named the Viennese Variation, deliberately gives up the f7 pawn to attempt to launch an attack on the White king on f1. White has multiple replies to this. 7. Nxf7 seems tempting — it wins the f7 pawn and traps the rook on h8. However, Black can start an attack on White's king with 7...b5! 8. Bb3 (8. Nxh8? bxc4-+ and Black is crushing white despite being down an exchange) Nh6! 9. Nxh8 Bc5! and White's king is struggling to survive. 7. Bxf7+ takes f7 with check but after 7...Kd8 8. d4 Nxe5 9. dxe5 Nh6 10. Bc4 Bc5 11. Qe1 g3! Black has a crushing attack on White's king that is survivable only with precision. 7. Nxc6 gives up the attack on f7 and instead trades knights, but it ruins the Salvio Gambit's idea of saving the knight and allowing Qh4+ to attack f7. After 7...dxc6, Black is better and simply fine. 7. d4 is the most accurate reply, taking the center and defending the knight. Black has a slightly better position after 7...Nxe5 8. dxe5 f3!, where 9. Bf4 is necessary because 9. gxf3?? leads a crushing attack on the White king with 9...Bc5-+.

rnb1kb1r/pppp1p1p/7n/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2.name: 6...Nh6
rnb1kb1r/pppp1p1p/7n/4N3/2B1Pppq/8/PPPP2.description: = Salvio Gambit, Silberschmidt Defense = Black chooses to defend f7 using their knight. This opening is called the Silberschmidt Defense. Despite the logicality and popularity of the move, this is not as accurate as the other main replies to 6. Kf1. 7. d4 is what most people play, taking the center and reinforcing the e5 knight. This is usually followed from the Black side by 7...d6 or 7...f3. 7. d3?? simply loses the knight to 7...d6!, trapping it as the d3 square is occupied by the pawn. 7. Nc3 is a minor try where after 7...d6 8. Nd3, Black has a slightly better position but White has more development.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/8/2B1Pp2/5p2/PPPP2PP.name: = 5...gxf3 =
rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/8/2B1Pp2/5p2/PPPP2PP.description: Black has accepted the Muzio Gambit and must play accurately. White may want to capture the pawn with 6. Qxf3.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/8/2B1Pp2/5Q2/PPPP2PP.name: 6. Qxf3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/8/2B1Pp2/5Q2/PPPP2PP.description: = Muzio Gambit = White recaptures with their queen and prepares to start a big attack as compensation for the lost knight. White attacks the f4 pawn and this is really a major threat; for example, 6...Nc6?, the so-called Holloway Defence, runs into trouble after 7. Qxf4! Qe7 (if 7...Nh6??, 8. Bxf7+! Ke7 9. Qf6# ends the game) 8. Bxf7+! Kd8 9. Nc3! (threatening Nd5). Black has two main options: 6...Qf6, the Sarratt Defence, is almost always played, defending the attacked f4 pawn while adding another defender to the weak f7 square and challenging White to prove sufficient compensation for the material loss. 6...Qe7, the From's Defence, has an interesting idea. If White gets greedy and captures the seemingly free f4 pawn, 7...Qc5+! picks up the bishop on c4.

rnb1kbnr/pppp1p1p/5q2/8/2B1Pp2/5Q2/PPPP2.name: 6...Qf6
rnb1kbnr/pppp1p1p/5q2/8/2B1Pp2/5Q2/PPPP2.description: = Muzio Gambit, Sarratt Defence = Black defends their f4 pawn and f7 pawn while developing the queen and blocking the f-file. This is the most testing reply to the Muzio Gambit as it forces White to prove sufficient compensation for the knight sacrifice. Black also carries the threat of 7...Qd4+ winning the bishop on c4. White must not let their attack fizzle out; for example, the most common move at club level is 7. c3, but this is too slow. There are other, better options available for White. 7. d3 is the soundest move for White in this position, but some players consider it slow. It allows the c1 bishop to view the f4 pawn, thus adding another attacker to it. 7. e5 often leads to chaotic play. More common that 7. d3 due to its aggressive style, this often leads to the Double Muzio Gambit, 7...Qxe5 8. Bxf7+, where White sacrifices their bishop as well. 7. Nc3?, the Bello Gambit, tries to distract the queen from defending the f4 pawn by tempting 7...Qd4+, but this simply does not work. After 8. Kh1 Qxc4, White can try either 9. Qxf4 or 9. Nd5 (the Baldwin Gambit), but they can be easily diffused: 9. Qxf4 Bd6-+ or 9. Nd5 d6-+ and Black is up two pieces. 7. b3!? is an extremely rare move which sets a somewhat dastardly trap; 7...Qxa1 8. Nc3 Bg7?? 9. Qxf4! and White is almost completely winning due to the undefendable f7 square and the queen on a1 stuck out of play, not able to do anything.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/6p1/4Pp2/2N2N2/PPPP2.name: 4. Nc3
rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/6p1/4Pp2/2N2N2/PPPP2.description: = King's Gambit Accepted, Quaade Gambit = With 4.Nc3, the Quaade Gambit, White indirectly defends against Black's threat of 4...g4 to kick away White's knight. Unlike the direct responses of 4.h4 and 4.Bc4, or the other indirect response of 4.d4, the move 4.Nc3 doesn't even seem to begin to defend against the threat of 4...g4, but it does. After 4...g4 5.Ne5 Qh4+ 6.g3 fxg3, the move 7.Qxg4 saves the day for White; best for Black is to trade queens and go into a queenless middlegame that is still incredibly tricky for Black. However, most people blunder with 7...g2+ 8.Qxh4 gxh1=Q, a tempting sequence that wins material but puts Black's king in severe danger. White is winning after 9.Qh5, threatening a Scholar's Mate. Black must find several only moves to defend an immediate mate, and even after a good defense, White's knight on c3 jumps to d5 with devastating effect, crushing Black. A better option after 4...g4 5.Ne5 is for Black to strike with 5...d5, immediately giving the pawn back. White still gets a very fun and violent attacking game. Instead of 5.Ne5, the move 5.Bc4 transposes to the McDonnell Gambit, and the move 5.d4 transposes to the Sorensen Gambit--both with the intent to give up the knight on f3 and go for initiative.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/6p1/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3PP.name: 4. d4
rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/8/6p1/3PPp2/5N2/PPP3PP.description: = King's Gambit Accepted, Rosentreter Gambit = With 4.d4, the Rosentreter Gambit, White indirectly defends against Black's threat of 4...g4. The most basic point is that White opens up their dark-squared bishop to recapture the f4 pawn. Most common by far is 4...g4 indeed, after which White has three very deadly options. The most played and trickiest option is 5.Ne5, and after the ensuing 5...Qh4+ 6.g3 fxg3, 7.Qxg4 saves the day for White. The point is that Black's tempting move 7...g2+ is not best; after 8.Qxh4 gxh1=Q, Black has won White's rook, but after 9.Nc3, Black's position is extremely delicate; the engine evaluates this as equal, and it's extremely easy for Black to blunder. This line demonstrates very well how 4.d4 indirectly defends against 4...g4. Another option is to play 5.Bxf4, the Testa Gambit; White sacrifices their f3 knight in similar fashion to the Muzio Gambit, looking for a deadly attack. The third option is 5.Nc3, the Sorensen Gambit; once again, similar to the Testa and Muzio Gambits in sacrificing the f3 knight, but trying to demonstrate counterplay with the c3 knight instead of the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5n2/4N3/4PppP/8/PPPP2P.name: 5...Nf6
rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5n2/4N3/4PppP/8/PPPP2P.description: There's a pawn on g4 if White wants to capture it, but it isn't a free gift: Black is counter-attacking e4. 6. d4 is the main line. White is attacking a pawn and Black is attacking a pawn, that's 1 pawn each, so rather than resolve either of those situations, White makes to 2 to 1 in her favour! This move also ensures that once Black kicks the knight away from e5 by playing ...d6, it will be able to retreat to d3 without blocking the d-pawn. Playing 6.d3 wouldn't have that advantage, and would also shut in the f1-bishop. 6. Bc4 was the move favoured by the world champion of the pre-World Championship era, Paul Morphy.
